📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the hair category is presently a hotbed for growth.
  • After 40 years in hairdressing, hairstylist and salon owner Charlotte Mensah has seen trends come and go, but notes that extensions have had enduring appeal.
  • “Full hair has always been in style,” notes Charlotte Mensah.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the hair category is presently a hotbed for growth. Alongside much innovation in existing products, the past decade has seen hair transplants, scalp serums, and novel treatment concepts like head spas surge in popularity. And the category holds appeal across many demographics, from the more traditional mid-life market to burgeoning legions of ‘looksmaxxers’ and ever younger consumers seeking interventions for early-stage thinning, pattern baldness and GLP1-induced hair loss. While many consumers are investing in supplements, serums or aesthetic treatments to address the issue, another cohort is spending substantial on extensions and wigs.

After 40 years in hairdressing, hairstylist and salon owner Charlotte Mensah has seen trends come and go, but notes that extensions have had enduring appeal. “Even with my clients that embrace their natural look, many are seeing value in adding volume/length and will request a weft that matches their hair texture to achieve this,” she explains. What’s more, extensions and wigs have become less of a secret, considered desirable across race, gender and other consumer groups. “The appearance of full, healthy hair is always fashionable. These days, we have latest methods like tapes and synthetic fibers that can simulate human hair, making hair extensions more accessible to everyone,” she adds.

“Full hair has always been in style,” notes Charlotte Mensah. “I’ve noticed clients are increasingly interested in extensions that mirror their hair’s natural texture.”.

In a recent development, as revenues go, the wig business is a lucrative business. The SKUs in this sector — wigs, wefts and other hair extension systems, such as lace toupees and semi-permanent, bonded K-tips — commonly necessitate multibuy purchases to achieve desired hairstyles and individually command price tags upwards of £250.

In a recent development, at the top end of the market, a single wig or set of extensions can sell for tens of thousands, with long extension lengths, made-to-measure customizations and laborious finishes justifying costs. Value perception is high, thanks to human hair’s product lifespan, reusability and styling versatility. Together with growing hair loss concerns, these factors encourage consumers to adopt an investment-purchase mindset that makes for higher average order values in the extensions space.

According to recent reports, having earned £20,000 through 30 orders in just 10 minutes on launch day, CEO Denise Nwogbu has honed a strategy for success here. Her wig brand Go Glueless positions its product offer as a “hair appointment in a box”, eliminating the friction associated with installing specialist extensions. Customers are drawn to the convenience and seamless nature of the wigs, which do not require adhesives to style — instead, they can be secured through elastic headbands on the wig’s interior that keep it fitted in place on the user’s scalp. She claims this ease of installation has driven high waitlist demand and often results in sellouts across the range on drop days.

Denise Nwogbu, CEO and founder of Go Glueless, has found success positioning her product as a “salon appointment in a box.”.

“We limit releases to four times a year and use a pre-order model. This allows time to carefully source single-donor, virgin hair, then handcraft and customize each bespoke unit,” Nwogbu shares. “Provenance is everything — I chose my supplier in Vietnam because she has a real relationship with each woman who grows and sells their hair for the production of the extensions. She does not delegate to hair collectors, she goes personally to the villages to find willing volunteers that have not been coerced into cutting their hair. She can tell you their exact age, name and lifestyle, and pays them fairly with an understanding of virgin hair value in the West.”.

By the time the hair reaches Go Glueless headquarters in Birmingham, it has been cuticle-tested to ensure quality and longevity. Then, a team of wig specialists construct, color and cut units to exact customer measurements. Attracting an affluent, often time-poor clientele of professional women and public figures, Go Glueless’s USP lies in doing the labor so the end consumer has it completely removed.

On launch day, Go Glueless made £20,000 in online preorders. Now, the brand has opened its first IRL space —a suite where customers can browse and get bespoke fittings for their wigs.

“It’s a salon experience with no skills needed, but education is also important: every customer gets access to exclusive tutorials through GG Academy, our online portal,” Denise claims. This in itself is a clever strategy, attracting large audiences already searching for terms like “wig install tutorial”, which has amassed 478,000 impressions on TikTok. “And we educate our clients about help available to them if they are buying wigs to manage medical hair loss — many with conditions like alopecia or cancer aren’t aware of their entitlement to VAT relief.”.

Industry observers note that in the wig business, hair loss sufferers are likely to be engaged, repeat customers, presenting major sales opportunities. But profits aren’t the only piece of the puzzle — the most impactful brands focus on corporate social responsibility, too.

Sources indicate that market leader Beauty Works, whose assortment includes both professional-grade extensions and DIY clip-ins, is a case in point. Its relationship with the charity Little Lady Locks, which provides free medical wigs and hair services to minors with medical hair loss, is symbiotic: the charity benefits from Beauty Works’s financial investment, resources and expert volunteers, while Beauty Works can exhibit purpose-driven values, benefiting from enhanced brand image and positive engagement within aligned communities.

Beauty Works donates hair extensions to Little Lady Locks, helping the charity provide free wigs to boost the confidence of hair loss sufferers under 18.

According to recent reports, elsewhere, the brand is big on avoiding ethical quandaries common to the hair trade by enforcing strict compliance throughout its supply chain. “Our human hair is voluntarily sold by individuals who are fairly compensated,” says Randilyn Dela Cruz, product architect and vice president of development at Beauty Works’ parent company BIG. “Our sourcing standards require a respectful process and prohibit child labor, forced labor and sourcing from regions where there are known human-rights violations,” she details.

Industry observers note that sourcing is an crucial aspect for any wig business to get right, especially given a black market of sorts exists. A far cry from the luxury products they’re promoted as in the West, some vendors acquire hair of dubious origin, obscure its imperfections and sell to unwitting customers overseas at a high markup. An ITV News exposé found this can include waste hair pulled from sewer drains in India, as well as “floor hair” collected from the ground of salons by cheap laborers desperate to cash in on the lucrative trade.

It has been revealed that “It’s ‘the fast fashion’ side of wigs,” Denise stresses, going on to explain that these vendors chemically relax the waste balls of hair — which are made up of several cut hairs with different properties because they are from multiple donors’ heads — to the point where it appears flawless. “They often then market it deceptively under names like ‘bone straight’. “You couldn’t tell with the naked eye, but when you use that kind of hair to produce hair extensions, time always tells. It frizzes up, tangles easily and is unpredictable after the chemical coatings wash off, and business owners risk having that happen in the hands of your consumer if you don’t do your due diligence at the point of sourcing,” she warns.

Hence, Denise insists on flying to Vietnam personally to inspect and test the quality of any hair used in the making of Go Glueless units. It’s expensive work, but something she recommends as worthwhile for newly introduced businesses hoping to break into the luxury wig space.

Another common source of hair that can pose ethical dilemmas is Indian temple hair. This hair comes from Hindu tonsuring ceremonies, in which some donors shave their heads under the religious belief that it releases past spiritual baggage. Others agree to shed their hair as a sacred sacrifice to be devoted to specific deities. These individuals are often left in the dark about the final destination of their hair and its huge monetary value if it is later sold on to wig companies at auction, and they often receive no part of the profits, according to a recent report from the BBC. Questions around exploitation in these cases can influence perception among discerning end consumers, and are worth investigating to reduce brand risk.

Model wears Synths 2: an extension that uses collagen-based fibers to add length and volume without the need for human hair or more toxic synthetic alternatives.

Recent findings suggest that to sidestep sourcing concerns entirely, Charlotte Mensah often opts for “man-made fibers that have been designed to perform like human hair and that can still be styled with heat tools” in her salon. This is an area of category expansion, with synthetic products from Outré reaching viral fame and plant-based hair brands like Rebundle, Knott and Ruka Hair attracting upcoming audiences with innovative alternatives to traditional human hair extensions.

It has been revealed that ruka Hair’s latest invention (a plastic-free, collagen-based braiding fiber called Synths 2) became the first-ever hair extension of its kind to land in Sephora doors this summer. Stockist support of this caliber affirms it: the wig business is significant business indeed, and with the right sourcing, can set savvy founders up for exponential growth.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • OPINION — Once again, the next Congress is going to be filled with losers.
  • This is not a personal judgment about their character or personality, but a simple recognition that many members have lost races before getting elected.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Capitol Dome is illuminated before dawn on Oct. 13. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

OPINION — Once again, the next Congress is going to be filled with losers.

This is not a personal judgment about their character or personality, but a simple recognition that many members have lost races before getting elected. And the incoming class is no different.

I’ve written many versions of this column for more than a decade, and yet the lesson always seems to get lost, no pun intended. Parties routinely attack candidates who enter a race with losses on their record. And, of course, it happened this cycle as well.

“We beat him once. We’ll beat him again,” National Republican Senatorial Committee Chairman Tim Scott declared when Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown declared his challenge to appointed GOP Sen. Jon Husted in the summer of 2025.

“Ohioans gladly sent him packing last year, and they’ll not hesitate to toss him aside again,” said a Republican strategist.

In a recent development, brown lost reelection to Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024 but came back to defeat Husted for the state’s other Senate seat. And Brown is far from the only candidate to avenge a loss with an electoral victory last week.

According to recent reports, the fact of the matter is that losing a race doesn’t have to be the end of a political career. Losses can lay the foundation for future success by building name ID or a fundraising network. Or sometimes it takes a change in the political environment or change in circumstances, such as running for an open seat instead of challenging an incumbent.

In addition to Brown, there are more than a dozen losers coming into the next Congress:.

In some instances, though, the losses are piling up.

Republican Rep. John James of Michigan now has three statewide losses on his record. He lost Senate contests in 2018 (taking 46 percent of the vote) and 2020 (48 percent) and came up short in his bid for governor this year (44 percent).

Republican former Sen. John E. Sununu of Latest Hampshire, who lost reelection in 2008 to Democrat Jeanne Shaheen, fell in his comeback attempt for the open seat last week.

Industry observers note that but they could take heart from another repeat loser. Charlie Crist, a former Florida governor and congressman, has had a handful of high-profile losses over the years, including for Senate and two gubernatorial comeback bids. He was just elected mayor of St. Petersburg.

So even though I know it’s a futile request, let’s have a bipartisan agreement not to attack candidates for past losses, because losing doesn’t mean they can’t later pull off a win.

Are You a Super Ager? This Competition Will Be the Judge of That

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1373 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that alan Krepack stands with his hands on his hips and takes a deep breath as he sizes up the Over Under: an obstacle with a high wooden box and low wooden beam spread 10 meters apart.
  • As soon as the volunteer notes “go” he sprints to the box, plants his hands, and hoists his feet up and over.
  • The challenge is just the first of eight trials Krepeck will tackle throughout the day alongside his sons, Harrison and Aaron, at the Super Age Games, a fitness and mental competition designed to assess abilities associated with healthy aging.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that alan Krepack stands with his hands on his hips and takes a deep breath as he sizes up the Over Under: an obstacle with a high wooden box and low wooden beam spread 10 meters apart. Music booms over the speakers and other competitors shuffle around the cavernous room of the Armory Track in Washington Heights, New York, but Krepack stays laser-focused, thanks to years of meditation practice.

As soon as the volunteer notes “go” he sprints to the box, plants his hands, and hoists his feet up and over. As he lands on the other side, he sprints to the beam, dropping down into an army crawl. “Take your time, take your time,” his son yells from the sidelines. Krepack reaches the far end, rushes back, and repeats the sequence again before crossing the line in 51 seconds. To cool down, he paces back and forth with his hands on his head. “I think I’m a sprinter, I’m a jumper, but then it’s like, fuck, no, I’m 73 years old,” he says, catching his breath.

The challenge is just the first of eight trials Krepeck will tackle throughout the day alongside his sons, Harrison and Aaron, at the Super Age Games, a fitness and mental competition designed to assess abilities associated with healthy aging. On November 7th, the inaugural day-long event drew 530 athletes from 42 states and 15 countries, and about 70% of participants were between the ages of 40 and 64. Krepeck agreed to let me shadow him to understand this latest event through the lens of someone who is, in fact, aging, and would like to do so gracefully.

The name of the Games comes from a buzzword that originated in the longevity world: super ager. The term was originally coined by Northwestern University researchers to describe adults over 80 whose memories rival those of people 30 years younger. These days it’s thrown around on podcasts and in books to describe anyone who defies both the typical trajectory of both cognitive and physical aging.

The inaugural Super Age Games drew 530 athletes from 42 states and 15 countries.

Industry observers note that from crawling across a cargo net to reading microexpressions, the challenges in the competition measure longevity markers like functional strength, aerobic capacity, balance, and cognitive skill. At the end, athletes see where they rank among their age group and receive their “Super Age,” learning how their body’s physical fitness stacks up against the general U.S. population’s.

According to recent reports, in an era where your average middle-aged midwestern dad is training for Hyrox, and a latest, outlandishly extreme challenge is being invented every few months, the Super Age games are a low-key counterpoint to raw, stunty, athleticism, born from the metric-obsessed fitness subcultures who prize longevity above all. And now that fitness trackers like Whoop or Apple Watch can track VO2max, heart rate variability, and resting heart rates, that group continues to grow. Along the way, these stats have become status symbols on par with owning a Lamborghini. And now that overall health is quantifiable, fitness values have become less about just how fast you run or how much you lift, but how slowly aging.

Sources indicate that it follows that, despite its name, Super Age Games isn’t just for aging athletes. The crowd there leaned middle-aged, and the youngest person at the competition was 21. As we stood by the dead hang station, Krepak pointed across the room at a brolic young man who looked like he could be an NFL prospect: “That dude’s a serious athlete,” he indicates, as we watched him run around the track cradling a sandbag on his shoulder.

Unlike competitions like Hyrox, where athletes race through a sequence of workouts against the clock, the Super Age Games allows competitors to rest as long as they need between trials. In fact, Junior Kennedy, the fitness program director for the Games, encourages it. “There's no rush,” he claims. “The goal is to get through each event as intentionally as you can. We need to understand what it means to recover.”.

In a recent development, each trial was developed with a certain longevity marker in mind, and developed with input from researchers at the Buck Institute for Research on Aging, a leading nonprofit research center based in Novato, California dedicated to understanding aging. The Over Under, for example, tests agility by judging how fast you can change levels and switch directions. Meanwhile, the Synapse, a challenge where participants track moving balls on a screen and identify them after they've been shuffled around, is meant to measure cognitive processing.

Challenges in the competition measure longevity markers like functional strength, aerobic capacity, balance, and cognitive skill.

It has been revealed that krepack, a psychologist and lifelong athlete from Mill Valley, California, first heard about the event through its founder, David Stewart. Stewart is a media founder behind two niche longevity platforms, AGEIST and Super Age, where he writes about longevity, wellness, and redefining aging (one of his website testimonial’s notes he has made aging “cool and aspirational.”). Krepack’s generally a skeptic of the profit-driven modern wellness industry—“I've always had a jaded view of all of that stuff,” he says—but he has followed both Stewart and the Buck Institutes’ work for years.

The competition appealed to Krepack, in part because he’s spent decades cultivating a consistent exercise routine he’s proud of. He played baseball in college and has spent much of his life skiing, cycling, and playing other sports. These days, his schedule revolves around a handful of rituals: bike rides on Mondays and Fridays, a Saturday hike with a friend, gardening, yoga, and Zen meditation most days. When he signed up for the Games in June, he altered his exercise routine, lifted more weights, practiced hanging from a bar, and experimented with the Neurotracker cognitive test online.

Sources indicate that yet all that training didn’t prepare Krepack for the biggest surprise of his day. After scoring well on both the Inferno (the assault bike VO2max test) and Synapse, next came the fourth trial: the “Tightrope,” a balance challenge that requires competitors to walk along a low beam while carrying a water-filled bag, taking as many consecutive steps as they can in two minutes without falling. He had expected to excel, thanks to years of skiing and yoga. Instead, he struggled to keep steady as the water shifted inside the bag. As his foot slipped off the bar, his eyes got wide. “I can’t believe my balance,” he notes. “That’s my one disappointment in life now.”.

Alan Krepack's sons Harrison and Aaron during the “tightrope” challenge.

Krepack was still hard on himself as we walked over to the dead hang trial. But after beating both his sons’ times, he seemed to get his competitive spirit back. He pushed through the remaining challenge determined to finish strong. And he did: By the end of the Games, he had placed second overall, with scores adjusted for age.

Industry observers note that A few days after the competition, I checked in with Krepack to ask him how he’d processed the event. He responded with screenshots of his scores. His highest score came from the cargo net, which he credited to sheer determination rather than any particular finesse: “due to my will and overcoming an unconventional and desperate style!” he texted me, “Plus my sons were great support and focus partners.”.

It has been revealed that but the Games were also a reality check about aging: “I left there feeling both young and old,” he tells me on a phone call. As he watched his sons rocket through the obstacles, he was forced to confront how much of his athleticism he’d lost. “They just flew over it. They were so fluid, and so fast,” he indicates. “I’m not 30 or 40 or 50 or 60 anymore.”.

Despite all the longevity industry's promises of maintaining youth, Krepack sees little value in denying the inevitable. Aging well, he notes, is about “accepting, improving, and doing your best. It’s not a denial of who you are at this point in life.” The goal, he says, is to make the most of what you’re still capable of.

#66169. From Practical Gifts to Wellness Moments: Holiday Trends to Watch for 2026

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2241 w)
📖 Baca

From Practical Gifts to Wellness Moments: Holiday Trends to Watch for 2026

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2241 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that as the holidays beckon, a younger, fashion-led contingent of consumers across the US and Europe are upping their spend despite inflation, higher living costs and economic volatility.
  • “[US consumers] are signaling that they’re going to continue to be resilient shoppers and lean into the holiday season,” states Brian McCarthy, Deloitte’s retail strategy leader, pinpointing millennials as the top spenders this year by a long shot — in part because of life stage.
  • Across the board, high-net-worth individuals (HNWI) are more discerning than ever — spending more where necessary, for gifts centered on individuality, performance, wellness and sentimentality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that as the holidays beckon, a younger, fashion-led contingent of consumers across the US and Europe are upping their spend despite inflation, higher living costs and economic volatility. The situation doesn’t make sense on paper, but on department store floors, the verdict is clear: The holidays are still significant business for luxury — they just look a little different.

“[US consumers] are signaling that they’re going to continue to be resilient shoppers and lean into the holiday season,” states Brian McCarthy, Deloitte’s retail strategy leader, pinpointing millennials as the top spenders this year by a long shot — in part because of life stage. “Millennials and Gen Z now have some discretionary spending, and they’re starting to hit the age where they have children,” he adds, advising that department stores focus on these two cohorts.

Across the board, high-net-worth individuals (HNWI) are more discerning than ever — spending more where necessary, for gifts centered on individuality, performance, wellness and sentimentality.

In a recent development, deloitte’s holiday report predicts that average household holiday spending in the US will increase 4% year-on-year to $1,654 per household in 2026. In Europe, shoppers are expected to spend 3.4% more year-on-year this holiday season, per data from Mastercard. In the US, millennials and Gen Z will make up 50% of spending — a first since the annual study began — with both groups upping their spend at a double-digit rate year-on-year. Most holiday shoppers expect to spend the most money at either mass merchants or online, followed by department stores.

McCarthy highlights some core stats luxury retailers must consider: 72% of Gen Z say they’re interested in purchasing luxury goods as gifts for the holiday season, followed by 61% of millennials, 40% of Gen X, and 29% of baby boomers. The data also reveals that 76% of Gen Z initiative on gifting clothing and accessories, up from 67% last year.

The K-shaped economy — where the top end of the economy grows, but the lower end lags as inequalities widen — will ultimately benefit luxury fashion retailers, many of whom rely on the top percentile spenders to turn a profit. Nonetheless, even HNWIs are not immune to the same financial pressures as the aspirational and middle class, confirms Mintel. Analysts agree that price, value, convenience and product will dictate consumption across demographics this holiday period.

Holiday shopping at Harrods is well underway.

“Financial pressures continue to influence holiday spending, creating a resilient but resourceful consumer who is looking for deals and becoming more deliberate about where they spend,” indicates Brittany Steiger, Mintel’s associate principal for retail and e-commerce, noting that 72% of US luxury shoppers say price alone isn’t an indicator of luxury, and 41% consider discounts notable.

According to recent reports, the macroeconomic environment is tricky, but it’s also a well-established mood of uncertainty. Per Mintel, 59% of shoppers admit financial stress is making it harder to celebrate in the way they prefer, but 39% are still willing to spend on truly meaningful purchases. Against this backdrop, the smartest retailers have risen to the challenge, aligning their product assortments with shifting consumer trends.

That stated, the rollout of Christmas shopping remains largely the same. “We typically see two distinct phases: the first is about preparation, with clients investing in their own wardrobes ahead of festive celebrations,” says Simon Longland, Harrods’s director of fashion buying, pointing to partywear, evening-wear, knitwear and exceptional outerwear. Then, “as Christmas approaches, the focus shifts toward gifting.”.

Below, Vogue Business collates this year’s key gifting predictions.

For retailers, occasion dressing continues to drive growth over the holidays, but shoppers are displaying a more playful, casual approach, tracking with a younger consumer skew.

At Bloomingdale’s, ritzy festive occasionwear will be a key driver. “This holiday, we can put the pursuit of the perfect wardrobe on hold for a moment and indulge in the sheer joy of fashion for fashion’s sake,” says fashion director David Thielebeule. “After seasons of restraint, fashion is remembering how to have fun. Rich color, sumptuous textures and a little extravagance are making getting dressed feel exciting again.”.

Sebla Refiğ Devidas, Turkish retailer Communité’s chief merchandising officer, reports a similar appetite for eveningwear this holiday period. “In womenswear, we expect party dressing to be a big part of holiday shopping, especially pieces with interesting details that can be worn in different ways,” she says. “There’s a sense of 1920s glamour in the lace, embellishments, fringed silk, and rich textures, reflected in pieces from Conner Ives, Dries Van Noten, Ann Demeulemeester, Simone Rocha, Anna October, Fforme and Enfants Riches Déprimés.”.

Industry observers note that at End, statement separates and directional designs from Simone Rocha, Cecilie Bahnsen, Rick Owens, Peachy Den and Gimaguas are outperforming traditional partywear. “We’re taking a broader and more fashion-led approach to occasion dressing this holiday season,” says Martin Wieczorek, End’s chief product officer. “We’re also seeing a notable shift toward separates over dresses, with customers seeking greater versatility and long-term wardrobe value, which is reflected in our assortment”.

In a recent development, within menswear, Longland notes that while established party-wear brands and tailoring services will continue to play a significant role for Harrods this holiday season, the store is already seeing clients explore more pioneering attire. “We believe menswear today is as much about individual expression as it is about the traditional codes of dressing,” he says. “The festive season is a particularly interesting moment for this, whether clients are discovering a fresh designer or investing in beautifully tailored pieces for a special occasion.”.

Even among luxury shoppers, practicality is becoming a core tenet of holiday gifting.

“Confidence is low and spending is still up, which tells you people are not buying less, they are buying more carefully,” reports Christophe Roberts, founder and CCO of New York-based concept store Seed. What’s working? “Shoes, outerwear and the good $50 gift. The one massive present is getting replaced by two or three smaller [practical] ones that actually say something about you.”.

British retailer End reports an uptick in pragmatic premium outerwear gifting from brands including Our Legacy, Stone Island, Salomon, Arc’teryx, Barbour and Damson Madder. “We’re seeing menswear customers gravitate toward two key style directions,” indicates Wieczorek, pointing to a continuation of outdoor dressing, functional accessories and hiking-influenced footwear. (In this vein, demand for Stone Island knits has grown 36% since October, per Lyst’s 2026 gift index.).

Sources indicate that on the other side of menswear gifting, End also reports a hunger for relaxed tailoring and elevated outerwear — “a long tailored coat is a must!” claims Wieczorek — from brands such as Studio Nicholson, Auralee and YMC. In keeping with this desire for lasting purchases, Mintel reports that 71% of US men see luxury purchases as a personal milestone or marker of achievement, which makes meaningful wardrobe upgrades and keepsake gifts especially resonant. “We’re seeing strong momentum across jewellery and watches, a category that continues to gain traction during the gifting season as customers seek elevated, personal, enduring purchases,” says Wieczorek.

Calvin Klein underwear remains a strong stocking filler, boosted by the brand’s hit campaign.

Sources indicate that in Fresh York-based concept store Essx, utility reigns supreme among menswear shoppers, bolstered by more experimental outerwear. “As the holiday season approaches, we expect to see a continued focus on utility shopping paired with experimental and statement outerwear. Leather has been one of our strongest categories over the past few seasons with VIPs and walk-in clients,” says Jackson Ray, store director. “We anticipate a continued desire for leather pants and jackets paired with sterling silver accessories and leather boots.”.

Essx also predicts keepsake pieces to perform. “Our customers always seek exclusive or limited items,” says Ray. “We have heavily invested in upscale accessories such as fine jewelry, eyewear, and footwear, which make for fantastic holiday gifts.

Unsurprisingly, underwear remains a trusty stocking filler for shoppers, especially this time round. Demand for men’s Calvin Klein underwear climbed 60% year-on-year in October 2026 versus October 2025, according to Lyst’s 2026 gift index. Following the Jude Bellingham campaign, searches soared a further 25% week-on-week (Nov 2-9 2026).

Womenswear shoppers are also seeking timeless gifts this holiday season. “For womenswear, quality, versatility and longevity can help justify the splurge,” states Steiger, noting that 76% of US luxury consumers prefer timeless or classic styles, where pieces feel special enough to gift but relevant beyond the holiday season. At Selfridges, HNWIs are showing strong interest in labels such as Phoebe Philo and The Row for this holiday season. “Investment dressing continues to be a key theme, with elevated knitwear emerging as a standout category,” notes Bosse Myhr, director of buying for menswear, womenswear and childrenswear at Selfridges.

It has been revealed that retailers still want to see newness within established brands, though. “This Christmas marks an crucial moment for womenswear at Harrods, as many of the collections introduced by newly appointed creative directors began arriving in store for SS26,” explains Longland. “These new creative visions are bringing fresh energy to established houses, and we expect the new icons emerging from these collections to feature prominently on Christmas wish lists.” Longland notes that Harrods’s clients are responding to pieces that feel distinctive, rather than plainly familiar.

Tried-and-tested holiday favorites will remain core across genders. “In our stores right now, we’ve launched cashmere shops, scarf bars, trench destinations and gifting at all levels of luxury prices,” remarked Burberry CEO Joshua Schulman, on the brand’s latest earnings call. Burberry just staged a takeover of New York hotel The Mark to promote its scarves and partywear with the all-key US consumer. Flannels features the Burberry scarf bars in-store, too. “You can’t go wrong with an iconic British scarf for Christmas. It’s one of those gifts that feels special but will be worn for years to come,” states Natalie Dickson, Frasers Group’s head of luxury brand partnerships.

According to PWC, 78% of US Gen Z consumers are seeking nostalgic, screen-free gifts. For US consumers gifting children (17 and under) in their family, clothing and footwear were the second most-cited category (60%), following toys (63%). Each of the top five categories are all analog.

In line with Gen Z and millennial households stepping into parenthood — and therefore becoming core gift-givers — childrenswear is showing more and more affinities with adult tastes. “There’s a growing crossover between adult and childrenswear, with families shopping the designer brands they know and love across the whole family,” reports Dickson.

In a recent development, at Harrods, a similar shift holds, with childrenswear holiday demand led by the same categories driving womenswear and menswear: partywear, pyjamas and outerwear. “Christmas at Harrods is one of those moments when dressing becomes a shared family occasion,” says Longland. “From special outfits for celebrations to beautiful winter pieces, clients are looking for clothing that combines practicality with a sense of occasion.”.

The newly introduced Burberry Christmas campaign.

One of the most notable areas of growth within childrenswear has been the baby category, which has significantly outperformed the broader children’s market at Selfridges this year, says Myhr.

It has been revealed that in the kids category, parents’ own memories of Christmas and holiday style guide product assortments. “There’s a wonderful nostalgia to dressing children for the holidays, and nobody understands that quite like Ralph Lauren,” says Bloomingdale’s Thielebeule, calling out Fair Isle knits, tartan and velvet. For him, these are tropes that “feel as though they belong in today’s family holiday card, but are just as lovely a generation later.”.

Last year, Ralph Lauren’s big Christmas push went viral. In response, Bloomingdale’s has invested in a special holiday partnership this year, entitled “A Treasured World”, which offers a whole family range of gifting and cozy seasonal wear, explains Thielebeule. It builds on the viral traction Ralph Lauren demonstrated last year with “Ralph Lauren Mom” creators on TikTok and Instagram presenting themselves as festive, old-money Americans, he adds.

Luxury brands have been ramping up their investments in wellness this holiday season — tapping into a market now valued at $2.7 trillion, according to McKinsey. This has trickled down into holiday offerings. “Wellness is opening newly introduced territory for luxury gifting, particularly as consumers increasingly invest in how they feel as well as how they look,” says Mintel’s Steiger, citing Dior’s “Haute Wellness” capsule, introduced in September, which comprises a Pilates and yoga mat, a yoga block, a Pilates ring, resistance bands and weighted wristbands.

In self-gifting, 32% of US shoppers cited health and wellness products as tempting — making them the third-highest-scoring category in Deloitte’s survey, after clothing and accessories, and electronics. Meanwhile, 44% of shoppers will gift products from the health and wellness category this year, up from 40% in 2025. Fittingly, one of the top brands in Lyst’s gifting index is Alo, with demand increasing 132% this year.

According to recent reports, the rise in wellness gifting aligns with another undercurrent. Per PWC, 81% of US Gen Z consumers are prioritizing offline, in-person activities this year, with 63% saying a shared meal would matter more as a gift than a physical present.

In a recent development, nonetheless, the bottom line remains the same across gift categories. “This holiday, the opportunity is in products that offer something beyond the price tag, whether that’s emotional significance, lasting quality, personal wellbeing, or simply something worth keeping,” says Steiger.

Upgrade: This story has been updated with Natalie Dickson’s correct title, Frasers Group’s head of luxury brand partnerships.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that this creamy, always comforting slow-cooked rice pudding is scented with cardamom and sometimes topped with nuts or dried fruit. Versions of it exist across South Asia and beyond, each one slightly different but speaking the same nostalgic language. I’m serving it with a little twist here—a brûléed top for that crackly crème brûlée moment, and a scoop of mango sorbet for brightness and as a nod to the classic sticky rice flavor.

In a recent development, note: If you are not using a nonstick pot, be extra careful and stir every 4 to 5 minutes; otherwise the rice pudding will definitely stick to the bottom. In the event it does, swiftly empty the contents into a new pot and start simmering from low heat again. If you do not have a kitchen blowtorch, you can skip the brûlée. Serve warm or chill for 2 to 4 hours and garnish with saffron threads.

Find more Rachel Gurjar recipes here.

To a medium heavy-bottomed nonstick pot, add 5 cups (1.2 L) whole milk, 1 cup (240 ml) water, one 14-oz. (415 ml) can sweetened condensed milk, 3 green cardamom pods, and one 1" (2.5-cm) cinnamon stick. Bring to a boil and add 1 cup (200 g) jasmine rice or any short‑grain rice, then turn the heat down to low and simmer, stirring often and scraping all the way down to the bottom of the pot to make sure the mixture doesn’t stick or scorch, until the rice is tender and the mixture is thickened, 50 to 60 minutes. Add ¼ tsp. fine sea salt and stir to combine. If the consistency feels too thick add, ¼ cup [60 ml] water and stir to reach your desired consistency.

According to recent reports, scoop the kheer into heatproof serving bowls and top each with 1 to 2 Tbsp. granulated sugar, ensuring the surface is covered completely. Then carefully brûlée using a kitchen blowtorch, moving in a circular pattern, until the sugar is melted and a deep amber color. (You want a thin, smooth crust that shatters when broken.) Top with a scoop of sorbet and serve immediately.

The Sussexes are in for a very British Christmas. After moving back in late August—following more than six years in California—Prince Harry and Duchess Meghan are ready to spend the holidays in England.

Per a new People report, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex are planning to celebrate both Thanksgiving and Christmas at their new home in the Cotswolds with their children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet. Meghan’s mother, Doria Ragland, is also expected to join.

A source told People that after her estranged father’s recent arrest, Meghan “wants the holidays to be as quiet and enjoyable as possible for the family.”.

“Traveling back and forth would be too much for everyone,” the source added. “She doesn’t want to add any more pressure right now.”.

It’s been a while since Harry and Meghan spent the holidays in the United Kingdom. In 2017, the engaged couple joined Harry’s royal family for Christmas at Sandringham. And in 2018, as a newly married couple, they attended the traditional Christmas Day church service at St. Mary Magdalene Church at Sandringham.

It has been revealed that in the years that followed, as the Sussexes stepped back from their senior royal posts, they spent their holidays in either Canada or the United States, which means this will be their little children’s first true British Christmas. We know they might not make it to town for the festivities (as they are trying to keep a low profile), but there really is nothing quite like a London Christmas.

The source told People that Meghan and Harry “really enjoy the privacy” of their upcoming home. “They can go out for lunch or dinner, and people give them space,” the insider noted. “With the kids back in school, they’ve been making time for each other and enjoying those outings together.”.

We already know Meghan’s Christmas table spread will include plenty of jam, flower sprinkles, and party bubbles. And we can’t wait to learn more about the family’s end-of-year celebrations.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, it’s possible that Rufus Sewell is having too much fun right now.
  • According to recent reports, wyler, of The Diplomat, is navigating how to work with the increasingly autocratic and bloody-minded President Grace Penn (Allison Janney) thousands of miles away from his wife Kate (Keri Russell), who is starting to exhibit some of his own manipulative behaviors she claims to abhor.
  • Sewell sat down for a long chat with GQ about the two series, the value of blending high silliness with high stakes in the same scene, and how bodily functions are an under-appreciated key to unlocking a character’s specificity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, it’s possible that Rufus Sewell is having too much fun right now. Between playing morally ambiguous Vice President (and husband to the U.S. Ambassador to the Court of St. James’s) Hal Wyler in Netflix’s frothy, prestige-y series The Diplomat and the beloved but deeply flawed Mr. Bennet in the streamer’s upcoming adaptation of Pride and Prejudice, he’s cornered the market on lovable rascals. He thrives on “exercises in gray” and relishes “when it goes wrong” for a character. “It’s the opposite of what you want in life,” he tells me. “You want drama, you want mistakes.” These roles offer plenty of both.

According to recent reports, wyler, of The Diplomat, is navigating how to work with the increasingly autocratic and bloody-minded President Grace Penn (Allison Janney) thousands of miles away from his wife Kate (Keri Russell), who is starting to exhibit some of his own manipulative behaviors she claims to abhor. Two centuries prior, Mr. Bennet is reckoning not with geopolitical crises and egomaniacal heads of state, but with the challenges his wife faces in marrying off five eligible, if dowry-poor, daughters.

Sewell sat down for a long chat with GQ about the two series, the value of blending high silliness with high stakes in the same scene, and how bodily functions are an under-appreciated key to unlocking a character’s specificity.

Rufus Sewell: The interesting question for me, for the second half of the season, was how much is Hal truly aware of everything that Kate and everyone else are noticing and concerned about with Grace's behavior. How much does he see? How much is he choosing to pretend not to see in order to stay in the room? He's always believed that access is all, but how much do you compromise in order to stay in the room? Where’s the point when you realize you stayed in the room too long without saying anything, and the moment’s passed, and you are just an accomplice? I found it very difficult to play his seeming unctuousness and obsequiousness with Grace this season, and to not be trying to protect my character in the wrong way, because I felt he was failing.

According to recent reports, he’s overestimated his ability to effect change with Grace. Hal was prepared to appear to be supporting her, when he believed in his ability to steer her in a better direction, and I think he goes past that point. When I read the final episode script and saw where he ends up walking out, it gave me the courage to really lean into how much he goes wrong, by his own standards earlier in the season. He begins to lose his way in a way that he never has done before. But I embraced it, knowing that the real gift of the part was getting to play him going wrong and then seemingly correcting himself. We actually shot a speech that he made, just to give us a sense of where the scene was headed and for me to know how to play it. They might end up using some of it in the next season, or they could end up completely changing what was written. Hal coming out of the summit is a momentous decision in terms of what that does for the future and I've got no idea what’s next—I can't wait to start filming season five to find out.

Industry observers note that I was always shocked when this show was described as a thriller because I always thought it was a kind of romantic sex comedy with extremely high stakes, because what it reminded me of firstly was some of the comedy of divorce screwball films of the 1940s. The characters may be divorced after a very tempestuous relationship, but they’re interlinked in a way that can never be undone. There's a romance to all of that history.

Recent findings suggest that the other thing that it reminded me of was the kind of films that were made in the '70s—French films where halfway through an argument one of the characters would sit down on the toilet, you know what I mean? The people inside these films remind you of your own relationships. Your long-term relationship might not go to the same extremes, it might not be in the same setting, but I think people are people. What I love about their relationship is their shared wonkiness, and the getting into the nitty-gritty of the politics and taking someone down and hatching a plot whilst fighting over pastries and getting crumbs on the bed—all of that is part of their foreplay.

In a recent development, that is what the show is about, as far as I'm concerned. These are people who wear suits that might stand at a lectern and be on TV, but the fact is, how do you scratch an itch? Do you smell? Do you need to go to the toilet? These are the things that the script leans into a lot, and it might put some people off, but I don't care about that. That's the thing that makes it feel real, and it's so refreshing to play.

Recent findings suggest that he'll flirt with anyone. We all know people like this. It's not even necessarily sexual, he just engages with people on that level and it's a natural thing for him.

Industry observers note that I would say Hal’s flirtatiousness being a problem is open for debate, because a lot of what we understand of him is via Kate’s descriptions of him and his behavior. I can and often do see it in a different way. Part of the story of seasons three and four is Kate’s realization that a lot of stuff she thought of as his personality was in fact the mantle of the job that he'd taken on, because we see her doing the same kinds of things now that she is an ambassador. They both have a lot of the same qualities. They're both killers in a sense, and it's been very convenient for her and great for the show for her to introduce the public to Hal through her descriptions. And yet, every time it seems like he's changed character, in fact, it is revealing something from a different perspective.

In a recent development, we learned pretty early on that we were going to be doing some very, very long scenes, and we were given the advantage of seeing the scenes very early so we could slowly gestate the performances. We needed that because Windsor Castle in the show was comprised of several different buildings and locations, some of them with oceans between them, so we’d be shooting some parts the next day, and other bits in four months’ time.

In a recent development, especially with a two-hander, with such long takes, you can go in and out of being relaxed, unrelaxed, free, slightly bound, and actually you get to the point where you stop worrying about it. It's like being on stage, because you end up too tired to be bad all the time and end up inhabiting the moment and things just happen. I love that all of it was a surprise to us.

It has been revealed that I think what is most vital in this particular iteration of the relationship between Mr. and Mrs. Bennet is that he comes to realize which ways he's failed his daughters. When Mrs. Bennet says to him in this version, it's easy for you to say that I’m silly or frivolous, but you try being a woman at this age with no means—this is the fight of their lives that he is making these jokes about. And yes, of course he's funny and right in certain ways, but he's also guilty of negligence of his family for the sake of an easy life for himself. The reason they have no money is that so much money has been spent on bonnets. Money could have been saved, but in order to have a quiet life, he's ducked out of fights in order to avoid responsibility.

In a recent development, exactly. It was a gift in this role to have that moment when he feels that, admits that, and gets to be slightly humbled in this idea of himself that he's been cultivating. He didn’t actively or consciously avoid having this revelation, but that’s the effect of staying in his study, and now he’s facing the consequences. To use very modern terms, he has a revelation of what his pattern has been. It made sense!

One could be forgiven for thinking that Mr. and Mrs. Bennet are two people that used to be attracted to each other and now have nothing in common and don't like each other. I think it's born out in the book, though, the idea that there is still a love there, and especially a shared humor between them, and a bit of a spark remains.

Industry observers note that I love the fact that we get to get drunk together and stuff like that. Olivia Colman and I worked on The Father together a few years ago with Anthony Hopkins, which was a very different kind of gig, but as is often the case with things that are very heavy and intense, we had a hoot doing it. I loved working with her, and was very excited about the chance to work with her again. I love the scenes between Mr. Bennet and Mrs. Bennet. They were such a treat for us.

Jennifer Lawrence has always leaned toward honesty in interviews, earning her a reputation as one of Hollywood’s most relatable celebrities. And as online chatter about plastic surgery—who did it, and what did they do—reaches a fever pitch, Lawrence is setting the record straight by openly discussing her “new” breast implants.

During an appearance on Watch What Happens Live with Andy Cohen, alongside her Hunger Games co-star Josh Hutcherson, Lawrence told Cohen offhandedly that she “has implants.” When Cohen asked, she said they’re new and credited Santa Monica–based plastic surgeon Steven Teitelbaum.

Lawrence went on to say she went with a full-C implant, restoring her breasts to the “same size they were”—meaning, before she had two kids. This is the second time in recent months that the Oscar winner has admitted to a postpartum plastic surgery procedure. In an interview with The Cut for her new haircare brand, Mes, Lawrence admitted to getting a breast lift following the birth of her second child. “Everything bounced back, pretty much, after the first one,” the actress told The New Yorker in October 2025. “Second one, nothing bounced back.”.

She took that sentiment even further on an October 2026 episode of Call Her Daddy, where she gave host Alex Cooper, who was then pregnant, a frank piece of motherly wisdom: “Your vagina will bounce back, your butthole won’t.”.

It has been revealed that lawrence is the latest in a string of A-list celebrities opening up about cosmetic treatments, like Kylie Jenner, who made waves last year when she admitted on TikTok to her exact implant size and surgeon. From Lawrence, the casual admission feels less like a calculated confession and more like advice from a trusted friend who doesn’t hold back about motherhood and pregnancy’s physical toll.

Is Merch Stealing Luxury’s Aspirational Consumer?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1492 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Typically, middle-income young shoppers have focused their fashion spending on accessible luxury goods or one-off splurges, like a Coach Tabby bag ($375) or a Longchamp Le Pliage ($165).
  • It has been revealed that however, among these groups, a growing faction is trading down, looking instead to the fast-developing category of merch to broadcast their affiliation to culture, whether it’s the newly launched Rhode windbreaker ($257) or last week’s frenzied release of a hot-pink GTA logo tee ($66).
  • Recent findings suggest that “Brands invest inordinate amounts of resources into product research and development to try and catch the ever-elusive hype cycle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Typically, middle-income young shoppers have focused their fashion spending on accessible luxury goods or one-off splurges, like a Coach Tabby bag ($375) or a Longchamp Le Pliage ($165).

It has been revealed that however, among these groups, a growing faction is trading down, looking instead to the fast-developing category of merch to broadcast their affiliation to culture, whether it’s the newly launched Rhode windbreaker ($257) or last week’s frenzied release of a hot-pink GTA logo tee ($66). While merch is nothing upcoming in the fashion market — Balenciaga relied heavily on it during Demna’s tenure between 2015 and 2025 — the playing field is changing, with a stronger focus on the temporal buzz of a new digital or game-based craze, the cult movie everyone’s watching, the fiendishly anticipated alt-rap tour, or a new milestone in a girl-boss beauty community’s trajectory — like Rhode founder Hailey Bieber’s 30th birthday.

Recent findings suggest that “Brands invest inordinate amounts of resources into product research and development to try and catch the ever-elusive hype cycle. But with [consumers] suddenly coveting more transient ‘merchandise’ over main line product ranges, is that investment misplaced?” asks Simon Richardson, group strategy director at creative agency Amplify. “What [brands] should be doing is creating a moment in time, not just a product line. Fans need more — all the time — to signal what they care about in a way that feels distinct, real and truly of a moment.”.

Outside the Selfridges GTA launch.

Sources indicate that recently, Jordan Firstman, director of buzzy gay drama Club Kid, called on Fresh York designer Emily Dawn Long — renowned among Dimes Square it-kids for her in-the-know screenprinted vintage tees — to design the merch for the film. The designer, known for her Spoiled Boys slogan tee, emblazoned the ragged tops with one of the film’s lines, “It’s like that every time”. In the film itself, Firstman also wore his own Emily Dawn Long tee, printed with the words, “Take off your clothes”. On Wednesday, A24 took over a downtown 1<3 NY souvenir shop to sell the capsule, before releasing a limited online drop (most styles are sold out).

A24 worked with designer Emily Dawn Long for fresh film Club Kid’s merch.

Sources indicate that tech bros are also tapping in. This year, Trump-contracted data surveillance firm Palantir released a chore jacket ($239) not dissimilar to those purveyed by cult restaurants, such as Sessions Arts Club and St. John. Reportedly, the tech giant’s broader apparel line is performing, especially in South Korea, where the windbreaker ($170) sold out. Much-talked-about corporation Nvidia — whose CEO Jensen Huang stepped down this week following his extramarital affair with a potential Chinese spy — also released a sweater emblazoned with a leather-jacketed cartoon of Huang ($178). The design is picking up strong resale value again following the scandal: one seller listed the design on Ebay for $2,500. And OpenAI offers a racing-style shirt ($75) not dissimilar to styles from Corteiz, Palace and Supreme — as well as bumper stickers ($10) and caps ($40), all sold on its website.

As luxury struggles to justify its price hikes — since the average price of personal luxury goods increased by 52% between 2019 and 2024, per HSBC — the merch market has swooped in to capitalize on the aspirational shopper. In the US, consumer sentiment is low, and yet spending is up. Indeed, across the US, Europe and China, shoppers are more cautious and discerning with discretionary purchases, guided by a brand’s value propositions. If a band tee, a Roblox hoodie, or a pair of GTA x Travis Scott Nike Air Force 1 sneakers can communicate cultural belonging, community adjacency, and lifestyle for a fraction of the cost of a luxury handbag, then merch wins.

In a recent development, indeed, in late 2025, 72% of Gen Z luxury shoppers told Vogue Business they would prefer owning a Walmart “Wirkin” over a genuine Hermès Birkin, and when interviewed, several respondents stated they deem spending lots of money on luxury distasteful and that luxury goods are not worth the cost. At the same time, beauty continues to boom with aspirational shoppers, but — unlike clothing and accessories — has only a handful of ways to turn its goods into walking advertisements. The Rhode phone case, seen in influencer selfies, marked the first step towards a solution, then came the wearable merch. Similarly, tech giants largely deal in intangible goods. But physical merch is a way for fans to display their favorite chip-maker or AI platform.

Hailey Bieber wears her latest Rhode windbreaker, which retails at $257.

For beauty, and even tech, merch gives brand fans a way to express their appreciation of the products and the communities around them. Companies recognize young people’s appetite to feel part of something.

Millennial readers will remember when “merch” referred primarily to band T-shirts. That playbook began in musical subcultures and has now transferred to a broader market. “Gen Alpha grew up inside worlds. For them, a ‘skin’ [Fortnite’s in-game outfits] is merch, a creator’s snack bar is merch, and a hoodie is the physical version of a world they already spend hours in,” says Jolyon Varley, co-founder of marketing agency OK Cool.

“Logos used to confer status and were a more reliable indicator of what you could afford or how you were living,” he adds. “Merch tells people what you’re into, and that’s become far more valuable. It’s a matter of signaling taste rather than wealth.”.

According to recent reports, varley points to the frenzy seen at GTA’s Selfridges launch, explaining that consumers now associate with much more than simply products, but instead entire worlds. “GTA isn’t just a game any more,” he claims. “Millions of people live in it. The launch week proved it.”.

Whether that’s an event exclusive, an IP artefact made real for the ‘heads’, or even a staff uniform, exclusivity and experience are major drivers of hype, indicates Amplify’s Richardson. “Something that says, ‘I was there’, not just ‘this is what I’m into’.”.

Richardson also notes that fandom thrives on shared codes and signals. So his advice for brands wanting a piece of the pie? “Bringing together your own lore, something that anchors your merch in time, and the right collaborators to bring it to life in a fan-first and agile way, can turn a small run of products into a mass-reach driver.” The Rockstar Games’s GTA takeover of Miami — a reported $3.9 million deal with Miami-Dade County — sets the bar, lighting up Miami Heat’s stadium, dressing players in black-and-pink jerseys, and activating across the city.

Merch’s appeal lies in the power of the brand and what that communicates. It’s a quick win to cross categories, too. “If you build a brand that is cool, interesting, culturally relevant, aspirational, it [almost] doesn’t matter what you’re selling, because what you’re selling is the aura — this ineffable, ‘it’, cool factor,” says Ursula founder and brand strategist Emma Hope Allwood. “Just practically, when you have these substantial cultural moments or launches like GTA, it makes sense to try to break it down into different categories — different ways for people to be part of it, rather than it just being a game.”.

Sources indicate that luxury brands that want to re-enter the merch market and cultural players looking to seize the growing momentum need to broach the sector carefully. “Not all merch is cool,” indicates Sara McAlpine, co-founder of brand and marketing studio Bikini, highlighting the recent tech brand plays. “There’s no reason to be producing a chore coat unless you’re trying to say you’re aligned with a Carhartt WIP and Japanese-denim wearing aesthetic-conscious crowd.”.

In a recent development, so what works? Influencer and DJ Leo Mandella visited the GTA Selfridges pop-up. He typically doesn’t consider merch cool — “[it] can look a bit gimmicky” — but the capsule delivered, he believes. “It’s very easy for gaming companies to mess up on the rest of the promo run, but Rockstar were absolutely incredible at creating a capsule of merch that was just as good as the game,” says Mandella, who spent £250 (roughly $329) at the pop-up. “I think merch is especially exciting when done well because you feel part of a moment. It’s not just a piece of clothing. Buying a Vice City tee or a Burger Shot uniform [the official in-game restaurant chain] makes you feel like you’re in this fictional world.”.

Inside the Selfridges GTA activation.

Nonetheless, for brands that still want to communicate esotericism, merch remains an astute method. Varley pinpoints the power of releasing one-off, friends-and-family T-shirts during events. He cites the Awake x Jordan T-shirts — art directed by London graffiti artist Fatzoo — given out during Notting Carnival at the Deviation stage. “That immediately orients you in a specific nucleus of that scene,” he says. “If you weren’t there — or don’t know the individuals involved — you didn’t get one.”.

  • Slow-roasting Japanese sweet potatoes flesh-side down releases their natural sugars, caramelizing and deepening their sweetness.
  • To a blender or food processor, add 2 bunches cilantro (about 6 oz.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, every cuisine has a sauce that’s an absolute essential—a ride or die, if you will. For South Asian food, this is a cilantro mint green chutney. It brings a punchy, herb-packed burst of flavor that goes with pretty much everything. This recipe combines cilantro, mint, and just the right amount of heat from green chiles, creating a balance of spice and freshness. Lime juice adds brightness, while cumin, sugar, and chaat masala add complexity. Use this as a zesty topping for your favorite dish or as a base for pani puri water (just add 1½ cups [360 ml] of water and strain), or make it creamy with yogurt or sour cream to use for spreading and dipping.

Slow-roasting Japanese sweet potatoes flesh-side down releases their natural sugars, caramelizing and deepening their sweetness. The flesh becomes incredibly tender, almost custard-like in texture, while the skin turns a rich golden brown and becomes slightly crispy. So don’t bother peeling them! Top them with tamarind concentrate (I like Tamicon, Cock Brand, Pure Indian Foods, or Dragonfly—anything without citric acid), green chutney, fresh onions, tomatoes, and cilantro for a chaat-inspired appetizer.

Find more Rachel Gurjar recipes here.

To a blender or food processor, add 2 bunches cilantro (about 6 oz. [170 g]), leaves and stems, 1 bunch mint (about 2 oz. [55 g]), leaves and tender stems, 6 green Thai chiles or 2 serranos, stemmed (more if you want it spicier), ½ cup (120 ml) lime juice (from about 5 limes), 2 tsp. cumin seeds, 1½ tsp. fine sea salt, 1 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. chaat masala. Pulse for a few seconds in intervals until the ingredients are pulverized into a smooth paste. Transfer to an airtight container and store until ready to use, up to 1 week in the refrigerator or 1 month in the freezer.

Preheat the oven to 375°F (190°C) and line a baking sheet with parchment paper.

Sources indicate that drizzle the sheet with extra-virgin olive oil and place 1½ lb. (680 g) Japanese or Korean sweet potatoes, ends trimmed, halved lengthwise, cut-side down. Bake for 60 to 70 minutes, until golden and caramelized on the cut side and cooked through and tender; a knife inserted into the center of the potato should slide through easily. Let rest for 5 to 8 minutes. Once cool enough to handle, cut the sweet potatoes into 1" to 2" [2.5 to 5 cm] pieces.

To a small bowl, add ½ cup (120 g) plain whole-milk yogurt or sour cream and ½ tsp. fine sea salt and whisk to combine. If you’re using sour cream, thin it out with a little water.

Recent findings suggest that place the sweet potatoes on a serving platter and drizzle the yogurt, ½ cup Evergreen Chutney, 3 Tbsp. tamarind concentrate or paste, and 2 Tbsp. lime juice evenly all over. Sprinkle with 1 medium red tomato (5 oz. [140 g]), finely chopped, 1 small red onion (7 oz. [200 g]), finely chopped, 2 Tbsp. chopped cilantro leaves and tender stems, 1 tsp. chaat masala, 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, thinly sliced, and crispy sev and serve immediately.

Do Ahead: You can make the individual components a day ahead of time and store them in airtight containers in the refrigerator, then assemble to serve.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, here at Harper’s Bazaar, we are game to try anything and everything in the wellness world—from daily digestion walks to a $500 full-body assessment, and even supplements to boost ferritin levels—to stay healthy. But, like anyone else, we’re always hunting for upcoming ways to avoid getting sick.

We’ve all been there: someone coughing on the subway immediately makes you jump, or you hear a friend you just sat next to at dinner has come down with a cold, and suddenly you’re overdosing on vitamin C. Warding off a cold or viral sickness is not always possible—especially once cold and flu season rolls around.

According to recent reports, there are classic tricks like upping your vitamin C intake, washing your hands frequently, and drinking hot liquids like soup and tea, but what about the extreme hacks that hit the SOS button on your immune system—those under-the-radar, witchcraft-adjacent tricks? We have tried almost every tip and trick in the book—some work like a charm, and others are all hype and anecdotes—but ahead are the 14 hacks our editors swear by for staying healthy this cold season—and beyond.

Industry observers note that “Tongue scraping has changed my life. Not only does it make your mouth feel much cleaner and support overall oral health, but I swear that since I started scraping religiously a few years back, I've been sick WAY less often. And I have a toddler! In daycare! My theory is that it scrapes away bacteria before it has a chance to settle in your throat—but who knows? No matter what the science says, there are only upsides—fresher breath, better teeth, and the satisfaction of seeing all that gunk removed." —Jenna Rosenstein, beauty director.

“As an out-and-proud hypochondriac, I have a long laundry list of cold-fighting hacks. The most crucial is washing my hands frequently (as soon as I arrive somewhere upcoming, after taking the subway, after touching a public surface, etc.) and avoiding touching my face. I keep a compact hand sanitizer in every purse I own in case of emergency!” — Olivia Alchek, senior designer.

Industry observers note that “I consider a good night's sleep a cure-all for just about anything, including incoming sickness. Not only does adequate rest help your body fight off infection by way of antibody and immune cell production, but it just makes you feel better in general, which is all you want when you're feeling borderline sick.” —Tiffany Dodson Davis, beauty commerce editor.

“Most of my heavy-hitting cold fighters are from Europe (they’re just exponentially better over there), but when it comes to sick solutions stateside, I always have Wellness Formula stocked in my house. I don’t know what sorcery is in these pills, but once I take this, whether it’s when a sniffle or tickle in my throat comes up, or if I am already deep into a cold, I feel better the next day. The pills contain all the gold-standard immunity ingredients: elderberry, zinc, propolis, echinacea, and vitamins C and D, plus vitamins and minerals that are good to take generally, like selenium, calcium, and vitamin A. The only downside is a pungent aftertaste (likely from the garlic bulb in the formula), and the daily dose is 6 pills, which is more than many can handle. If you don’t like pills, there’s a liquid version that works just as well, but I prefer the pills for when I travel.” —Katie Intner, beauty market and commerce editor.

According to recent reports, “Even in the post-COVID era, I still wear K-N95 masks on public transit. It’s the most successful way to avoid unwanted germs. Thinking about thousands of New Yorkers on a crowded subway, sniffling in the winter months—I’ll never go back to being mask-free again!” —OA.

“As soon as I feel a scratchy throat coming on, I break out the Vicks. Slather it on and let it do its old-timey magic.” —Lillian Dondero, assistant managing editor.

“When people say to ‘flush out a cold,’ they typically mean drink lots of fluids, but I love dry brushing to get the lymphatic system moving and grooving to rid any toxins from the cold. I do it for two minutes before I shower, and I instantly feel my lymphatic system activated and more energized. Plus, it doubles as exfoliation, which is key during the winter months.” —KI.

According to recent reports, “Throat Coat tea is my holy grail whenever I’m feeling under the weather. I love the subtle licorice flavor, and it’s incredibly soothing on an irritated throat. I always keep it stocked at home and reach for it at the first sign of a cold. Honestly, it’s so good that I even drink it when I’m not sick!” —Jackie Judd, executive assistant.

Recent findings suggest that “Whenever the thought ‘Oh, I think I might be getting a cold’ enters my brain, I immediately go to the pharmacy to pick up some Zicam. I don’t know if this is the official tagline, but in my head it is ‘stops a cold before you get it’ because IT. DOES! The trick is to buy the kind that goes up your nose—spray or swabs—and be diligent; your symptoms won't progress, and then they'll go away completely. It's magic!” —Laia Garcia-Furtado, deputy culture director.

“A shot before work is my way of staying healthy! My fridge is always stocked with Greenhouse Juice Co. dispensers because I truly can never live without them. A quick shot to kickstart my day is a great immunity boost, and the spice is a great bonus, as it always helps wake me up.” —Claudia Cruz, deputy visual director.

Industry observers note that “Liquid echinacea everywhere! I keep it in my bag and squeeze it into everything—even my coffee.” —Lynette Nylander, executive digital director.

Sources indicate that “I love Cymbiotika’s liposomal technology because the lipid base makes it more easily absorbed into the bloodstream and is therefore more effective. I always use these vitamin C packets when I feel a cold coming on or know I will be low on sleep, like while traveling, because they truly boost my immunity and taste like a creamsicle. Life is hard enough! I want a supplement that works and tastes good.

I will often couple the Cymbiotika vitamin C with a packet of the Armra Colostrum, which protects and boosts immunity.” —KI.

Industry observers note that “When I’m already experiencing cold symptoms? Downing a spoonful of honey—both anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial—with a squeeze of lemon does wonders for my itchy throat or stubborn cough." —TDD.

Industry observers note that “My most homeopathic tip whenever I start to feel symptoms is to eat raw garlic. Garlic contains a compound called allicin, which is released when you crush, chop, or chew it. Allicin is known to have immune-boosting, antimicrobial, and antiviral properties that may shorten illness. Does it actually work? Who knows! But it doesn’t hurt to crush a little garlic in olive oil for dipping toast. It’s a harmless, delicious extra step in my sick day routine.” —OA.

How to Grow a Beard

📅 20 Oct 2014 | ⏱️ 4 min read (888 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • So you want to learn how to grow a beard.
  • Recent findings suggest that “I’d say give it at least three to four weeks of solid growth before you even think about touching it with clippers,” Victor Mendoza, co-founder of beard care brand Viking Revolution, says.
  • It has been revealed that there’s a sweet spot between letting your facial hair grow out and knowing when it’s time to take the trimmers for the best results possible, even if you can’t go full lumberjack.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

So you want to learn how to grow a beard. First off, you should know that it helps to have the right genetics. Second, you have to stay committed to the endeavor. Too often, beard-growing attempts end before they’ve even had a chance to establish itself.

Recent findings suggest that “I’d say give it at least three to four weeks of solid growth before you even think about touching it with clippers,” Victor Mendoza, co-founder of beard care brand Viking Revolution, says. “Your beard needs time to actually show you what it’s going to look like, and that growth period lets you see the natural direction everything’s growing in. Plus, some hairs take longer to come in than others, so patience is key.”.

It has been revealed that there’s a sweet spot between letting your facial hair grow out and knowing when it’s time to take the trimmers for the best results possible, even if you can’t go full lumberjack. These are the best tips to maximize your hair follicles’ potential whether this is your first beard or your fiftieth.

There are many different beard styles to choose from; you don’t need to stick to neatly manicured, uniform look. Let your growth be influenced by the style you want to achieve.

In a recent development, “Your genes determine hair thickness, growth rate, density, and color,” Mendoza says. “If your dad or granddad had a thin beard, you’re probably dealing with the same hand, and that’s just life.”.

If your beard is patchy, or if it has a unique growth pattern (sparse on the cheeks, full on the goatee, for example), then you should set your expectations properly. This goes for beards substantial, small, and medium alike. And while nutrition is important for hair growth, you can’t cheat genetics with your diet.

Patience is a virtue. Not only can a little time help fill in some patchiness, but it’s also requisite for almost any style. A beard transforms into something newly introduced every week. So, if it’s seeming like you’ll never reach your goal—in particular if it’s a long beard—then you honestly might wake up one morning and realize that you’ve arrived at the destination.

Mendoza indicates to wait at least two weeks before you start to do a cleanup, but only around the ends, i.e. the hairs that aren’t within the perimeter in which you want your beard to grow. That’ll help you figure out your beard’s natural shape.

One of the tenets of beard maintenance is to keep it defined. In short: shave the neckline and clean up the cheek lines. These keep it more beard-like and less neckbeard-like—unless, for some reason, a wooly stoner beard is your aim. In that case, let it grow wild and free.

It has been revealed that the second way to keep things looking intentional is to sculpt and trim your beard as it grows. It might feel counterproductive—and counter to #2—but it’s the same way you need to get haircuts while growing out your hair. As Mendoza says, this helps direct the hair exactly where it needs to be: Fuller in some spots, less so in others. The styling products in the next tip can of course help influence things, but you foremost want to keep hairs in check as needed: This can mean spot-checking strays, snipping away split ends, or simply taking out some bulk. You’ll want a beard trimmer or a sharp pair of scissors.

There are a handful of beard products you should consider picking up if you’re serious about proper care and maintenance. A few drops of beard oil will absorb quickly and give your hair the right nutrients (plus a pinch of shine), while also making it less wild and frizzy. You can also swap in a beard balm or cream, something slightly heftier than an oil, to help style the beard and keep it in place all day. What’s vital is that you clean your beard every day with an actual beard wash and not just a regular shampoo, which Mendoza states will dry out your beard and your face.

According to recent reports, weekly maintenance will consist of a deep condition, which you can do in the shower. “If you’re doing those things consistently, your beard is going to look way healthier and fuller than most guys out there,” he notes.

Sources indicate that beard brushes help exfoliate the skin beneath the beard, for starters, which lifts dead skin cells and prevents future flaking. Moreover, brushing your beard at the end of each day will ensure its health and tame-ability in the long haul. This distributes the natural oils produced in the skin, which otherwise collect at the base of the shaft and only nourish the bottom of each hair. This oil distribution prevents breakage, frizzing, and split ends. (This is a great time to apply a few drops of beard oil as a booster, especially after a shower.).

Once your base has grown out—this can take months—it’s time to really make it yours. One of our favorites is to snip the bridge between the mustache and the chin, thus marooning the mustache. Or, pare back the beard itself, leaving a fuller mustache. You have lots of options, and it’s your privilege as a beard grower to flaunt it.
