  • But it’s hardly the only country that excels at this holiday event.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that there’s nothing quite like a Christmas market to set a joyful tone for the holiday season. Is there anywhere else where it’s acceptable to mill about with a hearty mug of glögg in one hand, an even larger potato pancake in the other, while exceeding your budget on handcrafted ornaments and posing for photos in front of a wooden sleigh? The answer, we can confidently say, is no.

If you’re especially fortunate, you might even find yourself exploring a traditional European Christmas market this winter—a bucket list item for travelers with a proclivity for all things merry and bright. A natural place to start when curating an itinerary is Germany, and for good reason: It is, after all, the birthplace of the Christmas market, with Dresden’s Striezelmarkt first springing up all the way back in 1434.

But it’s hardly the only country that excels at this holiday event. There are numerous other destinations scattered across the continent—some familiar, and some wonderfully under the radar—that deliver the festive goods. Here, find 22 storybook European Christmas markets to make 2026 your most memorable holiday season yet.

What to Expect: The Stortorget Christmas Market is held in Gamla Stan, Stockholm’s old town, that dates back to the 13th century and is encircled by historic merchant houses. It’s often snowy this time of year, so enjoy the crunch of fresh powder beneath your feet as you meander medieval alleys and peruse the market’s 41 chalet-shaped stalls. If you’re hungry, pick up a smoked sausage or some lussekatter, a brioche-like saffron bun. You can cross everyone off your shopping list with the cozy selection of hand-knitted sweaters and traditional ornaments, all illuminated by the market’s endless strings of festive lights. (And speaking of light, if your visit to Stockholm happens to land on December 13, don’t miss Lucia, the country’s traditional, candlelit festival.).

Where to Stay: Lydmar Hotel (12-minute walk).

It has been revealed that what to Expect: The term ‘fairytale’ gets thrown around a lot when speaking of Christmas markets, but in the case of Wroclaw, it’s simply the best way to describe it. This magical atmosphere—complete with gothic architecture and a 75-foot-tall (artificial!) Norwegian spruce—stretches across four interconnected areas: the market square (Rynek), the salt square (Plac Solny), Świdnicka Street, and Oławska Street. While exploring, don’t miss the opportunity to try oscypek, a smoked cheese from the Polish mountains that is served with cranberries and best paired with a glass of mead (Poland’s oldest traditional alcoholic drink).

Where to Stay: Hotel Altus Palace (15-minute walk).

Location: Place des Dominicains, Place Jeanne d’Arc, Place de l’Ancienne Douanne, Koïfhus, Place des Six Montagnes Noires, and Square de la Montagne Verte.

When: Ends December 29 (though the Gourmet Market runs until January 3).

In a recent development, what to Expect: There are six (yes, six) total markets in this little town, which looks like the missing chapter of a fairytale book even when it’s not covered in string lights and fir branches. They’re all scattered around the Old Town and serve slightly different purposes: The main one on Place des Dominicains is mostly arts and crafts themed, with a few kids’ rides spread; the Place Jeanne d’Arc market is set up to look like a traditional Alsatian village; the Marché Gourmand at Square de la Montagne Verte is the spot for scrapings of creamy raclette, rich tartiflette, and hot cups of mulled wine.

Where to Stay: Relais & Châteaux La Maison Des Têtes (3-minute walk).

What to Expect: Dating back to the 17th century, the Nuremberg Christmas market (“Christkindlesmarkt”) is one of the first on the continent, and the city certainly goes all-out in homage to this tradition. Nicknamed the “city of wood and cloth,” it stands out for its candy cane-striped cloth tents, each housing glass tree baubles, fresh-baked gingerbread, and handmade wooden trinkets. Traveling with little ones? The children’s Christmas market is just around the corner on Hans-Sachs-Platz, and includes everything from a lit-up merry-go-round to a bake house where they can roll out their own dough.

Where to Stay: Karl August (one-minute walk).

Location: On Barfüsserplatz and Münsterplatz in the historic old town.

What to Expect: In Basel, around 155 rustic wooden chalets are set against the backdrop of the city’s old town, set aglow with glittering lights. A magnificent Christmas tree is erected in the historic center with ornaments by local decorating legend Johann Wanner, while stalls are bedecked in string lights and tinsel at every turn. After picking up a few artisanal gifts and goodies, head for the 13-meter-high Christmas pyramid on Barfüsserplatz for mulled wine, followed by a stroll along the Rhine River.

Where to Stay: Les Trois Rois (10-minute walk).

According to recent reports, what to Expect: The Wiener Chriskindlemarkt und Weihnachtstraum Christmas market is perhaps the largest and well-known in Vienna, but with this precedent comes crowds. Instead, founder of bespoke travel company Black Tomato Tom Marchant points to the Christmas village at the Belvedere Palace as an in-the-know, less-trafficked alternative preferred by locals; here, you can wander around the palace’s lavish 18th-century Baroque architecture while indulging in mulled wine and delectable pastries. “Lots of locally crafted jewelry can be found in this area,” says Marchant. “Scented woods, ceramics, wooden hats, decorations, drinking horns—it’s quite a stunning place.”.

Where to Stay: Miiro Spittelberg (20 minutes by tram).

Location: The Grande Île (Old Town).

It has been revealed that what to Expect: Known by holiday devotees as the “capital of Christmas,” Strasbourg is home to the oldest holiday market in France, dating all the way back to 1570. Visitors to this picturesque city in the Alsace region can pop in and out of 13 quaint markets, all within walking distance of each other in the old town. The original, however, is known as Christkindelsmärik and can be found at Place Broglie—there you, can sip on a mug of vin chaud while zipping around tinsel-adorned chalets in front of the Gothic cathedral.

Where to Stay: Hotel Cour du Corbeau Strasbourg-Mgallery (15-minute walk).

Recent findings suggest that what to Expect: Christmas markets and Germany are inextricably linked—it’s been estimated that there are over 2,500 in the country alone—and one of the best places to begin your exploration of the region’s holiday traditions is in the fairytale fortress town of Heidelberg. The historic city’s landscape includes the Neckar River and Odenwald Forest, while it also boasts architectural landmarks such as the Old Bridge and a prestigious 14th-century university attended by everyone from Hegel to Hannah Arendt. Heidelberg’s Christmas market is scattered throughout the illuminated storybook alleys of the old town, where the smell of roasted nuts wafts in the air as you dip into huts for souvenirs. Kids in tow? Go ice skating on Karlsplatz, or take a spin on the antique carousel.

Where to Stay: Heidelberg Suites House of Hütter (10-minute walk).

Where to Stay: Telegraaf Hotel (5-minute walk).

Location: East Princes Street Garden.

In a recent development, what to Expect: With the unmistakable silhouettes of Edinburgh Castle and the Scott Monument in the distance, Edinburgh’s holiday market—located in the center of the Scottish city—imbues its ancient walkways with a lively charm. Take in bird’s eye views from atop the glittering ferris wheel or glide across the ice skating rink surrounded by 18th-century architecture. Afterward, trot around the cheery network of vendors serving Scottish delicacies and winter drinks, or pick up last-minute artisanal gifts and decorations at the market’s many boutique stalls.

Where to Stay: The Roseate Edinburgh (10-minute drive).

Location: Tivoli Gardens and Højbro Plads.

When: Ends January 3 and December 20, respectively.

What to Expect: Entering Copenhagen’s Tivoli Gardens during the holiday season feels like wandering into an undiscovered Nordic village. This 175-year-old theme park is transformed annually into a Christmas market with 60 stalls swathed in magical decor, including log cabins draped in pine cones and layers of snow—and that’s without mentioning the garden itself, which glows with over 70,000 Christmas baubles and 1,000-plus trees draped in lights. A 10-minute walk away, Højbro Plads also lures in visitors with 18,000 sparkling lights, plus live reindeer pulling a Santa’s sleigh.

Where to Stay: Villa Copenhagen (5 and 15-minute walk).

Sources indicate that what to Expect: If you’re looking for a more pastoral feel, head to the Cotswolds, England’s most romantic region of storybook countryside. “With quaint villages adorned in lights, caroling, and frequent dustings of snow, the Cotswolds evokes Christmas from the days of old,” Marchant notes. The ancient city of Bath sits on the region’s edge and is hosting the 20th anniversary of its annual holiday market this year. With over 150 stalls offering unique goods like pottery, hand-knit socks, artisan cheeses, and beyond, you’ll cross off your shopping list—and then some.

Where to Stay: Thyme (1-hour drive).

Location: Govone Castle and Asti’s historic center.

Recent findings suggest that what to Expect: Bordering France and Switzerland, Italy’s northern Piedmont region is a hotspot for wintry festivities—but the atmospheric Christmas markets of neighboring towns Govone and Asti are the real standout. In Govone, tucked away inside the 18th-century royal castle, is both the House of Santa Claus and an exhibition that timelines the city’s Christmas celebrations over the centuries. If you want to shop, however, nearby Asti is where you’ll find over 130 workstations of artisans and food and wine producers scattered across Italy; afterwards, visit the living nativity scene put on by nearly 100 local volunteers.

Where to Stay: Relais San Maurizio (30-minute drive).

What to Expect: If you ask Finns where Santa Claus comes from, they’ll proudly declare their country as the answer. (Lapland, to be precise.) This alone makes celebrating the holiday in the capital of Helsinki an exhilarating and celebratory affair. “This is one of the best holiday markets in Europe,” Marchant indicates. “The cathedral overlooks the Helsinki Christmas market, which has over 100 stalls and stands with hand-crafted gifts, ornaments, locally-grown produce, and fish and meats sourced hyper-locally.” What are you waiting for?

Where to Stay: Hotel Haven (5-minute walk).

Recent findings suggest that location: Vorosmarty Square and St. Stephen’s Basilica.

What to Expect: Brave the bone-chilling weather with a bowl of goulash soup or steaming chimney cake at Budapest’s beloved Christmas market located along the cobblestone streets of Vörösmarty Tér (Vorosmarty Square) in the heart of the city. About a 10-minute walk away you can also discover Christmas festivities in front of St. Stephen’s Basilica; the advent festival hosts around 100 craft exhibitors, an ice rink, and more. (It was named Best Christmas Market in Europe for three years in a row, if that sort of accolade piques your interest.).

Where to Stay: Four Seasons Hotel Gresham Palace Budapest (5-minute walk).

What to Expect: This century-old holiday fair has over 100 wooden stalls and is nestled in Madrid’s Plaza Mayor town square. The merrymaking vibes are cemented with a glowing carousel, nativity scenes (belénes), and loads of handcrafted ornaments and gifts to choose from. You can also savor seasonal Spanish flavors like churros con chocolate washed down with a cup of mulled wine.

Where to Stay: Rosewood Villa Magna (15-minute drive).

Location: Market Square and Simon Stevin Square.

In a recent development, what to Expect: Appointed the whimsical title of Winter Glow, the annual festival in the medieval city of Bruges is nothing short of magical. Begin your visit on the light trail; a walk along 10 illuminated installations, all connected by a wintry blue glow. Then head for the Christmas markets for festivities that feel plucked from a fairytale. Technically there are two markets—one in the Market Square and the other in Simon Stevin Square—but as they are situated less than a five-minute walk from each other, it’s easy to do both. Peruse the atmospheric stalls for handcrafted decorations, wool socks, and plenty of Belgian treats and mulled wine, followed by a spin around the ice rink.

Where to Stay: Hotel Van Cleef (10-minute walk).

Location: Roßmarkt, along the Zeil, down to Römerberg, and to the Main River.

It has been revealed that what to Expect: With origins dating back to the 14th century, the Frankfurt Christmas market is among the oldest in the world. As such, it’s also one of the most popular markets, attracting millions of festive guests each year and stretching across several parts of the old town. Meander through its many decorated stalls, make a pitstop at the tree in Römerberg square, and don’t forget to devour a bethmännchen (a marzipan pastry that is unique to Frankfurt and baked just for Christmas).

Where to Stay: Schlosshotel Kronberg (30-minute drive).

Location: Dom and Residenzplatz Square.

Recent findings suggest that what to Expect: This traditional market is cozied up in the heart of Salzburg’s UNESCO World Heritage Site and has origins that go back to the late 15th century. These days, Christmas lovers descend upon the market’s 100-plus stands in search of Austrian specialties, festive incense aromas, traditional crafts, and decorations for the tree—all found within traditional huts.

Where to Stay: Rosewood Schloss Fuschl (30-minute drive).

Location: Old Town Square and Wenceslas Square.

What to Expect: Soak up the magic of Czechia at Prague’s holiday market. Get into the spirit of the season as you hop from one decorated wooden hut to the next, purchasing artisan crafts and delectable treats along the way. Curious what you’ll be eating? Look to popular Czech dishes like šunka (big hams roasted on spits), klobása (barbecued sausages), and rybí polévka (a traditional Christmas soup).

Where to Stay: Four Seasons Hotel Prague (10 to 20 minute walk).

What to Expect: For those in search of something out of the ordinary, Valkenburg’s underground Christmas markets are a winning bet. The small southern Dutch town hits all the marks when it comes to setting the right tone for the season, but once you head into its caves and tunnels that’s when the magic truly begins. Bedecked in twinkly lights, these merry passages wind beneath castle ruins and offer stalls stocked with gifts and goodies. There’s even a cave with life-size sand sculptures and 3-D holiday paintings. Above ground, pay a visit to Santa’s Village, a more traditional market filled with chalets serving up hot drinks and Christmas trinkets.

Sources indicate that where to Stay: Château St. Gerlach (10-minute drive).

Where to Stay: Amerikalinjen (10-minute walk).

Industry News: Redistricting battle could spill into 2028

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • The redistricting fights that underscored this year’s battle for the House could continue into the 2028 election cycle, although lessons from last Tuesday will likely shape those efforts.
  • House Republicans had hoped that new congressional maps in seven states would help them limit losses in the face of an unfavorable political environment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that maryland Gov. Wes Moore, here at the Capitol in January, wants to see his state's congressional map redrawn. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

The redistricting fights that underscored this year’s battle for the House could continue into the 2028 election cycle, although lessons from last Tuesday will likely shape those efforts.

House Republicans had hoped that new congressional maps in seven states would help them limit losses in the face of an unfavorable political environment. But nearly a week after the election, the GOP appeared on track to flip just three redrawn seats while losing a host of seats in Texas, Florida, North Carolina, Ohio and Alabama that were reconfigured in their favor.

“The question is whether the results have let some air out of the [redistricting] balloon or not,” mentioned Erik Nisbet, a professor at Northwestern University’s School of Communication.

Republicans may question the utility of redrawing more state maps in the 2028 cycle, while Democrats will need to weigh how to spend their political capital. But the newly introduced lines approved over the past year could still prove more favorable for Republicans in future elections.

“This was a wave election, and there’s no guarantee that the Democratic generic ballot would be D+13 — which is the reason why redistricting didn’t work for Republicans — in the next cycle,” Nisbet added.

It has been revealed that new maps appear possible, if not likely, in at least a few states. Maryland voters last week approved an amendment that would clear the way for new boundaries ahead of the 2028 elections. Democratic Gov. Wes Moore, who easily won a second term last week, mentioned he hopes to see a new map, citing the threat of President Donald Trump continuing to push for friendlier lines in GOP-led states. Maryland Democrats could draw a map that would favor them in all eight of the state’s House seats, including the Eastern Shore district of Rep. Andy Harris, the state’s lone Republican in Congress.

Advocates for a new map in Wisconsin got a boost last week when Democrats flipped both the state House and state Senate, setting up a Democratic trifecta. Gov.-elect David Crowley noted he would sign a bill redrawing the state’s congressional map if legislators sent one to his desk.

In a recent development, republicans in recent years have had a lopsided edge in the congressional delegation for Wisconsin, a perennial battleground state. But Democrats flipped two House seats last week, with Rebecca Cooke and Mitchell Berman unseating GOP Reps. Derrick Van Orden and Bryan Steil, respectively, bringing the state delegation to an even 4-4.

Democrats could also look to redraw the lines in Newly introduced York and Virginia. Earlier this year, voters in the commonwealth approved a new map that would have given Democrats up to four pickup opportunities, but the Virginia Supreme Court later struck it down on procedural grounds. Even without the new map, Democrats flipped two House seats in Virginia last week and came within 2 points of flipping a third.

Democrats in Upcoming York, meanwhile, took initial steps toward mid-decade redistricting earlier this year, but 2028 is the earliest they could hold elections under a new map.

On the Republican side, several states have been mentioned as candidates for newly introduced maps in 2028.

Officials in GOP-led Mississippi have held hearings this year on redistricting, which could target Democratic Rep. Bennie Thompson. Republicans are also aiming to redraw the state’s legislative lines ahead of next year’s off-year elections.

Sources indicate that it’s not clear whether states that were unsuccessful in redrawing their district lines for 2026 will try again when their legislatures convene next year. Republicans in both South Carolina and Indiana fell short in their push to pass new maps and could decide to revisit the problem. But Democrats flipped a House seat in each state last week, and some Republican incumbents won reelection by narrower margins than usual. Still, Republicans maintained their legislative majorities in both states, though Democrats broke their supermajorities in the South Carolina and Indiana state houses.

An analysis by DecisionDeskHQ offers a potential warning sign for Republicans in the Palmetto and Hoosier states: Under the GOP-drawn maps that were not adopted for 2026, Democrats could have flipped even more seats last week.

Redistricting appears off the table in a handful of states where fresh maps for 2028 had once been considered possible.

Georgia’s outgoing Republican governor, Brian Kemp, said last week that he would not call a special session to address redistricting before the end of the year, after Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms was elected to succeed him.

There were no House flips in the Peach State in the midterm elections, though several Republicans won by closer-than-anticipated margins.

In Latest Jersey, Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill told the New Jersey Globe that she also did not “see a path forward for redistricting right now.”.

Democrats flipped two House seats in the Garden State last week. Navy veteran Rebecca Bennett defeated Republican Rep. Thomas H. Kean Jr., while Cape May Mayor Zack Mullock scored a surprise win over GOP Rep. Jeff Van Drew.

With their new majorities in Washington, Democrats could propose legislation to ban partisan gerrymandering.

That’s something John Bisognano, the president of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, anticipates happening, but he said Democrat-led states should be prepared to respond to newly introduced maps drawn in Republican-controlled ones.

“If they are going to continue to take those actions, Democrats in states across the country need to be prepared to respond, and we, of course, now have significantly more opportunities than we did before Tuesday to respond to those states,” he said.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you've spent any time on food TikTok, you've probably come across Glace's famous S'mores Hot Chocolate. The Newly introduced York City dessert shop has become a social media sensation thanks to its ridiculously rich hot chocolate, complete with a thick ring of toasted marshmallow fluff around the cup and hefty scoop of whipped cream to top it off. And now you won't have to book a trip to Manhattan and stand in line just to try it.

It has been revealed that glace has officially introduced its first-ever at-home hot chocolate mix, giving fans across the country the opportunity to recreate its signature drink without leaving their kitchens. And given how popular the in-store sensation has become, I'm guessing plenty of people will add this easy-to-duplicate version to their holiday wish lists.

It has been revealed that founded by Sasha Zabar in 2023, Glace first opened on New York City's Upper East Side, where its over-the-top S'mores Hot Chocolate quickly became the star of the menu. The drink, which features rich drinking chocolate surrounded by a toasted marshmallow rim, has attracted plenty of attention online.

Since then, the brand has continued to dominate social media with other over-the-top menu items like its à la mode Warm Brownie Pudding Cake and Matcha Fudge Sundae, and has also expanded with a seasonal holiday truck at Rockefeller Center and Glace Candy, a neighboring shop specializing in gummies, chocolates, and other sweets.

But its newest launch means you don't have to live anywhere near New York to get a taste of at least one of its viral treats.

The new Signature Hot Chocolate Mix costs $19.99 and comes with six individual sachets, each containing the same hot chocolate recipe served at Glace's shops.

According to recent reports, according to the brand, the mix is made with ground chocolate and A2 milk powder, without the cornstarch or powdered fillers commonly used in conventional hot chocolate mixes. The result is designed to deliver the same rich, glossy consistency that made the drink famous.

Preparing it is pretty straightforward: Simply whisk the mix over medium-low heat on the stovetop until it transforms into a thick, decadent drinking chocolate. Sadly, the at-home version doesn’t come with the shop’s signature marshmallow rim...at least, not yet.

Industry observers note that glace indicates it's planning to release its signature marshmallow fluff separately, allowing customers to eventually recreate the full experience at home, toasted marshmallow rim and all. The brand hasn't revealed an official release date for the fluff, but we're keeping an eye out.

For now, the hot chocolate mix is available for pre-order on Glace's website, with shipments expected to begin in early December.

The GTA Files: My Long-Lost Interview With the Brothers Who Founded Rockstar

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2562 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “You can’t fuck with Keith Richards.” That’s what Sam Houser told me when I asked the inspiration for his company name, Rockstar Games.
  • It was October 2002, just a few weeks before the release of their latest blockbuster, Grand Theft Auto: Vice City.
  • I continued reporting on them and their games during the raucous and turbulent years to follow: hitting over $10 billion in sales, getting compared to Balzac and Dickens in Time magazine, being sued (unsuccessfully) for causing real-life violence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“You can’t fuck with Keith Richards.” That’s what Sam Houser told me when I asked the inspiration for his company name, Rockstar Games. “I’m a huge fan of the classic golden era of rock stars—both the music, but also the life,” he went on. “You can't argue with Keith Moon riding in a Rolls Royce with a blowup doll hanging out the back and a woman in there screaming, ‘I'm being raped.’ The guy is the original punk rocker. And if we can bring a fraction of that to games, then we’re doing something.”.

It was October 2002, just a few weeks before the release of their latest blockbuster, Grand Theft Auto: Vice City. I’d come to their glossy loft in Soho, Manhattan to interview the elusive 30-year-old Houser and Rockstar co-founders, his younger brother Dan Houser and managing director Terry Donovan, for Rolling Stone. It would be one of their first, last and only in-depth sit-downs together before they decided that the world’s most successful and controversial video game required little explanation from them at all.

I continued reporting on them and their games during the raucous and turbulent years to follow: hitting over $10 billion in sales, getting compared to Balzac and Dickens in Time magazine, being sued (unsuccessfully) for causing real-life violence. As I investigated in my book Jacked: The Outlaw Story of Grand Theft Auto, they also triggered what remains the most outrageous and cinematic scandal ever to hit the industry: the discovery of a hidden sex scene in 2005’s GTA San Andreas that would inspire attempts to legislate and ban the game. As Hilary Clinton mentioned at the time, “The disturbing material in Grand Theft Auto and other games like it is stealing the innocence of our children and it’s making the difficult job of being a parent even harder.”.

With the gamer generation now grown up and in power, the Reefer Madness panic around GTA has finally given way to something more important: this little game out of Scotland has become the most successful and influential entertainment product of all time. Today, Rockstar returns to Vice City with the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI. More than a decade in the making, with a budget Rockstar has never disclosed but analysts put between $1 billion and $2 billion, the game follows Jason Duval, an ex-soldier, and Lucia Caminos, who phones him from prison, as they’re pulled into a criminal conspiracy across a send-up of Miami. Its first trailer has been viewed more than 300 million times on YouTube, and footage premiering on Netflix nearly crashed the streamer’s servers. Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar’s parent manufacturer, expects record revenue of $8.1 billion this fiscal year.

It has been revealed that for longtime fans, GTA 6 marks something more personal: the first game in the franchise since the original band behind it broke up. Following the departure of Donovan and other central figures, Dan Houser exited Rockstar in 2020, leaving his substantial brother Sam as the last founder still there. With Sam remaining notoriously quiet about the newly introduced game, I went digging through my old tapes and found my long-lost interview with gaming’s original punk rockers. During our two-hour talk, the young co-founders were brash, unrepentant, and championing a lifetime of obsessions, as Sam put it. “I wasn’t just obsessed about games,” he told me, “we were obsessed about everything—obsessive about music, obsessive about film, obsessive about fashion.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The one thing that can make classic apple pie better? Caramel! That it’s laced with a generous dose of bourbon vaults it straight into hall-of-fame territory. Made using a double batch of our never-fail Perfect Pie Crust, this pretty lattice-topped pie is a crowd-pleaser, familiar enough to appeal to the traditionalists with just enough of a surprise from the booze and the smoky burnt sugar to make the thrill-seekers come back for more. Like all good things, apple pie can’t be rushed. It needs time to chill, bake, and rest—so proposal ahead, especially if it’s for Thanksgiving.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

2 hours 15 minutes (plus 7 hours for chilling and cooling).

According to recent reports, whisk 3⅓ cups (417 g) all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 4 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces; rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 1¼ cups (2½ sticks) chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Recent findings suggest that make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ½ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Recent findings suggest that turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour; dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Divide dough in half and pat each piece into a ½"-thick disk. Wrap each disk tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Industry observers note that do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap each disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Recent findings suggest that place 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar and ½ cup water in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot and cover. Bring to a boil over medium heat (no need to stir); cook until sugar is dissolved, 4–7 minutes total. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring or swirling pot occasionally, until caramel turns a deep golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

According to recent reports, add zest of 1 lemon, 3 lb. Honeycrisp apples (about 6 large), peeled, cored, quartered, thinly sliced crosswise, ½ cup bourbon, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. ground cinnamon to caramel (it may become stiff). Cover and cook, stirring occasionally, until caramel dissolves and apples have released a generous amount of liquid and are tender but still retain their shape (they should look mostly translucent), 15–18 minutes.

Stir ⅓ cup heavy cream, 3 Tbsp. cornstarch, and 2 Tbsp. cool water in a small bowl until cornstarch is dissolved. Pour into apple mixture and cook (it should be bubbling), stirring often, until mixture is thick, about 5 minutes. Transfer filling to a large bowl; let cool. Cover and chill until cold, at least 45 minutes.

Meanwhile, let dough sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Unwrap 1 disk and roll out on a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1" overhang. Chill 15 minutes.

Unwrap remaining disk; roll out on surface lightly dusted with more rice flour to a 18x12" rectangle, about ⅛" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and transfer to a large parchment-lined baking sheet. Brush dough with a thin film of cold water; sprinkle remaining ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar over and press gently with your hands to cover dough completely in an even layer (coating dough before cutting into strips will give you the most even coverage). Chill 15 minutes.

Industry observers note that place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Spoon chilled filling into pie pan and smooth surface to level. Using a ruler, cut dough rectangle into 1"-wide strips. Lay 5–8 strips over filling, spacing evenly across surface to cover. Weave another 5–8 strips over, then under, alternating to create a lattice crust (you may not use all of the strips). Trim overhang to match bottom crust. Press edges of top and bottom crusts firmly together to seal, then trim again, leaving about ¼" overhang. Fold overhang up and over lattice so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers.

Sources indicate that place pan on a rimmed baking sheet (to catch drips) and bake pie until crust is set and golden, 45–50 minutes. Reduce oven temperature to 350°; continue to bake until crust is deep golden brown and filling is bubbling up through lattice, 40–50 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let pie cool in pan at least 4 hours before serving.

According to recent reports, do Ahead: Filling can be made 2 days ahead; keep chilled. Pie can be baked 1 day ahead; store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wendy’s is getting nostalgic this holiday season, and as someone who grew up eating in one of the chain’s iconic glass sunrooms, I’m particularly excited about this one.

The fast food chain just launched a limited-time Holiday Box complete with retro packaging, collectible knit hats, and a choice of some familiar menu favorites. And of course, two upcoming peppermint-inspired Frosty desserts.

Obviously, I had to try everything for myself.

Available beginning November 16 at participating Wendy’s locations nationwide, the Holiday Box starts at $11.99 and includes your choice of a Dave’s Double or 10-piece crispy or spicy chicken nuggets, small fries, a small soft drink, and one collectible knit hat.

The packaging is designed to resemble Wendy’s old-school Solarium restaurants, complete with the recognizable glass-walled dining area that became a staple of the chain beginning in the 1980s.

And I have to admit, this one hit me right in the childhood memories.

According to recent reports, growing up, I remember going to Wendy’s with my mom and sitting in that yellow, glass-enclosed sunroom. Seeing the design recreated as a miniature holiday box immediately brought me back to those visits.

Each Holiday Box includes one of four collectible knit hats featuring a retro Wendy’s design: Frosty, Biggie, the classic Wendy’s logo, or the famous “Where’s the Beef?” slogan.

The hats come in sealed mystery bags, meaning you won’t know which one you’re getting until you open it.

Thankfully, I ended up with the blue Frosty beanie, which was exactly the design I was hoping for.

Had I opened the bag to find a hat with “Biggie” written across my forehead, though, I think we would’ve had a problem.

The Holiday Box is available for a limited time while supplies last, and customers can’t select which hat they receive.

Alongside the Holiday Box, Wendy’s is introducing two limited-time desserts: the Peppermint Frosty Swirl and Peppermint Brownie Frosty Fusion.

Both are available with either a vanilla or chocolate Frosty base, so I decided to try one of each.

This was easily my favorite of the two.

The Peppermint Brownie Frosty Fusion combines Wendy’s classic Frosty with peppermint sauce and brownie pieces, creating a dessert that feels especially appropriate for the holiday season.

I went with the vanilla base, and I absolutely loved it.

Sources indicate that the peppermint flavor was strong and immediately reminded me of a candy cane or a York Peppermint Pattie. It had that recognizable minty sweetness I look for in a holiday dessert, without getting lost in the vanilla Frosty.

It has been revealed that the brownie pieces were another highlight, adding a nice texture and a layer of chocolate flavor to the mix. I particularly liked how the chocolate complemented the peppermint rather than competing with it.

For me, this is exactly what a seasonal Frosty should taste like. It’s festive, flavorful, and different enough from the regular menu to make it worth trying.

For my second dessert, I went with the chocolate Peppermint Frosty Swirl, which combines Wendy’s classic Chocolate Frosty with peppermint sauce.

My biggest piece of advice is to give this one a good stir before digging in.

When I first tried it, most of the peppermint syrup was concentrated toward the top of the dessert. Mixing everything together helped distribute the flavor more evenly throughout the Frosty.

Once I did that, I really enjoyed it.

The combination of chocolate and peppermint works well, although I didn’t find the mint flavor nearly as strong as it was in the vanilla Brownie Frosty Fusion.

According to recent reports, still, I’m happy to report that Wendy’s peppermint sauce works with both Frosty flavors. If you prefer a more straightforward chocolate-mint combination without brownie pieces, this is a solid option.

Personally, though, I’d go back for the Fusion.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • If it feels like no one’s talked about Movember for a while, that’s because the non-profit charity’s heyday online peaked in 2012.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani passed out water bottles to marathoners on Nov. 1, few clocked the newly mustachioned man as the city’s head honcho. After all, he’s the first bearded NYC mayor in over a century after, and his constituents had grown familiar with his signature look. When images of his new facial hair circulated, people wondered what inspired the change. Had the mayor been influenced by his hip Brooklyn constituents enough to grow his own on-trend mustache? As we learned the day after the marathon in an online video, the mustache was in support of a somewhat-ancient tradition: Movember.

If it feels like no one’s talked about Movember for a while, that’s because the non-profit charity’s heyday online peaked in 2012. That year, according to the Australian-based foundation, over 1.1 million people participated in Movember—a campaign that encourages men to grow mustaches to raise awareness and funds for men’s mental health, prostate cancer, and testicular cancer—collecting more than $126 million in charity. But like planking, “Gangnam Style,” and flash mobs, Movember eventually faded from the cultural conversation. Google Trends recorded a 10% drop in searches for the cause the following year, and by 2026, search interest had fallen 90% from its 2012 peak. Now, after Mamdani, alongside Council Member Rita Joseph, announced a $4 million investment in a new prostate cancer center at Brooklyn’s Kings County Hospital in honor of the hairy month-long social movement, interest in Movember has since climbed to its highest level since 2019, according to Google Trends.

While the mayor’s stubble has come and gone throughout the month, the heavy mustache has remained constant.

According to recent reports, the stubble around the mustache has come and gone during the month, but that thick mustache has remained a staple. He had it at a Veterans Day reception, during a plethora of press conferences, and when he announced the disbanding of the Newly introduced York Police Department’s controversial Strategic Response Group.

Politicians have long been defined, at least in part, by their hair: Donald Trump’s comb-over, Bernie Sanders’ horseshoe-shaped hairline, Gavin Newsom’s slicked-back locks. But facial hair is increasingly becoming part of the political image, too, as more men embrace letting their beards grow. Pete Buttigieg, once clean-shaven, grew a beard after leaving his post as Transportation Secretary; JD Vance became the first bearded vice president in decades; and Mamdani ended more than a century’s worth of clean-shaven NYC mayors.

And hey, what better time to revive an early 2010s tradition than following the Democrats’ historic victories in the midterm elections. Millennial woke optimism is back, baby, and so is growing facial hair for a charitable cause. If the mayor’s facial hair can turn a bygone internet fad into renewed attention for men’s health, it may be his most consequential grooming decision yet.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When you book something through our retail links, we may earn an affiliate commission.

In a recent development, there are two sorts of Parisian holidays. The first, an exercise in blissful escapism, where luxury hotels, gallery hopping, and lazy apéros à la terrasse all help you lean into the romantic undercurrent of the city. The second, an exercise in make-believe: You would not be the first person to plot a move to Paris halfway through your stay there, earmarking local boulangeries and wine shops as favorites and spending mornings chit-chatting with market vendors. If you lean toward the latter experience, this is where the best Airbnbs in Paris enter the picture. After all, what better way to cosplay a Parisienne than via a cozy flat of your own (albeit a temporary one)?

According to recent reports, our edit is an evolving one—there’s no shortage of stately Haussmann buildings available for rent—grouped by arrondissement. (There are 20 total, and while we haven’t hit on all of them, the below list includes several of the most popular for visitors.) Each spot has its own distinct flair, depending on what sort of Parisian you wish to embody. The chichi traveler with high-brow tastes will love the classic charm of the Left Bank; the arty fashion-lover will prefer the cozy studios of the Marais (as well as its proximity to some of the best vintage shops); the low-key bohemian will find respite in the hills of Montmarte, above the city’s lights. Grand architecture and bistro balconies, you’ll be glad to discover, have no loyalty to any particular arrondissement. They’re all good; you really can’t go wrong.

For anyone planning a trip to the City of Light, consider the roundup of properties ahead for a true immersive experience in one of the most stylish cities on the planet.

According to recent reports, for a grand apartment right in the middle of the historical center, book this ornate Airbnb. Travelers looking to see all the sights will appreciate its proximity to the Palais Royal, Centre Pompidou, and the Louvre; it’s also around the corner from the Les Halles shopping center, where you’ll find both great restaurants (Le Petit Bouillon Pharamond is a nice option for an affordable lunch and gorgeous interiors) and little shops (E. Dehillerin, Julia Child’s much-frequented kitchenware store, is a must). The home itself is no less impressive—high ceilings with crown molding, antique gilded mirrors, and parquet floors run throughout.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathrooms; sleeps 4.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer, indoor fireplace, long-term stays allowed, elevator.

In a recent development, exposed beams and parquet flooring set the scene for this typically charming Parisian apartment. There’s lots of space for making yourself right at home, including a stunning balcony that sits atop Rue de Rivoli so you’ll feel like you’re right in the middle of everything as you sip your morning espresso while mapping out the day’s itinerary. Then there’s the location: If it’s your first time visiting Paris, the fact that the Louvre museum, the Centre Pompidou, and the Seine are all within walking distance will be a massive bonus. Leave the complicated commutes for your sophomore outing; this home lets you walk everywhere.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 2.5 bathrooms; sleeps 4.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, blackout shades, Devialet Bluetooth sound system, television, air conditioning, kitchen, dishwasher, espresso machine, balcony, housekeeping available at a cost.

Best for: First-timers to the city.

Sources indicate that this sun-drenched two-bedroom near the Seine opens with a grand, golden-colored lobby, complete with a spiral staircase and tile floors. Upstairs, the duplex has lots of space to stretch out, from a dining table that doubles as a workspace to a bright living room to a small balcony. You’ll have both the fifth and sixth floors—but as there’s no elevator, prepare to get your cardio in. It’s in a fun area, too; Pizzeria Popolare, a great Italian restaurant, is just down the street, and you’re within easy exploring distance of all the boutiques and galleries the Marais has to offer.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathroom; sleeps 4.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, Bluetooth sound system, television, balcony, pets allowed.

Best for: A small group of friends—who still want their own space.

We’d book this Airbnb for the tiles alone. From the rainbow-colored bathtub to the celery green kitchen to the traditional tomettes that run throughout, it’s an effortlessly charming spot, located on the third floor of an 18th-century building. The enviable design continues from the baby blue bedroom to the painted furniture; it’ll be more than obvious that you’re staying in one of the more creative, artistic quartiers of the city. (And if you want to get some of your own work done, the dedicated office area is happy to oblige.) While it’s in a bustling neighborhood, the apartment itself is at the back of the property, so you’ll have quiet when you need it.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathrooms; sleeps 3.

Amenities: Bathtub, elevator, coffee maker, building staff.

In a recent development, if you picked the Marais because of its art scene, you might as well commit to the experience and book an Airbnb directly overlooking the Picasso Museum. Sought-after location aside, this duplex feels welcoming from the moment you step in the door. Hexagonal terracotta tiles line the floor, a large dining table is the perfect spot for a cozy night in, and every nook and cranny is filled with glass vases and art. When you want to head out for dinner, you’re spoilt for choice—but start with Chez Nenesse, a classic, red-and-white checkered tablecloth bistrot, that’s just four minutes away.

Rooms: 1 bedroom, 1 bathroom; sleeps 2.

Amenities: Kitchen, washer, Bose sound system, indoor fireplace, coffee maker.

The first thing this Airbnb has going for it is its location: It’s situated right on the Île Saint-Louis, one of the city’s two islands, and therefore has a more quaint feel to it than some of the busier arrondissements. (Plus you’re just five minutes from Berthillon, the best ice cream in the area.) The second thing, of course, is its style. The building itself is listed as a historic monument dating back to the 17th century, and interior highlights like a painted ceiling and gilded mirror amplify the antique appeal. Even the piano area, a tiny nook off one of the bedrooms, has a blue marble floor and matching tile mural—it’s all extremely decadent.

Rooms: 3 bedrooms, 2 bathrooms; sleeps 6.

Amenities: Washer/dryer, piano, indoor fireplace, parking, hot tub.

Recent findings suggest that we found your Parisian tree house. Tucked away near the busy Place des Vosges, the fourth-floor apartment is a calm respite, well-sized for a couple or solo traveler in search of more unique accommodation. Here, rustic wood beams accent nearly every ceiling and wall, textured brick flooring adds warmth, and a large, tiled tub looks out onto Haussmannian rooftops for a truly cozy stay. It even has two balconies—sure, they may be tiny, but the sweeping views of the city’s architecture more than makes up for their size.

Rooms: 1 bedroom, 1 bathroom; sleeps 3.

Amenities: Washer, television, piano, balcony, bathtub.

Best for: Those looking for a non-traditional vacation rental.

Recent findings suggest that A bedroom adorned in pink toile de Jouy print, a working fireplace in the living room, a dining room that’s overflowing with plants and dressed up with a gilded mirror: this apartment, to borrow some first-level French, is très chic. It’s deceptively spacious—thanks to a sofa bed, it can actually sleep up to six people—making it ideal for a girls’ trip to the city. With a spacious living area and a well-equipped kitchen, it’s certainly designed to handle a larger group. A nice bonus? You’re within walking distance of the beloved bookstore Shakespeare and Company for a souvenir you can employ on the long flight home.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathroom; sleeps 6.

Amenities: Kitchen, TV, fireplace, washer/dryer, bathtub.

Steps away from the bustling Odéon neighborhood and landmarks like the Pantheon and the Luxembourg Garden, this apartment is ideally situated for first-timers to the city of lights. With original 1930s features preserved and played up, it's also well-decorated: Art Deco details, like geometric borders, curved ceiling cut-outs, and arched doorways pop up throughout. (The turquoise bathtub nook is a particular highlight; the glass wall in the dining room is another.) This rental has tons of space for a family as well as several kid-friendly amenities available upon request; book it for a longer stay in the city.

Rooms: 3 bedrooms, 2 bathrooms; sleeps 6.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, piano, Bluetooth sound system, exercise equipment, television, high chair, board games, elevator, parking, pets allowed.

Location: By the Pantheon and the Luxembourg Garden.

Best for: Art Deco aficionados.

Sources indicate that this literary, light-filled Airbnb is located in a building that houses several artists studios—notes of which can be found everywhere from the airy, industrial-style layout to the perfectly imperfect collection of decor to the multi-colored tiles in the kitchen. (As for the literary tie-in: Bookworms will appreciate the massive wall of books in the upstairs bedroom. Take your pick.) The home is mere blocks away from the Jardin du Luxembourg, in Montparnasse. Browse the aforementioned bookshelf and grab a paperback, pick up a coffee from one of the many cafés in the area, and take a morning to yourself in the gardens.

Rooms: 1 bedroom, 1 bathroom; sleeps 4.

Amenities: Kitchen, washer/dryer, TV, crib, courtyard.

Location: Near Jardin du Luxembourg.

Best for: Avid readers always looking for a upcoming, picturesque spot to get lost in a book.

For the solo traveler who never wants to be too far from the sparkling lights of the Eiffel Tower, this little studio is a cozy cocoon just six minutes away. (Starting quite literally with the bed, which is cordoned off from the rest of the space by a chic glass wall and a gauzey curtain.) A tiny kitchenette stocked with all the essential appliances lets you make the most of local treats—helpful, as the famous Rue Cler street market is just around the corner, so you can stock up on cheeses, quiche, and even rotisserie chickens for quiet meals at home.

Rooms: 1 bedroom, 1 bathroom; sleeps 3.

Amenities: Washer, elevator, pet-friendly, housekeeping available at a fee.

Location: On Rue Amélie, a quick walk to the Eiffel Tower.

Best for: Foodies traveling alone.

Sources indicate that it’ll be hard to beat this central location: This sunny, spacious two-bedroom is situated directly at the base of the Champ de Mars, the grassy park that houses the Eiffel Tower. It’s as stately as its zip code implies—think, period-appropriate wall moldings that reflect its 19th-century origins and oversized windows, with the occasional unexpected pop of color (like a yellow window in the kitchen and pistachio dining chairs) to keep it from feeling stuffy. It also comes with an espresso machine, so if you ever tire of your local boulangerie—unlikely—you can start the day with coffee at home.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathrooms; sleeps 3.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer, elevator.

Location: At the foot of the Eiffel Tower.

Best for: Ticking the Eiffel Tower off your bucket list.

It’s conveniently located in the heart of Paris and stocked with modern creature comforts like a Nespresso machine and a Netflix-enabled television, but you really only need one reason to book this apartment: the massive terrace. Equipped with outdoor dining and seating, it’s a rare thing to find in the busy city (and, should you ever want a little quiet, an ideal spot to enjoy an apéro at home). Though it only has one proper bedroom, it can actually sleep four thanks to a sofa bed in the living room. For families looking for a comfortable spot near all the top sights, this is a great option.

Rooms: 1 bedroom, 1 bathroom; sleeps 4.

Amenities: Washer, blackout shades, HDTV, Bose sound system, exercise equipment, travel crib, kitchen, Nespresso coffee maker, dishwasher, terrace, paid parking available.

Location: In the Champs-Elysées area.

Best for: Travelers for whom a terrace with a view is a non-negotiable.

It has been revealed that staying in this palatial sixth-floor penthouse will feel like time travel—it sits within a historic Haussmann building and offers original details like 18th-century wood floors, hand-painted wallpaper, antique fireplaces, and a Napoleon-style oval room. It’s bourgeois luxury in every sense. The entire space enjoys plenty of light thanks to French windows opening onto three balconies, and amenities like a full kitchen and entry hall with a piano will make it difficult to venture outside (though you’ll want to—it’s in close proximity to some of Paris’s most coveted attractions like the Louvre, Opera Garnier, Champs Élysées).

Rooms: 4 bedrooms, 2 bathrooms; sleeps 8.

Amenities: Washer/dryer, piano, kitchen, elevator, balcony, antique fireplaces.

Location: In the Champs Elysées district.

Best for: Anyone who knows what a “Napoleon-style oval room” is (interior design buffs, this one’s for you).

On the fifth floor of a traditional Haussmann building (there is an elevator, don’t worry) sits this elegant sunny spot. A long balcony stretches outside and includes a small bistro set for breakfasts outside—though the spacious dining room is also an enticing option. From the red-and-cream checkerboard kitchen to the ornate crown molding in the living area, it’s endlessly charming. Montmartre is only 15 minutes away; perhaps more importantly, depending on what your itinerary priorities are, the famous bakery Mamiche is an even-shorter 10 minute walk. (The brioche and the ham sandwich alone are good reasons to make a daily pilgrimage there each morning.).

Rooms: 4 bedrooms, 2 bathrooms; sleeps 5.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer, sound system, board games, fire place, balcony, elevator.

Best for: Design inspiration and proximity to an incredible bakery.

Originally belonging to the painter Georges Braque back in 1911, this sweet studio has since been re-done and can now fit up to four guests (the sofa converts to a bed, if you don’t mind a slightly crowded living space). The renovation didn’t strip it of its character, though, and between the primary-colored kitchen storage cubbies and the floor-to-ceiling windows that let the light stream in, it’s one of the more unique apartment rentals in Paris. The bay windows look out onto a courtyard, so you’ll have plenty of peace despite being located in one of the city’s most bustling areas for nightlife.

Rooms: 1 bedroom, 1 bathroom; sleeps 4.

Amenities: Washer/dryer, kitchen, shared backyard, coffee maker, crib/travel crib/children’s books available upon request, balcony.

Location: In the Pigalle neighborhood.

Best for: Those hoping to experience the city’s artistic spirit beyond a visit to the Louvre.

In a recent development, right below Pigalle on Rue Cadet, this quiet one-bedroom is surrounded by bakeries, cheese shops, and greengrocers. Everything you’d need is within walking distance; head to Racines, a hole-in-the-wall Italian spot with a decadent tiramisù, for a date night in the neighborhood. Inside, a fully equipped kitchen and multiple workspaces ensure you have all the essentials to stretch out and make this temporary spot feel like home. With sloping ceilings and views onto the city’s greyscale rooftops, it feels like the coziest attic—peaceful, personal, and chic enough to make you want to stay awhile.

Rooms: 1 bedroom, 1 bathroom; sleeps 2.

Amenities: Washer, kitchen, dishwasher, coffee maker.

Location: In the Grand Boulevards area.

Best for: A cozy couples getaway.

In a recent development, if you can’t pick between the trendy 10th or 3rd arrondissements—don’t. This bright and airy one-bedroom is smack in the middle, in an ideal area full of hole-in-the-wall eateries and stylish spots to grab an apéro before a late dinner. Since it’s owned and designed by an architect, its interiors are especially appealing: The blend of vintage furniture and flourishing greenery might just inspire you to redecorate when you get home. In the meantime, you’ll feel right at home. The kitchen is significant enough to whip up meals of your own, if you feel inspired—or at least, a quick breakfast before heading out for the day.

Rooms: 1 bedroom, 1.5 bathrooms; sleeps 2.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer, blackout shades, HDTV, Apple sound system, piano, kitchen, dishwasher, Nespresso coffee maker.

Location: Right on the border of the 10th and the 3rd arrondissements.

Best for: Bookmarking design inspiration.

Sources indicate that overlooking the rooftops of Paris, this small but well-appointed apartment (yes, it has an elevator) is perfect for a couple. From a zellige-tiled kitchen to a teeny balcony where you can sip a cocktail during golden hour, you’ll find everything you need for a short stint in the city. But the best part is, hands down, its location: The home is right by the Canal. Here, you’ll find a livelier, younger scene, with natural wine bars, trendy restaurants, and an atmosphere that feels decidedly removed from the touristy center. (Early June, a local-favorite restaurant and wine bar with a rotating cast of guest chefs, is a leisurely 15-minute walk away.).

Rooms: 1 bedroom, 1 bathroom; sleeps 2.

Amenities: Washer, balcony, kitchen.

Location: Near the Canal St. Martin.

Best for: Proximity to your latest favorite wine bar.

For a vacation rental that feels designed by someone’s French grandma, choose this colorful, eclectic spot and make yourself at home. The kitchen, with its checkerboard-covered table, citron walls, and collected jumble of various tools and trinkets, is undoubtedly the center; but the bedrooms (there are three), with their massive windows and original terracotta floors are also nice—especially if you’re traveling with a big group, and want to make sure you each have enough space. When you do want to dine out, you’ll be well-positioned: Bistrot des Tournelles and Chez Paul, two wonderful traditional bistros, are located in this neighborhood.

Rooms: 3 bedrooms, 2 bathrooms; sleeps 5.

Best for: Cosplaying Julia Child for the weekend.

Not all Parisian Airbnbs involve ornate crown moldings and baroque antiques; some, like this loft, can lean quite industrial. Iron beams and high ceilings make it seem even more spacious (the space itself is located in an old printing house); glass windows overlook an internal courtyard, if you need a quiet temporary home. Sandwiched between République and Canal St. Martin, it’s in a fun, more local part of the city. If it’s warm enough, walk along the water in the afternoon before ducking into Chambre Noir, a little wine bar near the apartment, for small plates and a crisp glass of white.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathroom; sleeps 4.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, TV, air conditioning, pet-friendly.

Best for: Fans of industrial architecture.

In a recent development, this two-bedroom apartment may just house the best balcony in all of Paris. It’s well-furnished, with plenty of potted plants and a bistro set for taking your breakfast outside, weather-permitting, but the views of the Haussmann buildings and Eiffel Tower in the distance are what makes it really special. Inside, the design is cozy, with floral quilts and Art Deco-inspired lighting casting everything in a warm glow. Even the entrance to the apartment is special. While the fifth floor rental is accessible by elevator, you may just find yourself choosing to take the stairs, which are lined with stained glass windows.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathrooms; sleeps 4.

Amenities: Washer/dryer, Sonos Bluetooth sound system, indoor fireplace, air conditioning, coffee maker, balcony, outdoor furniture, elevator.

Best for: Morning coffee on the balcony.

Sources indicate that perched in the heart of Montmartre in the hilly, cobblestone-lined streets of the Abbesses neighborhood, this one-bedroom home is ideal for the couple who likes their decor collected, full of personality, and a tiny bit mismatched. Starting with the mix of antique furnishings in the living room (including a red velvet armchair) and going right through to the lemon-yellow bedroom, the design of this place will make you feel like you’re visiting your artistic Parisian friend—no cold, white-box rooms here. When you do want to hit the tourist spots, the Basilica of Sacré Coeur is just a 15-minute walk away.

Rooms: 1 bedroom, 1 bathroom; sleeps 2.

Best for: The eclectic traveler coming to Paris to peruse the flea markets.

Sources indicate that you’re alone in Paris, and you need an inspiring studio from which to focus on your creative project (or just finish your book in peace): This artist’s loft is it. Tall ceilings and an oversized window create a light-filled environment, while a dedicated workspace offers a quiet place to concentrate. There’s a small but well-appointed kitchen so you can cook your meals at home and truly feel at ease during your stay, however long it may be.

Rooms: 1 bedroom, 1 bathroom; sleeps 4.

Amenities: Washer, crib, coffee maker, shared backyard.

Best for: Anyone coming to Paris to get out of a creative rut.

Recent findings suggest that from the terracotta tomettes to the oversized windows, this sunny one-bedroom is perfect for the solo traveler or a couple. The building dates back to the 19th century, but the decor is firmly 21st: Butter yellow bedding and a mustard-striped kitchen skirt are design ideas to bookmark for when you get home. And you can’t trump the location: It’s right in the heart of Montmartre, only a few blocks away from Boulangerie Raphaëlle (one of the all-time best bakeries in the city—trust us).

Rooms: 1 bedroom, 1 bathroom; sleeps 2.

Amenities: Travel crib available upon request, coffee maker.

Best for: An extended solo trip.

According to recent reports, jeans and ballerinas are the unofficial uniform of the city (and, conveniently, make a comfortable ensemble for a day of shopping). Bring an extra-large tote as your personal item on the plane so you have plenty of space to shuttle back all your souvenirs… including some French pharmacy goodies, of course.

After combing through hundreds of listings in a destination’s most desirable neighborhoods, we narrow down our list by reviewing a variety of determining factors, from the logistics of price, location, and amenities, to notable details such as reviews and host information. From there, we take into consideration aesthetic details such as design, natural light, and overall look and feel of the home. The final edit is a well-rounded list that ensures booking a stay will result in a safe and stylish holiday.

Massie moves to force Hegseth impeachment vote

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1284 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thomas Massie, R-Ky., conducts a news conference outside the Capitol on Monday.
  • Thomas Massie, R-Ky., took to the House floor Monday to unveil a resolution that would impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and a vote on the issue could occur by Wednesday.
  • A draft resolution that Massie read aloud on the House floor on Monday accused Hegseth of eight violations of law or the Constitution, including that he violated the 1973 War Powers Resolution in his prosecution of the Iran war and acted illegally in military campaigns in Venezuela, Yemen, the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., conducts a news conference outside the Capitol on Monday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

In a recent development, rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., took to the House floor Monday to unveil a resolution that would impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and a vote on the issue could occur by Wednesday.

A draft resolution that Massie read aloud on the House floor on Monday accused Hegseth of eight violations of law or the Constitution, including that he violated the 1973 War Powers Resolution in his prosecution of the Iran war and acted illegally in military campaigns in Venezuela, Yemen, the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean.

It has been revealed that massie's resolution also charges Hegseth with disregarding protection of civilians in wartime and suppressing the free speech of a U.S. senator.

Massie confirmed his intention to file the resolution as a matter of the privileges of the House.

In a recent development, speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., will now have to rule as to whether the resolution constitutes a proper question of the privileges of the House. There is precedent from prior instances when impeachment was found to be valid as it relates to the House’s constitutionally granted powers.

He must schedule a vote to occur within two legislative days. Assuming that the speaker rules that Massie's resolution is privileged, the House could vote on the resolution itself, or on a motion to table it or refer it to committee.

If the House were to impeach Hegseth under this process, it would mark a historical anomaly. According to the Congressional Research Service, recent attempts to impeach an official as a matter of the privileges of the House have not resulted in approval of the resolution. In cases in which an official has been impeached, the House has nearly always chosen to conduct an investigation first.

Recent findings suggest that in an interview on Oct. 26, Massie put the chances of his resolution being adopted at 50-50.

In comments to reporters outside the Capitol after his floor remarks, Massie said he suspected some Republicans may back his resolution but he indicated he has neither asked for nor received any such assurances from any of them.

It has been revealed that he predicted there could be some GOP support in the Senate if Hegseth is impeached and it goes to trial. He noted that if the trial does not start until 2027, any Republicans who might vote to convict Hegseth would presumably be joined by most if not all of a more sizeable Senate Democratic caucus.

It has been revealed that massie's odds of success for his resolution may now be greater than his previous 50-50 prediction given the results of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, which gave Democrats control over both chambers in the next Congress — a vote motivated largely by opposition to the Iran war and its inflationary impact.

The questions now are, first, how many House Republicans will defy President Donald Trump and vote to impeach Hegseth; and, secondly, how many incumbents who lost their reelection bids on Nov. 3, a cohort that is disproportionately Republican, might be absent for the impeachment vote?

Massie stated some Republicans who lost their reelection bids may feel freer to vote to impeach Hegseth. And he also said Republicans who were reelected and will have to face voters in 2028 may also think about how their vote on an impeachment resolution would reverberate politically.

According to recent reports, "It's going to be everybody's conscience, and then they'll have to live with that vote," Massie said. "And they're going to have to live with that vote two years from now if they're not part of the retirement caucus. And if they were part of the retirement caucus, what do they have to lose?".

Asked why he did not bring articles of impeachment against President Donald Trump, Massie noted: "I think the president needs to see one of — this is a metaphor — one of his horses shot out from under him, and then maybe he'll he will see things differently.".

If the House does vote on Massie’s resolution, Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is expected to become the House speaker in the next Congress, noted on ABC’s “This Week” on Sunday that he would be a “hard yes” on it.

Hegseth has “got to go,” Jeffries said. “The so-called secretary of Defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe.”.

Most if not all House Democrats are expected to agree.

Last week, Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., the ranking member of the Armed Services Committee and its likely chairman in the next Congress, indicated in an interview with The Latest Republic that he would support Massie’s impeachment resolution, and he predicted it would be adopted.

It has been revealed that referring to Massie’s measure, Smith said, “By every estimation, it will pass and he will be impeached. And off that goes to the Senate. Then the Senate is legally required to spend all of their time dealing with that until it’s done with.”.

Industry observers note that "Every second Pete Hegseth remains at the top of the Pentagon, our servicemembers are at risk," Rep. Jason Crow, D-Colo., a senior member of the Armed Services Committee, remarked in a post on X on Sunday.

In a recent development, also on Monday, Everett B. Kelley, the national president of the American Federation of Government Employees, a union that represents some 820,000 federal and D.C. government employees, sent a letter to House members urging a “yes” vote on Massie's Hegseth impeachment resolution.

The letter cited the risks Kelley stated the Iran war has posed to the lives of the Defense Department's uniformed and civilian personnel, and the missive noted Hegseth's stripping of workplace rights and protections for the department's civilians.

"By adopting Rep. Massie’s resolution, the House can begin the long overdue bipartisan effort to reclaim its constitutional powers and authority, restore checks and balances, and take responsibility for the lives of military personnel and civilian employees that Mr. Hegseth’s capricious leadership has jeopardized," Kelley wrote.

Recent findings suggest that massie announced in mid-September his intention to file an impeachment resolution against Hegseth. But Johnson adjourned the House before the vote would have occurred.

Massie’s latest resolution is substantially the same as his earlier one, with the same eight articles of impeachment.

The first three of these alleges that Hegseth’s conduct of the Iran war violated the War Powers Resolution.

Massie's measure says Hegseth prosecuted the Iran war without congressional authorization and in the absence of an attack on the United States or an imminent threat.

Recent findings suggest that further, the measure alleges that Hegseth continued the war despite the House and Senate adopting in June a concurrent war powers resolution calling for the withdrawal of U.S. forces from the fight.

And, the resolution indicates, Hegseth continued the Iran war after the expiration of the War Powers Resolution’s 60-day termination period and any potential 30-day withdrawal period.

In a recent development, the House has only voted twice to impeach a member of the Cabinet. In 1876, Secretary of War William Belknap was impeached over allegations of corruption, and his abrupt resignation likely contributed to his acquittal in the Senate.

In 2024, the House voted 214-213 to impeach Alejandro Mayorkas, then-secretary of Homeland Security, for “willful and systemic refusal to comply with the law” and “breach of public trust.” The Senate dispensed with the charges without a trial.
