#66100. Why You Should Never Put Frozen Meat In A Slow Cooker, According To Experts

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (782 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Delish ↗ Open Full Page

Why You Should Never Put Frozen Meat In A Slow Cooker, According To Experts

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (782 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Delish

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that with busy schedules and limited time each day, slow cookers are key to getting dinner on the table.
  • Sources indicate that but think again.
  • Sources indicate that sorry to be the bearer of bad news: You should never put frozen meat directly into your slow cooker.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that with busy schedules and limited time each day, slow cookers are key to getting dinner on the table. They can take simple ingredients and transform them into a complete, ready-to-eat meal. Because the slow cooker does all the work for you, you may think that it can also handle defrosting meat.

Sources indicate that but think again. The idea seems convenient in theory, but in practice, it raises some serious food safety concerns. We consulted health experts to learn more about adding frozen meat to a slow cooker. So next time you strategy a hands-off dinner, you can make sure your food is delicious and safe to eat.

Sources indicate that sorry to be the bearer of bad news: You should never put frozen meat directly into your slow cooker. “I am all for cutting out unnecessary steps in cooking, but using frozen meat in your slow cooker is not one of them,” says Melissa Koch, RD, MEd.

Raw meat can carry harmful bacteria that cause foodborne illness. Freezing stops them from multiplying, but doesn't necessarily kill them. And because slow cookers heat food gradually, frozen meat can spend too long in what food safety experts call the “temperature danger zone.”.

Sources indicate that “The danger zone refers to a temperature range of 40°F (4°C) to 140°F (60°C) over two or more hours when harmful bacteria grow or multiply at a fast rate,” Koch explains. It can take hours for food in a slow cooker to move above the danger zone—and starting with frozen meat delays that process even further.

It has been revealed that “The appliance heats food slowly, and starting with frozen meat means the internal temperature may sit in the ‘danger zone’ for too long,” says chef and dietitian Sharniquia White. “This gives bacteria like Salmonella or E. coli more opportunity to multiply before the food reaches a safe cooking temperature.”.

What happens after eating food that has sat in the danger zone? The consequences vary based on your immune system, the extent of the contamination, and the strains of bacteria present. But none are pleasant, and some may even send you to the hospital.

“Symptoms of food-borne illness can include nausea, vomiting, stomach cramps, and fever,” Koch states. “You can experience the effects of food-borne illness within a few minutes to days after consuming a load of harmful pathogens or bacteria.”.

In a recent development, cooking frozen meat on the “low” setting of your slow cooker increases the time it spends in the danger zone, but the risk is present regardless. “The 'high' setting reduces the amount of time food spends at unsafe temperatures, but still doesn’t fully eliminate the risk when starting with frozen meat,” says White.

The ingredients you're using can also increase your risk. “Larger, denser cuts (like roasts or whole poultry) take longer to thaw and heat evenly, so they pose a greater risk of staying at unsafe temperatures for extended periods,” White explains.

According to recent reports, smaller pieces may thaw faster, but that doesn't necessarily make them safe to cook from frozen. White explains that ground meat is “particularly risky” because of the way it's processed, so it should be cooked thoroughly.

“I feed three young children at my home, so in my opinion, I wouldn't chance cooking frozen meat, no matter the size, in a slow cooker,” Koch states.

According to recent reports, the answer is simple: thaw your meat before turning on your slow cooker. But your ideal method depends on how much time you have.

The safest, easiest, and least involved thawing method is to put your frozen meat in the fridge. The cold temperature of your refrigerator lets your food defrost gently without entering the danger zone.

In a recent development, our editors recommend placing the meat on a plate or baking sheet to collect any juices and avoid contaminating other food in your fridge. This process can take anywhere from a couple of hours to a couple of days, depending on the cut of meat. “This requires some thought and effort, but in the long run it's worth your safety,” Koch says.

It has been revealed that no time for that? No problem. You can thaw meat faster by submerging it in cold water in a leakproof bag, changing the water every 30 minutes, or defrosting it in the microwave, though the latter can compromise the meat's texture. Both methods require cooking the meat immediately afterward. “Once thawed, meat should go directly into the slow cooker,” White explains.

It all takes a little extra effort and planning, but it's worth it to avoid getting sick from your slow cooker dinner.

One of them is District 12 tribute Haymitch Abernathy—a beloved figure from The Hunger Games trilogy—who fears being taken away from his loved ones, including his sweetheart, Lenore Dove. Even with an understanding that he could fail, Haymitch is determined to fight and see the games through. The Sunrise on the Reaping film adaptation, starring Joseph Zada as Haymitch, was released in 2026.

The Hunger Games is the book that started it all. Technically the first entry in Collins’s series, the novel introduced readers to Panem, a dystopian nation located where North America once stood, with 12 distinct districts and a Capitol. To keep the districts in order, the Capitol hosts the annual Hunger Games, a televised competition in which teenage boys and girls from each district fight to the death. One of those players—a.k.a. tributes—is 16-year-old Katniss Everdeen, who takes the place of her younger sister and must do everything she can to survive.

Fresh off her Hunger Games win, Katniss Everdeen faces an upheaval in her relationship with Peeta Mellark, her fellow District 12 tribute, and confronts the growing ire of the Capitol. Displeased by the last-minute move that allowed both Katniss and Peeta to win the games, President Snow has informed Katniss she must do everything she can to staunch the growing rebellion amongst the districts. But with another Quarter Quell looming, Katniss understands the games have only just begun.

Katniss is still standing, but at what cost? Her home is gone; the Capitol has captured Peeta; and a rebellion is underway in the districts. With the mysterious District 13 rising up to lead the revolution, Katniss must decide with whom her loyalties ultimately lie.

Gravy-Braised Turkey

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (572 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cooking a whole turkey is a commitment.
  • According to recent reports, this recipe will defy everything you have probably done to cook a turkey until now.
  • For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cooking a whole turkey is a commitment. Between the schlepping, trussing, and constant babysitting, it’s a serious investment—and one that doesn’t always pay dividends. For a more laid-back affair, and one that practically guarantees success, might we suggest turkey legs cooked directly in gravy? Yes, in the gravy.

According to recent reports, this recipe will defy everything you have probably done to cook a turkey until now. The first crucial step is searing the whole turkey legs for optimal browning. Now you are ready to create a base for the gravy with all those drippings and toasty bits left in the pot. No need to make a full-on roux either: Just sprinkle in the flour over the melted fat, whisk to combine, and slowly pour in the broth. Once the gravy is done, in goes the turkey and aromatics for braising. The rest is you worrying about something else, because that turkey will cook itself.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

It has been revealed that place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Season 4 whole turkey legs (thigh and drumstick; about 6½ lb. total), patted dry, all over with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large braiser or Dutch oven over medium-high. Working in 2 batches if needed to avoid overcrowding, arrange turkey legs, skin side down, in pot and cook, undisturbed, rotating pan on burner a few times to ensure even browning, until browned underneath and they easily release from pot, 8–12 minutes. Transfer turkey legs to a rimmed baking sheet, arranging skin side up. (No need to brown other side; turkey will still be raw at this point.).

Add more oil if pot looks dry; arrange 2 large oranges and/or lemons, halved, and 2 heads of garlic, tops trimmed to expose cloves, cut side down in pot and add 3 large shallots, peeled. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 2–3 minutes. Transfer each to baking sheet with turkey as they are done (it’s okay if some fall apart slightly).

Recent findings suggest that add 6 Tbsp. (¾ stick) unsalted butter to pot and cook until melted. Sprinkle in ⅓ cup (42 g) all-purpose flour and cook, stirring constantly, until no pockets of dry flour remain, about 1 minute. Gradually pour in 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth, stirring constantly to combine. Bring to a simmer and cook until gravy is just starting to thicken, about 2 minutes. Stir in 3 Tbsp. Worcestershire sauce and season with salt and pepper.

Recent findings suggest that nestle turkey legs into gravy, skin side up, then tuck oranges, garlic, and shallots around, arranging oranges and garlic cut side up. Add 1 small bunch thyme (about 10 sprigs), tied with kitchen twine, and cover pot tightly with a lid or foil. Braise 2 hours. (If your pot is too small to comfortably fit everything, transfer gravy to a 13x9" baking dish before adding turkey legs and aromatics.) Uncover pot and continue to bake until turkey legs are deeply browned, meat shreds easily off the bone, and gravy has thickened a little, 45–55 minutes.

Recent findings suggest that let turkey and gravy cool slightly before serving. Transfer to a platter if desired. (If gravy has excess fat on top, skim off with a spoon and discard before serving or spooning over legs on platter.).

Senate Majority Leader John Thune arrives for a GOP conference meeting at the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

But so far, no official candidate has emerged to challenge John Thune, R-S.D., for the post of minority leader in the fresh Congress.

Recent findings suggest that the conference was supposed to begin its leadership elections Tuesday morning, but pushed those back to hear from members still reeling from the midterm results, which saw the GOP lose their Senate majority. As the conference meeting turned into what some dubbed an “open-mic session,” they took a break to attend previously scheduled committee hearings, with a blueprint to return at 2 p.m. Next they must decide whether to forge ahead and pick leaders Tuesday or to punt those choices to a different day.

Industry observers note that sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., said the conversation taking place was “honest” and “frank.”.

“I will vote for the delay,” he remarked. “We’ve got a lot of things that we’ve got to think through, and I think to rush into this and to just ratify all the same leadership — I mean, what message does that send?”.

Sources indicate that “If you don’t think after losing seven seats minimum that we need to change course, I don’t know what planet you’re on,” he stated, adding he was frustrated that his party didn’t do more to focus on topics like affordability ahead of the midterms. “I know it’s easy to blame other people, but we need to look at what has happened here.”.

It has been revealed that sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., who is leading the charge to delay the leadership elections and collected signatures to call the conference meeting beforehand, called it “a very high-quality conversation” in which he was “leading.”.

Recent findings suggest that “People are voicing opinions on all sides of the challenges. It’s one of those times in the Republican conference where you kind of go, ‘We’ve got some smart people, and we’re having a very good, respectful conversation.’”.

Industry observers note that no challenger to Thune, the current majority leader, stepped forward during the closed-door meeting, several senators stated. Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., said “they’re not even criticizing Thune” inside the room. “It hasn’t been about John Thune.”.

“It’s been about the family,” Cramer mentioned, describing it as a “family discussion.” Thune and others in leadership had yet to speak, as the candidate forum hadn’t started yet.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said voters reacted to high gas prices, the war in Iran and the cost of living.

“The cost of living defeated us,” Paul mentioned. “I don’t think anybody in Texas who voted for the Democrat governor was voting against John Thune. If you diagnose that as a problem, you’re misdiagnosing the problem.”.

Sources indicate that hawley didn’t say how long he’d like to see a delay. “Long enough for people to think through this, and if there’s somebody else … or several somebodies who want to run for positions, let them think through it.”.

Cramer was asked if senators in the room were placing any blame on President Donald Trump over how he handled midterm messaging.

“There was a lot of discussion about the president,” Cramer remarked.

Sources indicate that “The area where I grew up, Belleville, is really different from the Hamptons,” noted Casablanca’s Charaf Tajer. “Growing up between Paris and Morocco, it seemed a very different landscape: it sounded very exotic to me.” Globalization might have shrunk the world—and flattened it too—but distance still creates room for the imagination to generate glamour. For this resort season Tajer projected his Casablanca formula on the Hamptons.

Sources indicate that his starting point was a survey of Jackie Kennedy and the milieu of American East Coast society during the middle of the last century. The seaside estates, sailing boats, country clubs, and sprawling lawns of this privileged playground offered a new destination for a brand whose MO has always been rooted in a romanticized dislocation. “It’s kind of near the cities,” Tajer said of the Hamptons, “but it has its own bubble.” Peering into that bubble through documentaries and archival imagery was an exercise in escapism, and Tajer intended this collection to be an escape route too. “It’s not that I don’t care: I’m really into the news. But I also feel like we need to care less, because the news can take us into a mental spiral.”.

According to recent reports, tajer presented the collection as the wardrobe of a dynastic clan on vacation, with each member bringing their own interpretation of American sportswear through a Casablanca-fied lens. Although shot in the UK, closer to Hertfordshire than the Hamptons, the images were cleverly set and staged. A scion crunched the gravel with a chunky laborador in a nicely homaged embroidered Skyliner jacket, wearing wide-leg chinos in one shot and skate shorts in another. Another lounged on a plump couch in seasonally-printed tennis gear, or lurked on the stairs in a camp collar shirt and embroidered wide-leg pants.

The women wore striped knitted separates, scarf-print silks, and tennis dresses, as well as a long black knitted dress that offered a more universal option for evening. Throughout, the preppy and streetwear references were blended and sometimes distorted through color, proportion, and the prints and embroidered illustrations created by the brand’s three in-house artists.

It has been revealed that the chinoiserie pattern adapted from a stately temple jar in this synthetic Camelot backdrop was prominently transposed into prints and patches. For Tajer, it served both as a hint toward a future project and as a reminder of how the decorative vernacular of one culture can become the status symbols of another.

It has been revealed that tajer said his ambition is to create a Casablanca wardrobe that can accommodate almost any occasion. The silk shirts that established the label have been joined by much more: This season’s additions included a leather tracksuit and fresh hybrid driving/boat shoe. Tajer cited Ralph Lauren as an inspiration, saying: “This is always what I wanted to create with Casablanca: a full, cohesive world.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gordon Ramsay has earned 17 Michelin stars throughout his career and still oversees nearly 100 restaurants. He also fronts prime-time TV franchises on both sides of the Atlantic and holds a couple of casual Guinness World Records (call him if you need to fillet a 10-pound fish in 1 minute five seconds).

This is a man who’s never met a goalpost he didn’t want to surpass. So it wasn’t entirely surprising when he posted a bare-chested shot of his six-pack to the grid earlier this month. What generated headlines was the occasion: his 60th birthday. “Gordon Ramsay thirst trap was not on my bingo card,” reads one comment. “My wife is on this app sir,” reads another.

According to recent reports, at home in London, he shows me the Insights section on his Instagram account, which reveals the photo has gotten over 62 million impressions. “It’s very strange,” he says. “I’ve had a lot of ribbing from my eldest daughter, Megan. She’s a police officer. She was like, ‘Dad, how can you do that to me?’ All her senior sergeants and officers were laughing and telling her to tell me they’re going for a run. They’re in their early 40s. And then my Royal Marines Commando son just sent me a message with: ‘WTF dad, what are you doing?’”.

Industry observers note that ramsay has been a pretty active guy for a while now, despite working in an industry typically associated with chaotic diets and zero time for exercise. He was a youth soccer player back in the day, before becoming a chef and then, in his 40s, going from weighing 252 pounds to competing in marathons and Ironmans.

All very impressive, but it’s even rarer to be this chiseled in your 60s (maintaining a low body fat percentage becomes harder as your testosterone and growth hormone production slows down). Read on to learn more about his preferred forms of cardio, his favorite pre-workout treat, and why he's established a daily cryotherapy routine. “I call it my freezer,” he says.

“15 minutes a day. It starts off with a quick two-minute stretch and 100 sit-ups every morning. Precore lifestyle is my ab cruncher thing—these things are fucking amazing, by the way. If I miss a day, then I have to punish it and do double the next day.”.

“It’s not physically hard with massive weights. These are 25 pounds. I’ll do a strength class once a week, 45 minutes. That’s it. Occasional push-ups and squats. No personal trainer.”.

“What’s helped tremendously, with no impact on any of the joints, is a lot of swimming. So I have an injury in my patella, my right knee, currently. So I just increased the swimming because that’s the only sport that can use every muscle in your body with zero impact. But cardio is off the charts.”.

“I have a Zwift bike, so I jump on that for 45 minutes. There’s no impact on that. I’ll do that Monday, Wednesday, Friday and gear up for 90 minutes on a Sunday. If I wasn’t injured, I’d be doing three 5K runs again, Monday, Wednesday, Friday, 20-minute runs. I’ve got my 5K back down to 21 minutes. The dream is under 20. I was running at 19 and a half back in July. A 5K run is easy to do in the morning before work, it’s done within half an hour. Once I do that, I can gear up for either a two-hour bike on a Sunday or a 90-minute run. I alternate. So, one Sunday’s run, one Sunday’s bike.”.

“10 years ago, I ruptured my Achilles. I invested in an AlterG, a beautiful running machine that takes your weight, so you get all the cardio you want and less impact on the joint.”.

“From the chef’s perspective, I call it my freezer. It’s the cryochamber. I do two sets of three minutes every morning. I try to go seven days a week in that thing, straight after [working out]. That is incredible. That’ll get up to like minus 160. For six minutes.”.

“I’ve invested in a tiny little red-light therapy sauna outside in the garden, and it seats two of you, and so [I’ll do] half an hour of that, every other day. This doesn’t need to be done every day. Three times a week’s fine. So when I’m not running, the other day I’ll sit in that red-light therapy and spend 20 minutes, 30 minutes in there, which is brilliant.”.

Recent findings suggest that “The older you get, the more you have to stretch. I use a lot of bands. And so after sitting and stretching, I had those incredible bands where you lift your feet up and pull and stretch. 5 minutes is always a nice stretch before you [work out] and then 10 minutes stretch after that. I’ve never been to a yoga class in my life.”.

Recent findings suggest that “I’m massive on oatmeal for breakfast, Monday to Friday. I indulge Saturday, Sunday. I will do [oatmeal with] blueberry compote, caramelized banana for my potassium, and then fresh blueberries on top with some—it sounds weird, but it’s delicious—hot honey.”.

“I have my friends at Precision. I’ll do one of their gels before I start that 5K, a protein gel, 30 grams, and then that sees me through the whole 45-minute routine. Coffee is just a full-fat, flat white, extra hot. Extra hot means I can sip it slowly. I cut out a lot of dairy, a lot of butter, a lot of cream. And so that treat in the morning with a flat white is that sort of, ‘I’ve earned this shit.’”.

It has been revealed that “I don’t overstress on that because I stay fit. I monitor what I eat, but if anything, I’ll do smaller portions now. I’ll involve a lot of spinach, involve a lot of salmon, chicken, especially thighs. We’re just smart with less cream, less butter intake. And then when we travel, we just keep it light.”.

Industry observers note that “I have a red wine with dinner, Californian, something light, something delicious. In 20, 30 years running restaurants, I’ve never gone around the room holding a glass of wine, holding a glass of champagne, sitting down, drinking with customers. Again, discipline.”.

“Just a couple of spoons of creatine, five mornings a week. A little scoop in my water.”.

“One thing I’ve learned in my 50s and my 60s—everyone noted the older you get, the less you sleep. I think it’s the other way around. I like to be in bed by 11, and I’m up at 6. My Oura ring for me has become my best mate, because it just gives me the proper day-by-day indication and then keeps you on track for sleep.”.

“No, no, no, no, no, no. Definitely not. No. I mean, no. My meditation is Kitchen fucking Nightmares. Dealing with some of those contributors on there and having to sit with them and talk with them. But no, not very good at sitting still.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that listen, we all know that stuffing is the best part of Thanksgiving dinner, but because of the butter, eggs, and chicken broth that usually go into classic stuffing, it's a dish that vegans can't always enjoy—until now! We created a stuffing that's so delicious, you might even be convinced to make a few of your other holiday classics into vegan Thanksgiving versions.

Start your stuffing off by preheating the oven to 200° and slicing the bread into roughly 1” cubes. Spread the cubes in a single layer on a large baking sheet and bake for about 20 minutes, until the bread is nice and crisp.

Remove the bread from the oven and turn the temperature up to 350°. Grease a 13” x 9” baking dish with cooking spray and heat oil in a large skillet over medium heat. Add onion to the skillet and cook for about 5 minutes until lightly charred in some spots, then add the celery and garlic and continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until the celery starts to turn translucent. Pour in the vegetable stock and scrape up any browned bits—this is where all the flavor is. Season with salt and pepper.

Mix the bread cubes and chopped herbs in the vegetable stock mixture until well combined, then transfer to the prepared baking dish.

Industry observers note that cover the dish tightly with aluminum foil and place it in the oven to bake for 40 minutes. Carefully remove the foil and continue baking for another 35 minutes, until the stuffing is golden brown and crisp on top.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

In a recent development, looking for more vegan holiday inspo? Whip up our cauliflower stuffing for a low-carb option, or try out our vegetarian mushroom gravy or vegan mashed potatoes to truly complete your spread!

Any leftovers can be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 4 days. You can also prepare this dish ahead of time, as it’s the kind of dish that we think tastes even better after sitting for a day.

The Best Drip Coffee Makers, Test Kitchen Vetted & Editor Approved (2026)

📅 22 Feb 2022 | ⏱️ 42 min read (8323 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~42 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ever since Starbucks started co-opting seemingly every street corner and strip mall and multiple waves of coffee snobbery (laudatory) have risen in direct opposition to mass market espresso, it’s safe to say the average consumer has changed what they expect from a cup of coffee.
  • The cliché of bad drip coffee from a cheap piece of plastic doesn’t apply anymore.
  • Our writers and editors have tested more than three dozen coffee makers over the years, and below we get into the ones that make a good cup of coffee, the ones that make a great cup of coffee, and the unfortunate ones that just can’t keep up with today’s coffee-brewing arms race.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ever since Starbucks started co-opting seemingly every street corner and strip mall and multiple waves of coffee snobbery (laudatory) have risen in direct opposition to mass market espresso, it’s safe to say the average consumer has changed what they expect from a cup of coffee. Just look at the coffee maker aisle in any massive-box store and, along with single-serve and pod machines and other barista-replacing gadgets, you’ll find a slew of coffee makers that promise to make you dozens of drink styles, froth up some milk, and bring you “instant” cold brew. But sometimes the simplest way to make coffee is still pretty darn good. What we’re saying is don’t discount the drip coffee machine.

The cliché of bad drip coffee from a cheap piece of plastic doesn’t apply anymore. And even lots of cheap coffee makers are so much better than they used to be. If you’re in the market for a lot of coffee with little effort, your options are now legion. Companies like Breville, Fellow, Oxo, and Ratio have joined the original king of drip, Technivorm, in making quality appliances that better control factors like water temperature, flow rate, and bloom time, several of which brew coffee that’s almost as good as what you can get with a kettle and a pour-over setup.

Our writers and editors have tested more than three dozen coffee makers over the years, and below we get into the ones that make a good cup of coffee, the ones that make a great cup of coffee, and the unfortunate ones that just can’t keep up with today’s coffee-brewing arms race.

Industry observers note that new in this update: We tested two new coffee makers with plastic-free brewing systems from Caraway and Simply Good Coffee. We also tested the new Braun OptiBrew Pro, which includes an onboard milk frother among other features.

Capacity: 10 cupsCarafe style: ThermalDimensions: 8.9" x 8.9" x 12"Weight: 9.6 lb.Features: Adjustable brew water ratio; adjustable temperature settings, flavor profile settings, programmable 24-hour timer; Wi-Fi connectivity; cold-brew capable; SCA Golden Cup capabilitiesWarranty: 3 years.

In a recent development, fellow has a knack for making coffee gear that’s both beautiful and effective, and its automatic brewer fits right in. The Aiden is as close to a perfect drip coffee maker as we’ve tested because its designers considered nearly every need. It offers brew profiles with different water temperatures and times for light, medium, and dark roasts, and it tells you exactly how much coffee to use in both grams and tablespoons.

Recent findings suggest that but even with all its bells and whistles, the Aiden still has to make coffee that tastes good. And it does. Senior editor Noah Kaufman compared it side-by-side to carafes of pour-over and found both hit fruity and caramel notes, with real nuance and depth of flavor.

What we love: The Aiden is customizable across so many parameters you might lose track: You can set water temperature (anywhere between 122°F and 210°F); the time and number of pulses of water (think of them as the individual water pours if you were making pour-over coffee); and bloom time that helps get rid of gasses that can make your coffee taste sour. This machine can also make a smooth pot of cold brew by slowly dripping water over the course of several hours. (Machines that claim they can make cold brew in minutes don't usually live up to their own hype.).

That sounds like a lot, but the Aiden is surprisingly easy to use thanks to a simple dial, a clear LCD screen, and straightforward instructions. And even though you can tweak your coffee in all the ways outlined above, you can also just use the Aiden like a basic one-button drip coffee maker. The Instant Brew option will use however much water is in the tank, brewing at water temperatures recommended by the Specialty Coffee Association (SCA) in its Golden Cup standards, which mark water temperature and coffee-to-water ratios for ideal flavor. To paraphrase Fellow’s founder, who visited us in the Test Kitchen, he wanted the machine to work for both coffee connoisseurs and total noobs.

Recent findings suggest that the Aiden also features a slew of carefully considered, where-have-you-been-my-whole-life details. Its two filter baskets—one for three cups or fewer and one for more than three cups—have spring-loaded seals to prevent drips when you remove them to empty the grounds into the garbage. It doesn't have a warming plate because it doesn't need one—the included thermal carafe kept coffee hot on the dining room table for around two hours. And the removable side water tank is easier to fill than either a built-in tank or one on the backside of the machine.

During the testing, we also tried Fellow’s Drops program. It’s not exactly a coffee subscription—you order via text on demand—but it gives you access to various rare and small-batch beans from Fellow’s roaster partners. The Aiden comes preloaded with specific brew settings for recent Drops offerings, adjusting water temps and pulse cycles beyond the standard light/medium/dark profiles and the resulting coffee produced using the Drops settings was truly excellent. Brewing the same beans with both the Drops settings and the regular settings make a real difference. It’s one of the closest ways to recreate that “rare pour-over at your favorite café” experience at home.

Check out an even more detailed rundown on the Aiden here.

What we’d leave: Compared to most of the drip coffee makers you’ll find at a significant-box store, it’s somewhat expensive. However, within the recent wave of better-quality drip coffee machines, it falls right in line with average pricing we’ve come to expect from a daily coffee workhorse that produces this level of coffee.

Recent findings suggest that in the long run: Noah has used the Aiden about five times a week for over two years, and it has lived up to its early promise. The coffee has remained consistently good, and we’ve had no concerns with the interface, plus the removable side water tank has continued to prove its convenience.

Sources indicate that the Aiden is a precision machine, and regular maintenance matters. Noah found this out the hard way after too many months of skipping descaling, which eventually produced a loud noise that sounded like the pump might be on its last legs. To get an unfiltered read on customer service, he reached out as a regular customer rather than identifying himself as a Bon Appétit editor. Fellow responded within two days, pointed him toward descaling as a fix, and after he sent a video of the machine in action, offered to replace it entirely. They also recommended descaling monthly going forward, which felt a little aggressive, but the clear instructions were appreciated.

It has been revealed that capacity: 8 cupsCarafe-style: Thermal Dimensions: 13" x 6.5" x 14.25" Weight: 8 lb. Features: Blooms coffee, SCA Golden Cup capabilitiesWarranty: 5 years.

Ratio has been trying to limit the plastic across its whole lineup and offers up this stainless steel dripper as an add-on to the Ratio 6, which ensures no hot water or coffee touch plastic during the brewing process.

The Fellow Aiden is a great coffee maker, but it has a lot going on. We know that some people’s ideal drip coffee maker is one you load up with coffee, turn on, and leave to do its thing. The Ratio Six (which is actually an 8-cup coffee maker, don’t let the name fool you) lets you do just that without compromising on the quality of the brew.

What we love: It’s got one button that begins the brew process. There is no water temperature to set, no flavor profiles to adjust. But the brewing process, like the Fellow's, is designed to mimic a pour-over. The Ratio first blooms the coffee, then it uses a slower flow to improve extraction. The resulting coffee is absolutely delicious and takes no effort on your part. The Ratio Six (Series 2) includes a thermal carafe that outperformed all the others we tried (the Fellow was a close second), keeping coffee hot for over two hours.

In a recent development, what we'd leave: The Ratio's fixed water tank at the back of the appliance is a real bear to fill. We either had to set the machine sideways on the counter or slide it out from under a cabinet to fill it with water. The brew basket also sits on top of the carafe instead of being attached to the body in any way. That made it easy to empty, but it was a little precarious to set up until we got the hang of it.

In the long run: Ratio’s 5-year warranty is longer than just about any other coffee maker you can buy (Technivorm’s Moccamaster is the only other one with a warranty that long), and it’s clear why the firm felt comfortable making such a long offer. This thing has turned out to be as reliable a small appliance as we’ve ever used. It makes the same quality coffee more than a year later than it did the day we unboxed it.

However, the things we found a little irritating about the Ratio’s design at the beginning did not get less irritating over time though. Unless it is set in an open space (i.e., not under a cabinet), filling the tank with water is cumbersome. And the small opening of the carafe demands a brush to properly clean it, which is not a deal breaker, but is a little annoying (especially compared to the wide opening of the Aiden’s carafe).

None of that takes away from the fact that, as far as small appliances go, this is as close to a buy-it-for-life pick as you’re going to find.

The Ratio was one of a small handful of machines we could really see working in the process.

A note on the wave of plastic-free coffee makers hitting the market: They’re not necessarily plastic-free. Countertop appliances are full of plastics, from their outer shells to their inner mechanisms because plastic parts are cheap, easy to mass produce, and, for many applications, durable enough. But a latest(ish) crop of brewers eliminated plastic anywhere water travels through the machine in an attempt to avoid any possibility of plastic leeching into the coffee.

Aside from the Ratio Eight (below), which has featured a plastic-free brew path since it was introduced over a decade ago, our social media feeds have been serving us ads for newer plastic-free brew path models from Simply Good Coffee and Caraway, both of which we tested in our most recent update to this article.

Industry observers note that how much does plastic in the brew path matter? As with coating technology on nonstick pans, the science is developing. On a more subjective level, many coffee drinkers do say glass and steel brewing—along with the ceramic used in pour-over—tastes better.

Capacity: 10 cupsCarafe-style: GlassDimensions: 13" W x 6" D x 14" HWeight: 13 lb.Features: Plastic-free brew path, warming plate, insulated stainless-steel basket, reusable filter, quiet operation, cleaning modeWarranty: 2 years.

Everything hot (and cold) water touches in this machine is either stainless steel or glass, including the embedded reservoir. Caraway also remains committed to cute colors and stylish aesthetic, as the new coffee maker’s four available colorways are matched to those in existing Caraway products.

Industry observers note that what we love: The Caraway 10-cup coffee maker is a simple setup, so there's not much to dislike. It has single push-button operation and brews between 195°F–205°F meeting Golden Cup Standards with an automatically programmed bloom cycle. The stainless-steel reusable filter (you can also use paper if you wish) does a sufficient job of keeping silt out of our cup while also brewing rich, flavorful coffee, and the insulated basket means little heat is lost while the blooming occurs. Speaking of the basket, Caraway designed it to fit in two perpendicular directions, meaning you can orient the machine with the short side facing out, perhaps nestled between two other appliances, or with the long side pushed back wider against the wall.

According to recent reports, even though it costs more than either of the two coffee makers recommended above, it is quite a bit less expensive than the Ratio Eight, which is why we’re choosing to recommend it here instead. From a pure coffee perspective we prefer the Ratio, but we don’t love its $700 price tag. The Caraway makes consistently good coffee with its plastic-free arrangement for $200 less.

What we’d leave: Considering the engineering it takes to produce a plastic-free brew path, we were left somewhat baffled by the lack of thought that seemed to go into the metal lid for the water reservoir, which just sort of sits on top—and loosely at that. The opening of the reservoir is nicely sloped so even a few errant drips will channel in. But the lid, which sits proud of the top surface of the unit and only slightly inset, can come dislodged just by shifting the machine (which you’ll need to do to fill it if it’s under a cabinet) or brushing your arm or hand across it too closely. Access to the reservoir is a bit limited as well, and while a water-only cycle is recommended weekly, plus a descaling for monthly maintenance, we’re a bit concerned about the prospect of something gunky getting in there and not being able to clean it out. Finally, there’s no option to preprogram the machine to brew automatically in the morning.

Capacity: 12 cupsCarafe-style: ThermalDimensions: 15" x 10" x 17"Features: Single-serve and half-carafe option, programmable timerWarranty: 2 years.

According to recent reports, we don’t have any real issues with the quality of the coffee or the functionality of either the Fellow or Ratio coffee machines, but neither of them count as XL coffee makers. The Oxo 12-cup machine gives you 20% more volume while still keeping the quality of the coffee very high. It uses a rainmaker shower head to evenly saturate the grounds, and the resulting coffee is the kind of nuanced, fresh-tasting carafe we’d expect from something at this price point. There are a couple other features that push this one to the top of the pile.

Recent findings suggest that what we love: First is its range. It can brew anywhere from a single cup of coffee all the way up to 12 cups with no sacrifice on flavor or aroma. (Entertainers, take note: This means you can use the same machine to fuel both your normal weekday mornings and the occasional group brunch.) The Oxo also comes with a well-insulated stainless steel carafe that keeps coffee warm enough to drink for almost two hours and has an intuitive digital interface with a dial and a brew button that make it easy to schedule your coffee ahead of when you'll need it.

This coffee maker also has plenty of the little design touches that define Oxo products, including a removable shower head for easy cleaning and filter holders that are flat on the bottom so you can set them on the counter or in the sink after a brew without them spilling everywhere.

What we’d leave: The water tank is built into the body of the machine, and while the opening isn’t too small, it’s still not as easy to fill as a removable reservoir.

Braun BrewSense 12-Cup Drip Coffeemaker.

Capacity: 12 cupsCarafe-style: GlassDimensions: 7.9" x 7.9" x 14.2"Features: 1–4 cup options, adjustable brew strength, programmable timer, water filter, adjustable hot plate temperatureWarranty: 3 years.

Let’s get something straight about budget coffee makers: they don’t produce coffee on the same level as machines that precisely regulate water temperature and flow rate. These are the kind you might find at an adequate but not exceptional Airbnb. So we didn’t judge the Braun against the Fellow or the Ratio, but rather against the Mr. Coffees, Ninjas, and Black & Deckers of the world. By that measure, it did an admirable job. For a machine you can sometimes find on sale for $80, the coffee came out bright rather than stale or watery.

What we love: There are a few ways you can tell a good cheap coffee maker from a bad one. One, it will produce water hot enough to actually extract flavor from ground coffee. When we measured the temperature of water as it ran through the Braun, it was more than 10℉ hotter than many of the other cheap coffee makers we tried. Another is that it will evenly distribute water over the coffee. Even if a coffee maker looks like it has a shower head that can spread water across the coffee bed, you still might end up with a machine that creates deep channels. Basically, a situation where streams of water get drilled through narrow areas of coffee. When we looked at the coffee bed of the BrewSense after making a pot, the coffee was evenly wet.

The proof will always be in the taste of the coffee, though, and the BrewSense pulled out many of the flavor notes we got from the Fellow and Ratio, though in a more muted way.

Also, for such an inexpensive coffee maker, the BrewSense came with some nice features, like the ability to slow down the water flow in order to brew small batches and a hot plate with adjustable temperatures to keep coffee from getting burnt while it sits.

Industry observers note that what we’d leave: The glass carafe wasn’t our favorite. It flipped open a little too easily, which seemed like it could cause spills. And, frankly, a thermal carafe would have been nice. Some other budget machines have them.

EC-DAC50 Zutto 5-Cup Drip Coffeemaker.

Capacity: 5 cupsCarafe-style: GlassDimensions: 9" x 6" x 10.75"Features: Hot plate, removable water tankWarranty: 2 years.

What we love: This little thing? Makes good coffee? Grading on an appropriate curve for something that costs less than $100, it absolutely does. Its design is unlike any other machine we tested, with a brewing cone that sits inside the carafe. That’s one way to achieve a small footprint. But it also keeps the coffee closer to the shower head, which helps maintain a hotter temperature than it otherwise might.

The coffee is not what you will get if you brew with the Fellow or the Ratio, but it can produce a more flavorful pot than any other sub-$100 machine we used (the Braun above is sometimes less than $100, but retails for more). And because it comes from well-respected Japanese brand, Zojirushi, the name behind our forever-favorite rice cookers and coffee tumblers, we trust it’s as high quality as something in this price range can get.

It also has a removable water tank that makes filling it each morning a much less irritating task, and is rare in cheap coffee makers.

What we’d leave: This is a small machine, only five cups. That may not be enough even in a two-coffee-drinker household if those two people need much more than eight ounces of coffee apiece. It also only has a single switch, which, on the one hand, makes brewing coffee easy (flip switch, brew coffee), but can lead to a bit of confusion. That switch also adjusts the temperature of the hot plate, but that isn’t made clear either on the machine or in the instructions. Zojirushi has famously dense instruction manuals that can be hard to follow, and that’s true even for something as simple as this.

In short, we made copious amounts of coffee in these machines. To keep the brewing process as consistent as possible, we used the same beans or grounds from the same roaster in each test—usually a blend of Counter Culture coffee beans, freshly ground with a Fellow Ode burr grinder. If the coffee maker came with a reusable filter, we used that; otherwise, we used standard Melitta paper filters.

If machines had features like a “bold” setting or the ability to brew half batches or single cups, we tested them to see what kind of difference the setting made (this was a particularly involved test with the Fellow and the Breville machines).

For machines with thermal carafes, we used probe thermometers to test how long they kept coffee above 110℉.

Sources indicate that the single most key thing you want from a drip coffee maker is a pot of coffee you actually want to drink. We looked for coffee makers that provided the most depth of flavor and nuance to their coffee. We discounted anything that made coffee that was burnt or watery.

Industry observers note that the point of a drip machine is to deliver your morning coffee in large quantities with minimal thinking from you. That means it should be easy to fill and easy to operate. If a machine has lots of customizable options like the Fellow Aiden, using them should still be straightforward enough that we could pick up their operation quickly.

Do they have special features, and do those features work?

A number of machines offered the ability to precisely regulate temperature. Some came with thermal carafes. Most had the very basic, but very crucial ability to schedule a brew ahead of time. We used every single option available.

How do they look? How do they feel?

Sources indicate that as drip coffee makers have advanced technologically, they have also advanced aesthetically. We tested a number of machines that looked quite handsome on the countertop. We also noticed that a lot of the inexpensive machines felt too light and flimsy, which we’d consider an indicator that they may not last very long.

These machines, which include several of the fancier SCA-certified brewers as well as a number of simple, cheap ones, didn't make the short list of top picks, but they did well enough that we think you'll be happy if you pick one up.

Moccamaster KBGV 10-Cup Coffee Maker.

Sources indicate that A longtime darling of both online coffee publications and coffee lovers, Technivorm Moccamaster machines were some of the first to stake a claim on good drip coffee. They were actually the first to receive the SCA Golden Cup standard stamp of approval. And indeed, the coffee from the Moccamaster is tasty. It’s also simple in the way you’d traditionally expect a drip coffee maker to be. Just an on-off switch and a full pot–half pot switch.

Recent findings suggest that despite those two very big pluses, there are a few things that land the Moccamaster down here instead of up with our top picks. One is its look. Compared to the Ratio machine, which is just as simple but also offers extras like bloom time in the brewing process and a thermal carafe, the Technivorm takes up more counter space and doesn’t look nearly as sleek. But if you’re into the Technivorm’s diner coffee maker aesthetic (and I totally respect it if that’s your thing) it is a high-quality, long-lasting coffee maker (the Test Kitchen has had the same one for more than four years).

Ratio Eight Series 2 Coffee Maker.

An OG in the plastic-free brew path drip coffee space, the only problem with the latest Ratio Eight is that it’s pretty damn expensive. But it’s also part coffee maker, part art object—with wood accents and a hand-blown glass carafe—so for the right person, the price may well be worth it. The coffee it brews is superb: evenly bloomed, well-extracted, and just as easy to make as with the Ratio Six thanks to the same single-button operation.

In a recent development, the upcoming version of the Ratio Eight adds a half-carafe mode (just long-press the brew button) that adjusts bloom time and flow depending on the batch size. It also comes with the thermal carafe to end all thermal carafes; it’s one of the heaviest we’ve ever used and kept water above 120°F for four hours.

Sources indicate that beautiful, functional, and built to last, this is a great machine. But with a price around $700, it’s in that echelon of luxury goods that isn’t accessible to a wide enough audience to make it a top pick.

8-Cup Coffee Maker with Podless Single-Serve.

If you want to join the ranks of “better” drip coffee but don’t like the idea of spending $300 or more on your coffee maker, this mid-size, mid-priced machine from Oxo is a good choice. It gets water hot enough extract good flavor from ground coffee (we measured it at 196℉, which is on the low end of the acceptable range) and distributes it nicely thanks to Oxo’s showerhead design. It also blooms the coffee, though you might not know that if you don't read the fine print in the manual.

The Oxo has settings for a full 8-cup pot, a half pot, and a single cup. Oxo touts that single-serve capability as a major feature in its own description of the coffee maker, and it’s…fine. The individual cup didn’t brew up as flavorful as the full pot nor as flavorful as the single cups brewed by some other coffee makers, like the Fellow or Oxo’s higher-end 12-cup machine. But it does make good coffee, has a relatively small footprint, 7 inches wide and 10 inches deep, and feels well-built, as many Oxo products are. You can upgrade this coffee maker with a stainless-steel carafe which we didn’t test, but other Oxo insulated carafes performed well in our testing over the years.

OXO Brew 9 Cup Stainless Steel Coffee Maker.

The Goldilocks size of the three Oxo coffee makers we tested ticks the main boxes for a high-end drip machine: It has good temperature control between 197℉ and 204℉, comes with a thermal carafe that keeps coffee warm for well over an hour, and it blooms the coffee. And like so many of Oxo’s products it comes with some subtle but smart design choices like keeping the lid of the grounds container attached to the machine, choosing a dial controller instead of a lineup of buttons, adding a freshness timer so you know how long the brewed coffee has been sitting, and a cleaning indicator to let you know when it’s time for descaling.

On the flip side, the opening of the carafe is pretty narrow, so you’ll need to clean it with a bottle brush. Technically, this machine does not have the Golden Cup standard (though it does keep its water in the proper temperature range). It also offers fewer options than the Fellow, but isn’t as simple as the one-button Ratio.

Industry observers note that if you like the look of the Moccamaster but want something plastic-free (inside, at least), Simply Good Coffee’s The Brewer looks like a near-duplicate that comes in both a programmable and simpler on-off model. At nearly $400 for the latter, we think the similarly priced Caraway is a better plastic-eschewing choice. But it doesn’t let you set a brewing time, so if that’s vital to you, then the programmable model at $40 more might be right for you. While it produced acceptable coffee overall, the parts felt a little flimsy at times with the reservoir lid not quite sitting flush or other pieces twisted slightly out of alignment out of the box. It takes #4 cone filters, like those used in pour-over setups, and one nice feature is that the filter basket sits flat on the counter or on a coffee scale, making measuring out grounds directly into the filter super easy. And there are gram ratios printed right on the reservoir to help you remember how to math when you’re still groggy. Lastly, one slightly confounding aspect is the inclusion of a Bloom switch, which must be turned on and, when engaged, produces markedly better tasting coffee. Which begs the question why not just have the “good coffee” mode be the only mode? “Very dark roasts and older, degassed beans benefit the most from skipping or heavily shortening the bloom phase,” Dean Rotchin, CEO of SimplyGoodCofee, told us. “While blooming is standard for fresh pour-over coffee to release trapped carbon dioxide (CO₂), certain roast profiles and conditions make it unnecessary or even counterproductive.” Lastly, this machine has a lot of parts (lids, filter holders, etc) which, generally, will just sit in their respective places most of the time, but if you have to this one in a cabinet, it can be a lot to keep track of.

Breville Luxe Drip Coffee Machine.

Seattle Coffee Gear (glass model).

Recent findings suggest that released in 2025, Breville’s Luxe Brewer has the look and feel of something designed specifically to compete in this world of increasingly customizable, increasingly high-end drip coffee makers. It offers the ability to set bloom volume, bloom time, water temperature, and flow rate. Plus, it makes cold brew overnight.

It has been revealed that this is a very good coffee maker, and once someone learns how to use it, they’ll be pleased with what they get. However, it costs almost the same amount as the Fellow Aiden, and it doesn’t give you quite as much. Bloom volume and flow rate, for example, can only be set to low, medium, and high. And while that might be plenty of optionality for most people in most situations, the point of having all these settings is to offer the ability to tease out exactly the flavor you want from any batch of beans. And we think the Fellow’s more precise capabilities are worth an extra 20 bucks.

The interface of the Breville is also a little confusing. When you turn it on, it’s not immediately clear whether you’re adjusting settings or starting a brew cycle, and many of the customization options are represented by unlabeled icons. In an era of increasingly complex appliances, an intuitive, user-friendly interface is more crucial than ever, and that’s where the Luxe Brewer falls short.

Zojirushi Dome Brew Classic Coffee Maker (Stainless Black).

Industry observers note that with more than twice the capacity of the Zojirushi Zutto, the Dome offers a more traditional drip coffee maker experience. Like the Zutto, it produces coffee that punches above its weight for its price point, and the simplicity of a single switch that both brews coffee and turns on the warming plate. The removable showerhead does a nice job of fully saturating the coffee grounds, and a “bold” setting concentrates the water to extract bigger flavors. A standout design detail is its silicone gasket, which seals the top of the carafe during brewing to help keep the coffee at temperature as it drips through. If you’re looking for a straightforward, no-fuss machine that makes great coffee without breaking the bank, the Dome is an excellent pick.

Café Specialty Grind and Brew Coffee Maker.

The Grind and Brew effectively toes the line between a simple, self-contained coffee maker and a techy, customizable one. The built-in grinder has six grind sizes and, while it’s not so nice or versatile that we’d pick it over a stand alone burr grinder, it gets the job done.

According to recent reports, this machine has variable temperatures between 185℉ and 205℉ and can brew using the SCA’s Golden Cup standard. That made its coffee both very good and very consistent. And it's a nice touch that you can easily switch between a setting for single cups and one for full carafes. Ultimately, it ended up in this middle space of not being able to do as much as the Fellow Aiden but holding a price tag that keeps it out of what we’d consider a “budget” range.

Café Specialty Drip Coffee Maker.

This is basically the Café Grind and Brew without the grinder or the single serve option, and the glass carafe model is actually priced low enough that we’d recommend it for someone who thinks the Fellow or the Ratio machines are a bridge too far for their wallet.

Like the Grind and Brew, you can use the SCA Golden Cup settings or customize water temperature between 185℉-205℉. Also like the Grind and Brew, the wide shower head evenly wets the coffee grounds and produces a high-quality pot. If you already have a solid coffee grinder or are willing to invest in one, this is a drip machine to consider.

GE Profile Smart Grind & Brew Coffee Maker.

In a recent development, GE is the parent company of Café, so it wasn’t surprising that some of the technology found in the Café Grind and Brew coffee maker used by the mother brand. The Profile features one significant improvement over the Café Grind and Brew: It shrank its countertop footprint. Instead of stretching out horizontally across the counter like the Café, the GE better integrates the water tank snugly into the back of the machine for a coffee maker that fits much more comfortably in a variety of kitchens.

In a recent development, otherwise, it operates much like the Café. It allows for freshly ground single serve coffee, features an SCA Golden Cup setting, and has a user-friendly app that will get a fresh pot of coffee going from anywhere in the house. Like the Café version, we think the GE is good, but not great, and for just a little bit more money, you can get one of our top picks. After spending many months with both the Café and GE Grind and Brew models, we’ve found that the washable mesh filters let too many grounds wiggle their way into the coffee and regularly found sediment at the bottom of our cups.

Yet another machine that meets the Golden Cup standard (it’s become table stakes for “good” drip coffee makers at this point), the Zwilling Enfinigy makes coffee on par with the Café and Technivorm machines and is less expensive than all of them. Despite a high end look though, it’s also lighter weight, which makes it feel cheaper by comparison.

It has a number of standard features: the ability to brew between 2 to 12 cups, a timer to plan brews ahead, and a keep warm function. Like the Simply Good Coffee machine above it also offers the curious feature of a bloom function that you can toggle on and off. Blooming coffee seems like all upside and no downside, so we can’t think of a good reason you’d ever want to toggle it off. Maybe you like off flavors in your coffee?

The Aarke machine is a beautiful, high-quality coffee machine, no doubt about it. It brews coffee with temperature control precise enough to earn it a rating from the Specialty Coffee Association and has a couple other nice features like a bloom function that you can toggle on or off by holding the single button on the machine. It's most effective when paired with Aarke's burr grinder, which can read how much water is in the dripper and grind coffee to match. You can read our review of the complete system here, but you don't need the grinder to make use of the brewer.

According to recent reports, the issue with the Aarke is that it's not as customizable as the Fellow and, if you want a thermal carafe, will cost you quite a bit more than the Ratio Six. But if you're focused as much on aesthetics as you are on coffee, you might be ready to swallow the price bump.

Braun PureFlavor 14‑Cup Programmable Coffee Maker.

In a recent development, first the good: As programmable coffee makers under $100 go, they don’t come better than this Braun model, consistently priced below the Braun BrewSense we recommend up above. It can draw more flavor out of ground coffee than anything in this price range has business doing. The coffee bed showed no channeling, meaning even water distribution and better extraction. The machine has an alarm setting so coffee will be ready when you wake up and has three different brew settings, including “bold” and over ice (which produced better iced coffee than some much more expensive machines).

So why does the Pureflavor miss out on a spot as the top budget pick? Because of a design you might actually like but we do not: It has a touchscreen. Unlike the BrewSense, which uses tactile buttons, the Pureflavor has a touchscreen interface. That’s not a problem in and of itself—some people like touchscreens, some don’t. It does raise durability concerns though. We’ve used enough touchscreen items in our product testing (and had enough fail) that seeing one at this price point makes us cautious about recommending it.

Calphalon Programmable 14-Cup Coffee Maker.

The Calphalon’s coffee was just as good as what we got from my favorite Braun machine: rich, flavorful, more than we typically expect from a cheap coffee maker. It also had the same features, including the different settings for the hot plate. We thought the Braun’s interface was a little easier to use—all the buttons are clearly labeled and in one line as opposed to the Calphalon, which has a couple buttons that felt sort of hidden away at the top of the machine. And while prices on these coffee makers can bounce around a little bit, the Calphalon is typically a little bit more expensive than the Braun.

Sources indicate that mr. Coffee Stainless Steel 10 Cup Programmable Coffee Maker.

Mr. Coffee is sometimes used as shorthand for a cheap, meh coffee maker. But the brand has come a long way from the basic machine on your parents' or grandparents' counter growing up. This is still a very affordable machine, but comes with a thermal carafe that kept coffee warm for about an hour and a detachable water reservoir that makes it easy to fill without spilling. The coffee itself was on the watery side, but was still perfectly drinkable.

Kenmore 12-Cup Drip Coffee Maker.

It comes with fewer features than either of the Braun coffee makers, but it produced coffee that ran close to them in terms of flavor. It has bold and 1-4 cup brew settings, making suitable for large or small coffee drinking households, and a simple interface that requires no explanation. It feels quite cheap—thin plastic and glass—but it also costs less than just about anything else we’ve tested, so in that way it meets expectations. If you’re looking for an alternative to the Zojirushi for some reason that’s just as inexpensive, you should be satisfied with this Kenmore.

Cuisinart Perfectemp 14-Cup Coffee. Maker With Glass Carafe.

In a recent development, the major selling point of the Cuisinart Perfectemp is its size. It can brew 14 cups of coffee (that’s coffee-sized cups—five ounces, not eight ounces). It makes adequate tasting coffee, and the 1-4 cup setting, which adjusts the extraction time for less water, still produces flavorful results. We didn’t notice much difference when switching between regular and bold strength though. Ultimately, testers liked the flavor and the extra features of the Braun, which put it over the top here.

Even though some of the coffee makers on this list make coffee that’s tasty enough, they either lack the features, design, or value of the machines up above.

Braun’s OptiBrew Pro is trying to do a lot, and there are some aspects we loved, including smart water consumption from the reservoir (it only uses the amount for the desired cup or carafe size you select), sleek interface, and decent customization and programmability. However, among its many promises, it tries to masquerade as an espresso maker with “single shot” capability and an attached, foldaway milk frother. But the faux-spresso we got from it wasn’t satisfying enough to make us ditch our espresso machine. And wand-style milk frothers can be bought for under $10 and take up little space. We found the OptiBrew Pro’s operation a bit finicky, including the rear-mounted water tank and brew basket lid, which snapped closed and required a bit of effort to open. In other words, the lack of endorsement here does not come down to it being necessarily a bad coffee maker. Its added features just didn’t work well enough to justify paying more than you would for the BrewSense.

Ninja 12-Cup Programmable Brewer.

Industry observers note that as budget coffee goes, what I got from the Ninja was good, not great. It was a little more watery, and even on the “rich” setting tasted flatter than some machines’ regular coffee. The removable side water tank is a nice design touch, it’s easy to take off, refill, and replace. But there’s better cheap coffee out there.

Industry observers note that this is, to my knowledge, Mr. Coffee's first attempt to really play in the luxury coffee maker space. And retailing at $200 at the time of writing, it's definitely got the price tag to be there. In terms of performance the coffee was on par with lots of the mid-tier machines I tested—nuanced, sometimes fruity. It too uses SCA standards for its brewing.

The thing that should justify the jump in price from say, the $150 Zwilling machine above, is the Mr Coffee’s ability to make quick cold brew in under 10 minutes. But I found the cold brew a little bit flat in flavor. Fine in a pinch, and if you didn’t want to go to the trouble of using a cold-brew coffee maker, but not what you’d expect from immersion cold brew. If you’re planning to spend in this price range, a number of the coffee makers above will serve you better. Do note that this Mr. Coffee also has tea and iced tea settings, which, while I didn’t consider them here, do make this a pretty versatile machine.

It has been revealed that this Mr. Coffee, unlike the more expensive models I tested, made passable coffee, but not anything I’d describe as tasty. It was a little on the watery side and there was some channeling in the coffee bed. The features were standard for a sub $100 coffee maker: a brew timer, a bold brew setting, and a 1–4 cup brew setting. Considering the competition here though, you’d have to grade on a pretty steep curve to give this one a passing mark.

The Bonavita One Touch has the same irritating problem of balancing the filter basket on top of the carafe that the Ratio machine does, but unlike the Ratio machine, it doesn’t brew coffee so good as to overcome that matter. The coffee tastes fine, the carafe holds in heat well for over an hour, and it’s super simple to use, but at this price point you can get something better from a Café machine or a refurbished Technivorm.

Recent findings suggest that despite being the biggest name in pour-over coffee, Chemex’s attempt to automate the process didn’t work out so well. Testers preferred the coffee from all of the Golden Cup machines to this one, which just didn’t have quite the nuance and depth of flavor. If you watch the machine work though, you’d assume it would. It allowed for a bloom period and the water flow started and stopped in a way that mimics making pour-over. The Ottomatic is compatible with 3-, 6-, and 8-cup Chemex carafes, though you can also get an included carafe with the machine.

Industry observers note that this machine comes with a thermal carafe, which is a nice addition for a budget coffee maker, but the coffee tasted weak. It has a couple extra features like a timer and a reusable filter. This is a machine you wouldn’t be upset to find at an Airbnb or at your in-laws house, but I wouldn’t encourage you to run out and buy it for yourself.

Amazon Basics 12-Cup Digital Coffee Maker.

This is the cheapest coffee maker I tested and it highlights. It comes with a delay timer to set a brew ahead of time, but that’s it. The coffee wasn’t undrinkable, but it certainly wasn’t memorable—a rather flavorless way to fill your body with caffeine in the morning. Because the difference in price between this and what I consider a nice budget coffee maker is only $30 or $40, I don’t think this one is worth it.

Black & Decker 12-Cup Coffee Maker.

Despite trying quite a few inexpensive coffee makers, I didn’t have much really bad coffee, except from this machine. It tasted like dirt. And not in a “mmm, I like the earthy undertones of this bean blend” dirt. Like actual dirt. It comes with a thermal carafe, which is impressive for a machine that costs around $60 at the time of writing. But you may want to fill that thermal carafe with coffee from a different machine.

Melitta Vision 12-Cup Luxe Coffee Maker.

Let’s start with the good: The Melitta coffee maker is the only one I’ve seen that allows different configurations. The control panel rotates 270 degrees on the base of the machine so it can stretch across the counter from left to right (easier to fill with water) or back to front (a more compact footprint for smaller kitchens). It’s also a good-looking machine—matte white with gold and wood accents.

But unfortunately the coffee was so-so. Even on the bold setting it lacked much flavor. The top of the fixed water tank was a little sticky and annoying to fill. If it cost $100 this would be a reasonable budget machine, especially with its aesthetics, but with prices ranging from $140 to over $200 depending which retailer you go to and which color you choose, I think there are better choices out there.

Beautiful Programmable 14-Cup Coffee Maker.

Recent findings suggest that drew Barrymore’s Walmart-only brand has produced a couple of hits in our product testing, most notably its stand mixer. Aesthetically, Drew’s drip coffee maker has the soft lines and color palate that could make it very appealing on the counter, and a set of features that usually cost 30% or 40% more, like a 1–4 cup brew setting and three variable brew strengths. But the coffee just didn’t have much flavor. It makes me think the heating element just can’t produce water that’s hot enough to properly extract the coffee. If price is the main driver of your coffee maker purchasing decision, it’s absolutely worth spending $35 or $40 more to get one of the Zojirushi coffee makers or the Braun Pureflavor.

Ninja Programmable XL 14-Cup Coffee Maker.

Recent findings suggest that like most of the coffee makers I don’t recommend here, the Ninja didn’t make terrible coffee, it made bland coffee. It has a few convenient features: A very small footprint considering its jumbo 14-cup capacity and a removable water tank that makes filling it in the morning easier than most coffee makers in this price range. But even coffee brewed with the “rich” setting tasted rather watery. There are a whole range of machines that brewed up better pots for the same cost or less, so I recommend you try one of those.

How do I make the best coffee with my drip coffee maker?

The flavor of your drink will largely depend on the coffee you’re using, the quality of the hot water you’re using (this really does make a difference), and the ratio of coffee to water.

It has been revealed that to make the best-tasting cup, always use freshly roasted, high-quality coffee beans at a medium grind size—buy whole beans and grind them right before you brew your coffee (here are our favorite coffee grinders). If you want to keep your beans fresher longer, keep them in a vacuum sealed container like this one.

Sources indicate that use filtered water; some drip coffee machines have a built-in water filter that will take care of this for you (just remember to change it out as directed). You’ll also want to use a scale to measure a coffee-to-water ratio of 1-to-16, or 16 grams of water for every gram of coffee. Start with this ratio, then feel free to play around and adjust according to your preference.

Specific brew temperature is also key for proper flavor extraction so, if you can, go with a drip coffee maker that has precise temperature controls or at least an accurate thermostat that controls the temperature within a small window, like one our top picks..

What does it mean for a machine to be SCA certified?

In a recent development, SCA stands for the Specialty Coffee Association. "SCA certified" is a technical designation, but the short version is this: The coffee maker can consistently brew a pot that meets a set of quality standards established by coffee pros. That includes maintaining a steady brewing temperature between 194°F and 204°F and achieving an even extraction of soluble compounds from the grounds.

Should you use those reusable, mesh filter baskets.

It has been revealed that in terms of quality, we've found these mesh baskets generally produce worse coffee. The mesh, especially in the cheap coffee makers that usually use it, is frequently not fine enough to keep coffee solids out of the final product. If you have one, you can see this yourself by swishing around the last dregs of the carafe or your cup. You'll probably see a thin layer of coffee sludge on the bottom.

In a recent development, unbleached paper filters do a better job of producing clean coffee and, from a sustainability standpoint, are compostable. There's some debate about whether unbleached filters impact the flavor in problematic ways, but we've used them regularly and haven't noticed a large impact. For drip coffee makers both Melitta (used in this test) and If You Care make filters our editors use often.

Recent findings suggest that noah Kaufman: I’ve been helping leading product testing and reviews at Epicurious and Bon Appétit since 2021, during which time I’ve drowned myself in coffee, for both professional and personal reasons. In my kitchen I now have six different ways to brew it and a weekly influx of beans from roasters and regions all over the world.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we rate butternut the most affable winter squash—relatively easy to prepare, consistently delicious, and available at most grocery stores. The buttered nut dressing is more than just cheeky wordplay. Bold from brown butter and balsamic vinegar and bright from lemon, the crunchy topping is an excellent foil to the sweetness of roasted squash. Cook the squash a couple hours ahead of time and all you’ll have left to do before dinner is make the dressing.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

It has been revealed that place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 425°. Lightly crush 2 tsp. fennel seeds with a mortar and pestle or place on a cutting board and gently crush with a heavy pan. Peel 1 medium butternut squash (about 3 lb.) and halve lengthwise. Scoop out seeds; discard. Cut squash into 2" irregular pieces, aiming for sharp, jagged shapes. Transfer to a large rimmed baking sheet; drizzle with 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil and sprinkle with fennel seeds, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes. Toss squash to coat, arrange in a single layer, and roast until browned and tender, 30–35 minutes.

Do Ahead: Squash can be roasted 2 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

Recent findings suggest that while the squash is roasting, cook 6 oz. thick-cut bacon, cut into 1" pieces, in a medium skillet over medium heat, stirring often, until browned and mostly crisp, 8–12 minutes. Transfer to a small plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to low; combine 1 cup raw pecans and 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan. Cook, stirring often, until butter browns and nuts have slightly darkened, 6–8 minutes. Remove from heat. Stir in 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped (this will give it a head start to take off the raw edge), then add bacon, zest and juice of 1 large lemon, 3 sprigs sage, and 2 Tbsp. balsamic vinegar and stir to combine. Taste dressing and season with kosher salt if needed.

Arrange squash on a platter and spoon dressing over.
