There are others (cast-iron nerds and collectors) who swear by the superior quality of their vintage pan from Griswold or Wagner that they found at a scrap yard, de-rusted in a bucket with a DIY electrolysis setup, and seasoned with a proprietary oil blend in the furnaces of their bespoke restoration workshop.

Industry observers note that to these two camps of people I say: “I don’t want to fight you, and I already know why you feel the way you feel. Please do not send me any angry emails.”.

Recent findings suggest that if you’ve been loyal to your own cast-iron pan for years—or decades—I don’t expect to change your mind. My goal is merely to provide recommendations for cast-iron cookware based on side-by-side testing and the input collectively provided by members of our staff. Agree with me and my team or don’t; either way, I’m happy if people are passionate about cooking with cast iron because I too enjoy it a great deal.

Cast-iron frying pans were the original nonstick pans, before ceramic nonstick and PTFE rolled around, and unlike modern nonstick coatings, a cast-iron pan’s surface actually gets more nonstick over time rather than degrading week by week. This is because, through continued cooking, thin layers of oil polymerize to the surface of the pan, creating a glassy nonstick surface that improves with continued use. They are also strong enough to handle metal utensils. The same can’t be mentioned for that Instagram-famous nonstick pan (you know the one).

In a recent development, yes, there are ways you can damage this seasoning layer, but these pans are far more resilient than lots of people think, and they aren’t actually all that difficult to care for. Talk to cast-iron enthusiasts and they’ll tell you the best way to season a cast-iron skillet is to just keep cooking with it.

Recent findings suggest that and cook with it you can. Cast-iron pans are amazing for fried eggs, skillet hashes, cornbread, and sautéed greens. At a high heat, they do an incredible job searing strip steaks, London broil, and chicken thighs, giving you a burnished crispy exterior.

Bottom line, cast-iron cooking is an absolute joy, and every kitchen tool kit should include some cast iron alongside its stainless-steel and carbon steel pans and enameled Dutch oven.

In a recent development, what I loved: Because they’re much more expensive than the Lodges folks got used to, many feel a certain type of way about the upcoming era of smooth, vintage-style cast-iron pans that includes this Lancaster. But when you have the opportunity to test a bunch of these pans side by side, you really get a sense of their differences (however small), and you’d be surprised by the things you notice. It was in this apples-to-apples testing that this pan, manufactured by a small firm based in Southeastern Pennsylvania, really set itself apart.

Industry observers note that the Lancaster is the lightest cast-iron pan I’ve tested, weighing in at 4 lb. for the No. 8 (10"-diameter) pan. Most cast-iron pans of a similar size are around 5 lb. or more—a seemingly small difference in number that makes a surprisingly substantial difference in hand. When laid out next to a dozen pans in the Test Kitchen, multiple testers singled out this pan as being the most comfortable to hold and maneuver.

Sources indicate that it has thinner walls than a typical cast-iron skillet, which allows it to heat up faster. In testing, it came to temp over one minute faster than pans with thicker walls. We were concerned this would mean a reduction in the level of heat retention you’d want to crisp up the edges of some skillet cornbread, but we didn’t find that to be a problem at all. The cooking surface also demonstrated relatively even heat for a cast-iron pan (you really can’t expect too much from cast iron, though; cold spots are sort of inevitable with the material).

The pan comes pre-seasoned, but as is the case with most smooth cast-iron pans, this seasoning layer isn’t nearly as robust as what you’d find on a conventional Lodge or Victoria pan. The polished surface does aid in the pan’s nonstick properties, though, so we found the pan was exceptionally nonstick right out of the box.

Other testing sites have criticized this style of smooth cast-iron pan for getting stained after cooking, but to that we say: This is the process of seasoning developing on the pan. That staining is a feature, not a bug.

Industry observers note that an earlier design of this pan didn’t include a helper handle, a feature we missed but forgave because the pan was already so easy to wield. However, Lancaster recently updated the design to include one—all the better in our book. Check out my full review of the Lancaster No. 8 here.

What I’d leave: The main drawback here is the cost. This pan will set you back $175, a steep price for cookware with a reputation for being budget-friendly. I’ll just say this: People happily pay comparable prices for nonstick ceramic cookware that lasts only a year or two at best. This pan, provided you don’t drop it in an industrial crucible, will last a lifetime.

Recent findings suggest that in the long run: I have more patience than a lot of people when it comes to taking care of pans. So I will concede that the out of the box seasoning isn’t that robust. Some tasks, like searing off meat, can strip the seasoning slightly at first. With the Lancaster, I’ve found that this doesn’t impact the pans overall nonstick-ness. It does, however, mean you have to keep an eye out for rust until it gets a couple uses under its belt.

Below you’ll see two Lancaster pans. The left is four years old and the right is fresh from the box (you can tell because the earlier generation of pans didn’t have the helper handle). These are the pans after searing off two chicken thighs. You can see how the pan on the left has a robust, established seasoning, while the one on the right has some gray patches where the chicken skin pulled off some of that seasoning. From experience (I am the owner of the pan on the left), I can say that all you really need to do is keep cooking with it to get that seasoning back, but if you want to do a whole round of seasoning in the oven yourself, it certainly won’t hurt. Honestly, had I just sautéed some onions in the rendered schmaltz after cooking the chicken, those spots would be taken care of.

For comparison, I seared some chicken thighs in both pans. The factory seasoning might get patchy after the first use. Don’t let that scare you, just keep cooking with it. If you’re really worried about rust, just wipe down the surface of the pan with a tiny bit of neutral oil, buff off the excess, and put it over the heat for a few minutes.

Sources indicate that some people complain about the cosmetic changes to these smooth pans when breaking them in To reiterate: It does not impact the performance of the pan. If it bothers you, I encourage you to think about how it’s a record of use and proof that it’s growing and developing alongside you. Or, if you’re just an unsentimental aesthete, perhaps read up on the concept of wabi-sabi. I personally think that my pan is the most beautiful piece of cookware I own!

Industry observers note that if you want a high-quality pan that’s not only a pleasure to cook with, but can serve as a family heirloom for generations to come, consider this one. If you’re just looking for a workhorse that won’t break the bank, go for the budget option below.

But in my testing, the Victoria edged out the fan favorite on two separate metrics. Victoria pans are pre-seasoned with flaxseed oil and arrive glossy and exceptionally nonstick. Having a more thorough pre-seasoning is more crucial on cast-iron pans, as they are prone to sticking early on. We found the Victoria pan’s factory seasoning slicker than Lodge’s, which made frying potatoes and eggs ever so slightly easier. Do all cast-iron seasonings improve with continued use over time? Yes. Heavier skillets are cheaper and easier to produce, so it’s a trade-off you’ll have to accept if you want a less expensive piece of cookware.

I omitted enameled cast-iron skillets like those made by Le Creuset or Staub because enameled surfaces offer a different experience in terms of both cooking and care. I also chose to exclude any cast-iron griddles or grill pans since they are too different functionally.

In a recent development, sizing is a bit different from company to company, but I chose to stick with a 10"-diameter skillet—a No. 8 in traditional cast-iron sizing—as it is the most common size available.

How nonstick is the pan out of the box?

In a recent development, I should clarify that cast-iron pans aren’t nonstick in the sense that you can cook an egg in the pan without any oil and slide it around. A really well-seasoned pan that’s a glossy lacquered black from years of use might get close, but the seasoning really just helps food release more easily from the pan—and the more seasoning there is, the less oil you’ll need for food to release.

I evaluated the pans on their out-of-the-box factory seasoning, because having a solid seasoning layer to start with diminishes the amount of time you need to break in a pan. This matters more with cheaper, rough textured cast iron, which is more prone to sticking when it lacks proper seasoning. For polished or vintage-style cast-iron pans (like the Lancaster), factory seasoning is nice, but the smooth surface also aids in preventing sticking, so it isn’t as crucial in the beginning stages of using the pan. That is why, throughout this review you see more emphasis on factory seasoning when discussing budget pans.

Is the pan designed in a way that makes it easy to use?

I counted form and design heavily in how I judged these pans. I wanted the pan to be comfortable and easy to maneuver, so I looked for pans that were lightweight (relatively, we’re talking about iron here) and had handles that were comfortable to grip. If the pan was heavier, I wanted a helper handle for moving it from the cooktop to the oven. I didn’t place an emphasis on whether handle was designed to stay cool, because even a handle billed as “stay cool” will get dangerously hot when cooking for long enough, so I feel it’s better to just make a habit of always using an oven mitt or cloth to grab a cast-iron handle.

Industry observers note that heavy-duty, even-heating, satisfyingly weighty skillets are staples in the BA Test Kitchen because of their versatility. Stainless-steel and carbon steel frying pans get hot promptly, but they don’t always have the heat-retention capabilities of cast iron. And while nonstick pans are nice for scrambled eggs and crispy-skinned fish, many are not oven-safe and should never be exposed to high temperatures, so you can’t sear safely with them.

Stargazer Cast Iron Skillet - 10.5".

If you know cast-iron pans, you might see the Yeti cast-iron skillet and might find that it looks somewhat familiar. This is because Yeti acquired cult-favorite Butter Pat several years ago. The Yeti skillet is just the Butter Pat by a newly introduced name, and apart from the logo, the finish, handle shape, and overall design remain unchanged. When you first get your pan, you’ll want to season it. We recommend this even when the pan comes labeled as pre-seasoned. To do this, just lightly rub a bone-dry pan with a thin layer of high-heat neutral vegetable oil and place it upside down in a very hot oven—450°F–500°F should do the trick. Leave for an hour, turn off the heat, let it cool completely in the oven (you should be able to take it out without an oven mitt or towel), rub with a tiny bit more oil, and store. You can season cast iron as many times as you’d like to build up a glossy nonstick surface; when the pan looks dull or dry, it’s time to moisturize.

Sources indicate that no, you can’t chuck it in the dishwasher, and you won’t be using your normal hand-wash methods, but a cast-iron skillet really doesn’t require much love. When it’s time to clean up, simply wipe a damp rag across the surface of your pan, then dry it thoroughly. Often, that’ll be enough. But if there are any crusty bits, try pouring coarse salt in there and going at it with a Tawashi scrubber, which has soft bristles that whisk away any detritus. Many will tell you to avoid soap at all costs lest you ruin your careful seasoning, but a little dish soap is fine—just don’t let it sit in hot water. (Read our complete guide to cleaning cast iron.).

It has been revealed that for really baked on crumbs, try The Ringer, a handy chain mail scrubber that easily rinses clean between uses. After cleaning your cast iron, be sure to wipe your fry pan very dry—this is key for preventing any rust spots. Then take a teeny bit of neutral cooking oil (like canola or vegetable), smear on a paper towel, and give it a light coating. Take care to get the handle and the bottom as well as the cooking surface, as rust can crop up anywhere. And you’re good to go! It sounds involved, but it really only takes a few minutes. A well-seasoned pan takes virtually no time at all, so dutifully season and you’ll be rewarded.

Tossed your skillet in the sink absentmindedly or left it out in the rain only to find it’s developed a layer of orange rust? Don’t panic—rusting can happen pretty easily if you allow your pan to come into contact with water for an extended period of time (it is made of iron, after all). But that doesn’t mean it’s ruined. A salt scrub will help with most small spots, while a vinegar soak is the cure for more serious cases. (Read more on dealing with pesky cast-iron rust patches.).

If, after all of that, you’re still intimidated by raw cast-iron cookware, you might want to consider an enameled cast-iron skillet. It offers all of the heat retention and distribution of a well-seasoned cast-iron pan, plus it has a porcelain enamel to prevent rusting. Unlike a Le Creuset Dutch oven, enameled cast-iron skillets, like Staub’s, have a dark textured enamel that helps with browning and crisping.

In a recent development, wilder Davies: I have been Epicurious and Bon Appétit’s resident cookware tester and researcher for over six years. I have cooked with hundreds and hundreds of pans and have asked chefs, materials scientists, and manufacturers far too many questions about things that go clank in the kitchen. I am a massive apologist of nonstick alternatives, and strongly believe in a buy-it-for-life ethos when it comes to outfitting your pantry.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • This recipe is one of BA’s Best, our vault of the Test Kitchen's definitive takes on iconic dishes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Unlike many iconic Italian recipes, this luxurious union of silky broccoli rabe, chile-flecked sausage, garlic, and curvaceous pasta is a weeknight hero. You can make it start to finish, in about 30 minutes. The key to successful execution is to go way beyond blanching when it comes to precooking the broccoli rabe in boiling salted water. For tender rabe that melds seamlessly with pasta and sausage, start by separating the thick stems from the rest of the stalks and giving them a head start before adding the rest. It removes any unpleasant bitterness and also means the rabe will cook into the saucy base of browned sausage and sweated garlic in just minutes.

While orecchiette is the traditional pasta choice, any short pasta will work. Sausage has become a popular addition to the true original Pugliese dish of stewed broccoli rabe with pasta, but a tin of anchovies makes a great substitute for added oomph and intensity.

This recipe is one of BA’s Best, our vault of the Test Kitchen's definitive takes on iconic dishes.

Cut 2 large bunches broccoli rabe, trimmed, in half crosswise to separate thick stalks from thinner stems and florets. Cook thicker stalks in a medium pot of boiling salted water until crisp-tender, about 5 minutes. Add thinner stems and florets and cook until all of the broccoli rabe is tender (the tip of a paring knife should slide through the stalks with little to no resistance), about 3 minutes. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet with tongs; let sit until cool enough to handle (no need to squeeze out excess water unless dripping wet). Coarsely chop into bite-size pieces.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, cook 1 lb. orecchiette (little ear-shaped pasta) or other short pasta in a second medium pot of boiling salted water until al dente (or use same pot with fresh salted water). Drain, reserving 2 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Industry observers note that heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 1 lb. hot Italian sausage, casings removed if needed, breaking up with a wooden spoon, until golden brown and nearly cooked through, about 5 minutes. Add 1 head of garlic, cloves separated, peeled, thinly sliced, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, breaking up sausage even finer if needed and stirring often, until garlic is golden brown and softened, 3–4 minutes. Add broccoli rabe and cook, stirring occasionally, until very tender and wilted, about 5 minutes.

Sources indicate that add 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter, cut into pieces, pasta, and 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Cook, stirring often and adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is coated in a clingy sauce. Taste and add some crushed red pepper flakes if desired. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup), and stir, adding more pasta cooking liquid a splash at a time as needed to keep sauce smooth and shiny, until incorporated; season with salt.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan.

Sources indicate that florida Rep. Darren Soto, here at a hearing in July, has won a sixth term representing the 9th District. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

Florida Rep. Darren Soto, the most vulnerable House Democrat running for reelection, narrowly won a sixth term Tuesday in a district that state Republicans redrew in their favor.

Soto was leading Republican Navy veteran Dan Green by less than a point when The Associated Press called the race for Central Florida’s 9th District a week after Election Day. His margin of victory was above the 0.5 percent threshold that would trigger a recount under state law.

House Democrats have so far flipped more than 40 seats and appear on track to hold their biggest majority in the chamber in decades. Soto’s win means that no House Democratic incumbent lost to a Republican in the general election this year. And Florida Democrats defended all four seats the GOP had hoped to pick up under the state’s latest Republican-drawn map.

Recent findings suggest that democratic Reps. Kathy Castor and Jared Moskowitz both won reelection from districts that shifted red, while Democrat Pia Dandiya, a former high school principal, defeated Republican Marine Corps veteran Casey Askar for a redrawn open seat in South Florida.

Soto, who declared victory last week, had been seen as the most vulnerable of the targeted Florida Democrats. The new map reduced the Hispanic population of his district as the seat shifted from one that Kamala Harris would have carried in 2024 to one that Donald Trump would have taken by 18 points.

It has been revealed that “Despite the Florida Republican legislature’s efforts to redraw me out of this district, my record of delivering for Florida indicated voters that I am a reliable fighter for them in Congress,” Soto said in a Nov. 4 statement.

In a Tuesday memo detailing how House Democrats secured their historic majority, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee took aim at Republicans’ mid-decade redistricting efforts, saying their “attempts to steal seats … supremely backfired.”.

Sources indicate that while Florida Republicans were unsuccessful in flipping the four Democrat-held seats, the party held all of its House seats in the Sunshine State. Republican Rep. María Elvira Salazar narrowly won reelection in the Miami-area 27th District over Democratic challenger Eliott Rodriguez, the AP reported Tuesday. In the 7th District outside Orlando, Republican former TV news anchor Ryan Elijah defeated Democratic Navy veteran Bale Dalton, a former NASA chief of staff who conceded Tuesday.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that these maple-glazed carrots don’t hold back on the butter—or the brown sugar. Roasted with pure maple syrup and crushed red pepper flakes, they turn tender and glossy with a sweet-hot kick that complements everything from ham to lamb to green bean casserole.

The recipe began with Barbie—not the doll, but Andy Baraghani’s cousin’s former girlfriend. Her syrupy-sweet carrots became a fixture at family Christmas dinners. Some dishes are meant to last; some relationships aren’t.

Recent findings suggest that for BA’s version, Andy traded the original’s hours-long cooking time for a hotter roast that gives the carrots browned edges and a buttery glaze. There’s no separate sauce to simmer: Everything goes straight onto a foil-lined (for easier cleanup) rimmed baking sheet, with regular tossing to coat the carrots in syrup as they cook. Finish with flaky salt for crunch and a welcome contrast to the sweetness.

Recent findings suggest that no. This recipe calls for scrubbed, unpeeled carrots—give them a thorough cleaning and leave the skins on.

How do I keep the glaze from burning?

Keep the carrot pieces similar in thickness, halving or quartering larger ones lengthwise. Check the glaze each time you toss the carrots, especially once the edges begin browning: The sugars can darken quickly. Use tenderness and browned edges as your guide rather than waiting out the clock if the carrots are already done.

For a more savory version, try our Easy Roasted Carrots.

It has been revealed that place rack in middle of oven and preheat oven to 400°. Line a rimmed baking sheet with 3 sheets of foil (you’ll need it!). Cut 2 lb. medium carrots, tops trimmed to about ½", scrubbed, on a diagonal into 3" pieces (halved or quartered lengthwise if large).

Spread out carrots on foil. Evenly top with 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, ⅓ cup (packed; 70 g) light brown sugar, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, and ¾ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes. Season with kosher salt and toss to combine.

Recent findings suggest that roast carrots, tossing every 20 minutes, until tender and browned around the edges, 50–60 minutes. Watch closely as the carrots begin to brown; the glaze can darken swiftly. Transfer to a platter and drizzle with any remaining syrup. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt (if using).

#66052. Spinach Artichoke Baked Potatoes

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (470 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Epicurious ↗ Open Full Page

Spinach Artichoke Baked Potatoes

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (470 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that this baked potato stuffed with spinach-artichoke dip is the ultimate solo comfort meal.
  • Industry observers note that the rich, velvety filling that melts over top comes together in moments while your spud cooks.
  • It has been revealed that most recipes serve multiple people.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that this baked potato stuffed with spinach-artichoke dip is the ultimate solo comfort meal. Classic twice-baked potatoes require two trips to the oven to deliver a pillowy, gussied-up filling and crispy skins all in one bite. Here, I’ve streamlined the workflow with a microwave. By zapping your spuds to start, you can reduce the overall baking time without sacrificing texture. Pick a large russet (or Idaho) for the best results; their relatively high starch and low moisture content helps them bake up airy and light, not gummy.

Industry observers note that the rich, velvety filling that melts over top comes together in moments while your spud cooks. Cream cheese and mozzarella pack in enough dairy richness for a satisfying cheese pull and mellow out the subtle bitterness of baby spinach and nutty tang of artichoke hearts. (It’s important that your cream cheese is room temperature before you mash it in with the veggies. If it’s still got a chill from the fridge, it won’t fully incorporate.) The Worcestershire sauce is optional, but just a few shakes from the bottle bring instant savory depth to the filling.

It has been revealed that most recipes serve multiple people. In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one. That's you! Because whether you live solo (almost 30% of Americans do) or are enjoying a night to yourself, sitting down to a meal should be something to look forward to.

Preheat oven to 425°. Poke 1 large russet potato (about 12 oz.) all over with a fork; rub with avocado or vegetable oil to coat and sprinkle with kosher salt. Microwave potato on a microwave-proof plate on high 5 minutes. Turn potato over and microwave on high until fork-tender, about 5 minutes more. Let potato sit until just cool enough to handle.

Industry observers note that while potato is cooling, microwave 5 oz. baby spinach with 2 Tbsp. water in a medium microwave-proof glass bowl until wilted, about 2 minutes. Carefully press leaves to release as much liquid as possible, then drain off liquid. Coarsely chop spinach.

Mix 2 Tbsp. cream cheese, room temperature, in a medium bowl until smooth. Add spinach, 4 quartered artichoke hearts (from a 14-oz. can), coarsely chopped, 2 Tbsp. finely grated Parmesan, 2 Tbsp. coarsely grated mozzarella, ½ tsp. garlic powder, and ¼ tsp. Worcestershire sauce (if using) and fold to combine; season with salt and freshly ground pepper.

According to recent reports, slice potato in half lengthwise and lightly fluff flesh in each half. Set on a small foil-lined rimmed baking sheet. Divide spinach mixture between potato halves, piling high (don’t pack too tightly). Sprinkle more Parmesan over. Bake potato halves until very tender when squeezed and skin is wrinkled and crisp, 20–25 minutes. Let cool slightly before eating.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This past weekend the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen in Upcoming York City opened its doors to the public for Bon Appétit Live, an immersive day of cooking demos and classes, talks with chefs and recipe experts, Test Kitchen tours, games, prizes, and plenty to eat and drink.

The day kicked off with a warm welcome from Bon Appétit’s editor-in-chief Jamila Robinson, who exclaimed that “the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen is the heart of our brand.” Robinson also shared that Bon Appétit just launched a new cooking app containing tens of thousands of recipes from the Test Kitchen archives.

Guests fueled up with an impressive array of curated breakfast treats alongside refreshing beverages from S.Pellegrino, before moving on to interactive experiences.

In the first class of the day, baking novices and aficionados alike joined senior Test Kitchen editor and BA Bake Club expert Jesse Szewczyk in the Test Kitchen for Pie Crust Fundamentals, presented by East Fork. The hands-on class featured guest Keia Mastrianni, brand storyteller and “unofficial pie lady” of East Fork. Mastrianni proclaimed her enthusiasm for pie making: “I love preaching the gospel of pie. My favorite thing is teaching people to make pie dough with their hands.” Szewczyk agreed, emphasizing the tactile nature of the process: “It’s a very physical thing to do…a recipe can be written, but teaching someone to make pie dough requires demonstration.” Participants were in luck as Szewczyk and Mastrianni demonstrated a buttery pie crust fortified with cream cheese, a recipe ideal for Thanksgiving developed by former senior Test Kitchen editor Shilpa Uskokovic. After Mastrianni shared crimping tips, participants made their own pie dough at stations throughout the kitchen, with Test Kitchen editors on hand to offer guidance. One participant, James, was particularly excited to be working with director of cooking Emma Laperruque. He enthused, “Before Emma’s and Chris [Morocco’s] recipes, I would burn water. [Bon Appétit] has made cooking really accessible, and I built a lot of confidence. I love the simplicity of Emma’s recipes…they are all so flavorful and so good.”.

It has been revealed that each guest left ready for holiday baking season with newly introduced pie-making skills, and a ceramic pie dish from East Fork’s new bakeware collection, featuring clay and glaze made in-house with materials sourced in the Southeast. Before moving on to their next experience, Mastrianni encouraged everyone to keep honing their skills, emphasizing, “Practice makes pie. Progress, not perfection.”.

Meanwhile, in the neighboring Demo Kitchen, a Pasta Boot Camp was underway with Bon Appétit senior cooking editor Kelsey Jane Youngman and chef Stefano Secchi. Secchi, chef and partner of Latest York City’s Rezdôra (recipient of one Michelin star) and Massara, honed his craft in Modena, Italy, under legendary chef Massimo Bottura.

In a recent development, after walking guests through the fundamentals of making and shaping fresh pasta by hand, Secchi demonstrated a filled ravioli dish aptly named Holiday in Parma. Made with 00 flour and egg dough, the ravioli was piped with a chestnut and Parmesan filling and served with a rich reduction of chicken broth, butter, and saba (a traditional Italian syrup made from slowly simmered grape must).

It has been revealed that while guests savored their pasta in the Demo Kitchen, a lively panel discussion was underway on the 34th floor. Moderated by editor-in-chief Jamila Robinson, the Bringing Culture to Cooking panel featured chefs Fariyal Abdullahi (executive chef, Hav & Mar, NYC), Nicholas Bazik (chef and owner, Provenance, Philadelphia, a Bon Appétit Best New Restaurant of 2025), and Vijay Kumar (executive chef and partner, Semma, NYC, a Best New Restaurant of 2022). The conversation explored how culture, identity, and personal experience inform each chef’s cooking. The chefs shared some of their favorite home-cooking ingredients, such as Chef Bazik’s fermented lime juice, a versatile seasoning made by combining fresh lime juice with salt at a 2% ratio by weight. Chef Abdullahi championed berbere, the Ethiopian spice blend she likened to “Ethiopian salt” for its ubiquity in the country’s cooking. Abdullahi cautioned that store-bought blends are convenient but not necessarily of the highest-possible quality. “You should make it at home!” she encouraged.

Back in the Test Kitchen, Visit Maine hosted Lobster 101, a hands-on lobster class and oyster tasting with Bon Appétit’s manager of audience strategy Carly Westerfield and Krista Tripp, founder of Aphrodite Oysters in South Thomaston, Maine. Each participant received a whole, steamed Maine lobster and the ingredients and tools needed to transform it into a creamy, decadent lobster dip. Under Westerfield’s guidance, the class learned how to break down their lobsters, extract the meat, and assemble a dip made with cream cheese, mayonnaise, celery, chives, and lemon juice. The approachable demonstration demystified the process and showed guests how easily they could prepare a luxurious appetizer at home, just in time for the holidays.

Industry observers note that participants worked with hard-shell lobsters, but Tripp encouraged them to visit Maine and sample both hard-shell and soft-shell varieties. She explained that soft-shell lobsters, typically in season from July through August, have a sweeter, more tender meat. The two are actually the same animal at different stages of its molting cycle: a soft-shell lobster has recently shed its old shell, leaving a newer, more pliable one that is easier to crack. The class concluded with a tasting of Aphrodite Oysters, grown in the waters off South Thomaston, Maine. The medium-size oysters were briny and subtly sweet, reflecting the cold, brackish waters of the Lower Weskeag River where they were grown. A small squeeze of lemon was all that was needed to enhance their flavor as guests tilted their heads back, slurped, and allowed themselves to be transported to the rugged coast of Maine.

Meanwhile, in the Demo Kitchen, Bon Appétit director of culture Joseph Hernandez was joined by Matt Conroy, chef at Washington, DC’s Maison Bar à Vins, for a live cooking demonstration of one of Chef Conroy’s favorite dishes. Named one of Bon Appétit’s Best New Restaurants of 2026, the restaurant pairs French-inspired cooking with an eclectic wine list and seasonal cocktails. Chef Conroy prepared a new fall salad made of chicory, pear, and smoked blue cheese, finished with a Banyuls vinaigrette.

In the cafeteria, guests gathered for a live version of the Dear Bon Appétit advice column. Bon Appétit director of cooking Emma Laperruque presented questions about home cooking and holiday entertaining to chef Amanda Freitag. One attendee asked Freitag how to handle undercooked turkey legs and thighs each year. Freitag recommended removing the legs and cooking them separately, as in this BA recipe for Gravy-Braised Turkey from Jesse Szewczyk.

Recent findings suggest that next, food stylist Thu Buser showcased her exceptional culinary artistry by decorating an elaborate “snake cake” with vibrant green swirls and flowers. Then, a break for lunch with BA’s Best Mozzarella Sticks, a variety of salads and skewers, hot honey salmon, smoothies, and a cranberry maple mule.

While attendees grazed and mingled, Jamila Robinson joined legendary chef and restaurateur Marcus Samuelsson to discuss Back to Green: Rediscovering a World of Delicious, Healthy Eating, his latest global plant-forward cookbook coauthored by Robinson. Samuelsson captured the atmosphere of the event, remarking, “What a party we are having here…the energy is amazing!”.

The final demonstration of the day featured Cornmeal Shortcakes with Blueberry Compote presented by Visit Maine with Jesse Szewczyk and Ron Howard of Brodis Blueberries. Featuring a recipe from Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firsker, the shortcakes showcased farm-fresh wild blueberries grown on a ninth-generation family farm. As Szewczyk prepared the recipe, Howard discussed the importance of wild blueberries to Maine’s agricultural heritage. A native crop, they can be traced back to the end of the last Ice Age, predating lobster as a symbol of the state. “Everyone should think of wild blueberries as the ultimate Maine crop,” Howard explained. After tasting the shortcakes, attendees would be hard-pressed to disagree. Szewczyk noted that compared with conventional blueberries, the wild blueberries produced a more saturated color and tasted more distinctly of blueberry.

Recent findings suggest that the day ended on a sweet note with pastry chef Eunji Lee, winner of North America’s Best Pastry Chef Award from The 50. Attendees had a chance to meet Lee and sample pastries from Lysée, her pastry boutique influenced by Korean and French culture and inspired by Upcoming York City.

Recent findings suggest that bon Appétit Live brought together chefs, culinary personalities, and food editors for a day of conversations, cooking, tasting, and learning. Attendees experienced the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen firsthand, learned directly from chefs and editors, and engaged with the people and products behind the food. As editor-in-chief Jamila Robinson noted, “Food is always an invitation…we are so happy to give everyone access to the same experiences we have.”.

The best barn coats for men are a close cousin of the chore jacket—similar in spirit, but built tougher. They’re heartier, heavier, better insulated, and usually more water-resistant. Where the chore jacket belonged to the factory floor, the barn coat was made for the fields: a layer you could shrug on to tackle chores outdoors.

But ever since the ’80s and ’90s, the barn coat has been finding a fresh audience of urbanites who understand its utility, even on mean city streets. Today, alongside the waxy Barbour zip-ups and dad-approved L.L. Bean riffs, a ton of capital-F fashion labels—The Row, Auralee, Prada—have been herding the barn coat back into the center of the style conversation.

Reading to buy your first barn coat? Make sure it’s cut with enough room to comfortably slip a sweater beneath it, and that its craftsmanship ensures it’ll remain a reliable rotation beater for years to come. The former, of course, might demand some trial and error on your end, but the latter is exactly where we come in. These are the absolute best barn coats for men on the market right now, from the genre-defining joints you already know to the sleeper-hit versions you probably don’t.

Deep, easily accessed pockets? A warm corduroy collar? A charming plaid lining? This jacket from J.Crew is, quite simply, the platonic ideal of a barn coat. It has all the details dialed in, built upon a sturdy, 100% cotton washed canvas body that will only soften and feel more like your own in time. Originally launched over 40 years ago, there’s a reason J.Crew is still able to sell it four decades later. And we didn’t even mention the hook on the back, so you can hang this up with ease as soon as you enter your bustling, warm, overcrowded local bar. It’s the little things.

Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In the large bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment, combine the egg whites and salt.
  • Sources indicate that in a medium pot, combine the sugar, corn syrup, and water.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Divinity candy is a classic Southern dessert. If you haven't heard of it yet, I promise you'll be coming back to this recipe over and over again after making it just once! It’s a simple confection made of sugar, eggs, and corn syrup that looks like clouds, with the crunch of meringue and the chew of a perfect marshmallow. It does require a candy thermometer and a bit of patience, but once you know what to look for, it’s extremely simple to make.

In the large bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment, combine the egg whites and salt.

Sources indicate that in a medium pot, combine the sugar, corn syrup, and water. Attach a candy thermometer to the pot before you go any further. Heat the mixture over medium-high heat, undisturbed, until the thermometer registers 250°, which should take about 10 minutes. When the thermometer registers 235°, start whipping egg whites on high speed until stiff peaks form, which should take another 2 to 3 minutes.

Industry observers note that with the mixer running on medium speed, carefully add sugar syrup to egg whites in a thin stream. Make sure to go slowly! The whole process should take about 1 to 2 minutes. Then beat in the vanilla extract.

Proceed to increase mixer speed to high and continue to whip until the mixture comes together and loses some of its gloss, which should take approximately 5 to 10 minutes. Let it all cool until the mixture is slightly thickened and holds its form when spooned onto parchment, another 1 to 2 minutes.

It has been revealed that grease 2 spoons with cooking spray, and working rapidly, spoon candy onto a parchment-lined baking sheet. Swirl it as desired to make the shapes you want! Immediately top the dessert with sprinkles. (The sprinkles won’t stick if you wait too long!).

Let the candy sit until it’s completely dry, just about 2 hours more. Store in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 1 week and enjoy!

The candy can be made 1 week ahead. Store in an airtight container at room temperature.

Thune will lead Republicans through the minority

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1073 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., leaves a meeting in the Capitol on Tuesday, before his election as incoming minority leader later in the day.
  • Senate Majority Leader John Thune was reelected as the Republican leader on Tuesday and will steer the conference through their time in the minority.
  • The South Dakotan ran uncontested despite a push from some of his colleagues to delay the leadership elections following Republicans’ stunning defeats last week in the midterms, which saw them lose at least seven seats and the majority.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., leaves a meeting in the Capitol on Tuesday, before his election as incoming minority leader later in the day. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

Senate Majority Leader John Thune was reelected as the Republican leader on Tuesday and will steer the conference through their time in the minority.

The South Dakotan ran uncontested despite a push from some of his colleagues to delay the leadership elections following Republicans’ stunning defeats last week in the midterms, which saw them lose at least seven seats and the majority.

Recent findings suggest that “Obviously, the election result was not what we hoped for,” Thune told reporters, referring to the midterms. “But I think it’s notable that we take the lessons from that and internalize the message the American people were sending to us.”.

While he and the rest of the leadership slate sailed through the conference contests by voice vote, it wasn’t without drama.

Industry observers note that before the leadership elections began in the Old Supreme Court Chamber early Tuesday morning, the conference held a meeting at the request of a group of GOP five senators, led by Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis.

The conversation, which several senators described as “frank,” ended up pushing back the leadership elections by a few hours. But they were not postponed to another day as some had hoped.

According to recent reports, “This has never been anything against John Thune,” said Johnson, as he made good on his commitment to leave the room early if the conference proceeded with its election. “What I didn’t agree with was holding the election right away, giving nobody an opportunity to really challenge any leadership position.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Part of the problem here is who wants the job? God bless him for serving,” Johnson added.

The conference conversation Tuesday morning turned into an “open-mic” with both conservatives and those who lost their elections speaking, according to senators.

In a recent development, sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., told reporters, “To rush into this and to just ratify all the same leadership — I mean, what message does that send?”.

But no contender to Thune emerged despite the angst, and a motion to proceed to the election, introduced by Thune’s fellow South Dakotan Sen. Mike Rounds, was accepted.

Industry observers note that sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., mentioned voters who rejected Republicans last week were reacting to high gas prices, the war in Iran and the cost of living, not to how Senate leaders were running the conference.

“I don’t think anybody in Texas who voted for the Democrat governor was voting against John Thune. If you diagnose that as a problem, you’re misdiagnosing the problem,” Paul remarked.

Whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo., was reelected to his position, as was the chairman of the Senate Republican Conference, Tom Cotton of Arkansas. Sen. James Lankford of Oklahoma was again selected as vice chair of the conference, while Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia was reelected as Republican Policy Committee chair.

“Our first step is to make sure the American people know that we heard what they said, and the American people’s priorities are our priorities. That’s the way we regain their trust,” Barrasso said afterward.

It has been revealed that sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio got the nod to chair the National Republican Senatorial Committee, meaning he will helm the campaign arm as the party looks ahead to the uncertain waters of 2028.

According to recent reports, moreno mentioned, “I was in the retail automobile business, so when you don’t listen to your customers, your customers punish you. I think we have to own it, and I think we have to learn from it.”.

In a recent development, sen. John Kennedy, R-La., said on Monday evening, “What we as a conference right now need is honesty. We need focus. We need to try to reach a consensus on what we need to change.”.

Kennedy was among those pushing to delay the leadership elections and told reporters on Tuesday he voted present instead of yes on whether to proceed to them.

In a recent development, sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., who ran for GOP leader twice — once in 2022 against Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., and in 2024 against Thune — declined to run again to challenge Thune. But in a Dear Colleague letter on Monday, he detailed what he’d like to see in the lame-duck session before Democrats take power, including confirming every nominee President Donald Trump has sent to the Senate, funding the government without an omnibus, banning stock trading, passing the permitting bill that is advancing this week in the Senate, passing the National Defense Authorization Act, balancing the budget and pushing through a sweeping voter ID bill known as the SAVE America Act.

Senate Republicans on Tuesday also voted on a resolution on their path forward that was spurred by a motion from Scott, aides stated.

“It is the sense of the GOP Conference that we will maximize the 54 days we have with congressional majorities, to confirm every judicial nominee and every executive nominee that the conference approves of, to pass our core Republican priorities, and to do everything humanly possible to pass a reconciliation bill before Jan. 3,” the resolution reads in part.

Sources indicate that that long list of goals highlights the expectations Thune has faced as leader, where he led one-third of Republicans’ trifecta in Washington. In the next Congress, Democrats will hold the majority in both chambers of Congress after their larger-than-expected wins, while Trump finishes out his term as president.

Thune noted he told his conference: “As I look back on the last couple of years, my question is, what would you have me do differently?”.

“Given the constraints we had to deal with, all the stuff that was coming at us on a daily basis, a narrow margin in the House, the White House, the Democrats over here who were obstructing two long government shutdowns — I think we came out of it as well as could have been expected, and got a lot of stuff done,” Thune told reporters.

“If you believe the exit polls, it was the war, it was the economy, it was inflation, it was fuel prices,” Thune added. “So no, I wasn’t apologizing for anything that we did. And I think on the political side, I don’t know what else I could have done.”.

There’s a time and place for classic cheesecake, but it’s hard to resist a handheld dessert. These irresistible cheesecake bars are the solution. They’re like traditional cheesecake’s cool older sister, and she’s invited to your holiday party this year. These bars perfectly balance creamy, rich cheesecake with the tartness of fresh cranberries and the nuttiness and warmth of a pecan streusel topping, with none of the intensive labor required for traditional cheesecake.

Industry observers note that the bars:In this recipe, the cheesecake filling rests in a simple graham cracker crust, and swirls of homemade cranberry sauce weave their way through each bar, adding a burst of flavor and a beautiful marbled effect that makes them almost too pretty to eat—almost. Fresh orange juice and zest bring the cranberry sauce to life and add another layer of brightness and complexity to the bars. The streusel topping, made from a mix of pecans, brown sugar, and cinnamon, adds a satisfying crunch that contrasts beautifully with the creamy cheesecake filling.

The cranberry sauce:If you like, you can simplify this recipe further by using 1 (14-oz.) can of whole berry cranberry sauce rather than making homemade cranberry compote.Storage:Whether you’re making them for a holiday gathering, a potluck, or just because you deserve a delicious treat, these cozy bars are sure to impress. If you’re lucky enough to have any left over, they’ll be amazing with your coffee in the morning; store them in an airtight container in the refrigerator for a few days.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How to buy and store fresh cranberries.

Look for firm, glossy cranberries and discard any that are soft, shriveled, or bruised. A few pale pink berries are nothing to worry about.

Keep unwashed cranberries in their original bag in the refrigerator for up to four weeks, though they’re best used sooner. To stock up, freeze them in their original packaging or spread clean thoroughly dried berries on a baking sheet until frozen, then transfer to a freezer bag. They’ll keep their quality for up to a year. Many cooked cranberry recipes work with frozen berries straight from the freezer; check the recipe before thawing.

It has been revealed that that vivid magenta filling is no food-coloring trick: Cranberries and plenty of lime give the curd its electric hue and tang. Let the pie set overnight, then pile on billowy meringue and break out the kitchen torch.

Sources indicate that A 12-oz. bag of cranberries, sugar, orange zest, and about 10 minutes at the stove are all you need for this tangy Thanksgiving essential. Make it up to five days ahead and save any leftovers for turkey-cranberry sliders.

Layers of tender buttermilk cake, tart cranberry jam, and silky white chocolate frosting make an excellent argument for serving cake on Thanksgiving. The sugared cranberries on top are like little sour candies.

It has been revealed that imagine Key lime pie dressed for the holidays. The punchy cranberry-lime curd meets a crisp press-in crust made with gingersnaps and pecans. A generous dollop of whipped cream rounds out the tartness.

Sources indicate that here’s a reason to keep canned cranberry sauce around after Thanksgiving. Jellied sauce melts into a glossy, sweet-and-sour glaze that coats chicken and green beans. Think orange chicken, with a cranberry twist.

Sources indicate that cranberries turn this classic upside-down apple tart a beautiful rosy pink while cutting through its buttery sweetness. Homemade rough puff pastry supplies the flaky base; vanilla ice cream is very much encouraged.

According to recent reports, canned whole-berry cranberry sauce becomes a punchy dressing for pleasantly bitter endive and frisée. Add crunchy candied pecans and salty Manchego, and suddenly cranberry sauce is doing salad duty.

Two layers of buttery, crumbly walnut crust surround a tart cranberry filling in this striking take on a Linzer torte. Save it for a holiday dessert table—or any occasion that calls for something special.

Recent findings suggest that dress crisp-bottomed Persian rice with dried cranberries, saffron, and fragrant herbs. The berries plump in ghee alongside rosemary, sage, and thyme, adding little pops of sweetness against the savory rice.

If the wobble is the best part of canned cranberry sauce for you, this homemade version delivers. It’s sliceable, deeply fruity, and subtly fragrant with cardamom and bay leaves. Bring on the ridges.

Roasted brussels sprouts get a lively companion in cranberry mostarda, a sweet-tart condiment with mustard seeds, prunes, and a little brandy. Make extra mostarda: It belongs on more than just sprouts.

Industry observers note that A warm cranberry-apple topping brings plenty of tart fruit flavor to this crowd-friendly baked oatmeal. It’s a welcome breakfast when the house is full and everyone seems to wake up hungry at once.

Rum, hard cider, cranberry juice, ginger ale, and lime make a lively batch cocktail. Cranberry-studded ice cubes do double duty, keeping glasses cold and making the punch look party-ready.

Jalapeño and lime give classic cranberry sauce a bright, spicy kick. It’s especially good alongside roasted meats or piled onto a leftover turkey sandwich when you want something with a little heat.

In a recent development, forget the giant roast bird for a minute. These tender, gravy-coated turkey meatballs come with a cranberry-orange marmalade jam that stands in for traditional lingonberries. A heap of mashed potatoes completes the picture.

Sources indicate that fresh ginger gives this cranberry relish some zip, while golden raisins and allspice round out its tartness. Spoon it onto a cheese board or save the leftovers for French toast the next morning.

In a recent development, herbs in the dredge give this crunchy fried chicken Thanksgiving energy, but the quick cranberry-mustard dipping sauce is the real holiday flourish. It’s a compelling alternative to roasting an entire turkey.

Recent findings suggest that homemade cranberry-thyme syrup, Campari, and Champagne make a sparkling cocktail that’s fruity, pleasantly bitter, and dressed for a party. Make the syrup up to two weeks ahead; the drinks come together in minutes.

Boxed stuffing mix gets a serious upgrade with aromatic vegetables, dried cranberries, and the savory drippings from crisp-skinned chicken thighs. It’s Thanksgiving-adjacent comfort food, made in one skillet any night of the week.

Roasted sweet potatoes and delicata squash get a glossy, sweet-and-sour cranberry sauce made with red wine vinegar and thyme. Make extra: The agrodolce is just as good spooned over Thanksgiving turkey.

Sources indicate that whole orange and a cinnamon stick give this chunky cranberry sauce its fragrant warmth. Blanching the chopped orange first keeps bitterness in check, while a little butter softens the berries’ sharp edge.

A buttery, lemony custard studded with tart cranberries gives this Southern classic a holiday spin. The berries stay mostly intact, offering juicy little bursts of tartness against the rich filling.

Dried figs bring earthy sweetness to this bold cranberry chutney, while ginger, vinegar, and whole grain mustard keep it lively. It’s the sort of condiment you’ll want beside roast pork as much as turkey.

Dorie Greenspan’s warmly spiced Bundt packs in fresh and dried cranberries, toasted almonds, and a little five-spice powder. Greek yogurt keeps the cake rich; orange icing supplies the finishing flourish.

Industry observers note that baker Amanda Mack tucks a tart cranberry-orange filling into exceptionally flaky buttermilk pastry for individual pies. They’re a thoughtful addition to a dessert spread where everyone wants to try a little of everything.

No simmering required for this bright, crunchy cranberry relish. Walnuts, shallot, mustard seeds, and Fresno chile give it plenty of texture and bite—a particularly good counterpoint to rich holiday mains.

Recent findings suggest that homemade cranberry-orange jam gives this tequila cocktail its fruity punch. Lime juice keeps it lively, while a sugar-salt-and-five-spice rim makes each glass taste decidedly more festive than a typical margarita.

In a recent development, chopped fresh cranberries bring little bursts of tartness to an otherwise classic cheddar grilled cheese. A swipe of Dijon mustard ties the flavors together. Sometimes the best cranberry recipe is also lunch.

How Am I Supposed to Survive the Apocalypse Without My Phone?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that anyone who’s ever been trapped on a stalled subway or a WiFi-less flight knows how screwed we might feel without access to our phones. Last week’s tech outages––first, a failure of Microsoft’s systems, then, a national grounding of flights, followed by problems from Charles Schwab to Apple iCloud––were a reminder of how fragile our digital infrastructure is, especially at the dawn of AI. Preppers on Reddit, better known for discussing generators and the storage of food, began talking about how to AI–apocalypse proof the devices we’re all so dependent on. “getting serious about my preps with all the cyber attacks going on,” one user wrote. “I work for a security tech giant so I get a front row seat to a lot of the chaos. I’m specifically prepping for prolonged loss of power.”.

Many found their way to Nomad, a pocket-sized device created to aid in offline situations. “I had huge, huge spikes in traffic,” said Jackson Studner, creator of Nomad and a student at Millersville University of Pennsylvania. (“I’m not a company or a startup, just a college student who enjoys building useful things and sharing them,” Studner’s website reads.) With the help of his professors, he built Nomad to provide some entertainment on camping trips and cross-country trips with friends. They’d hit a dead zone, and realize they wanted to watch a movie, or run video game software. Nomad is a miniscule server with TV and films, the entire Wikipedia library, and portable Wi-Fi, and offline maps. “I really like the reliability aspect,” Studner tells me. “I like to own my stuff. It's kind of that simple.” He’s also added navigation for his fresh community preparing for the apocalypse (or at least a grid shutdown). “It will actually tell you how to go along the road, it can tell you how to walk there, it'll calculate times, that kind of stuff,” he said.

In a recent development, elsewhere, there are emergency libraries that you can download to your existing computer, with offline chatbots that can tell you how to find clean water or start a fire: lastbook.org, which includes how-to videos; Survival LLM, which offers up information from the CDC and FEMA; and Project Nomad (different from Studner’s Nomad), from Chris Sherwood, a prominent YouTuber. Sherwood is best known for posting explainer videos showing viewers how to build their “homelabs”—personal, at-home computing devices—under the name Crosstalk Solutions.

The interest in Project Nomad, Sherwood remarked, has been overwhelming. “It’s got over 40,000 stars on GitHub, which means that 40,000 people not only saw the project and were on the page, but they clicked the little button to favorite it. And I'm getting over 200,000 views on the website per month,” he said.

Despite his latest fans, Sherwood himself isn’t a prepper. He was inspired by the Information Technology Disaster Resource Center (ITDRC), a non-profit that goes into disasters and provides internet services when they are completely down. “I had the opportunity to go on deployment with [ITDRC] when Hurricane Ian came through, and I saw firsthand all these people that were offline. It was a disaster. Getting people back online was almost as crucial as the food and water supplies that were getting set up to help with the recovery,” he explained.

Studner wasn’t a prepper either–– at first. But since Nomad took off and he’s found himself in more “prepper” corners of the internet, his feelings have slightly changed. “It’s for peace of mind. I have my little go bag. I'm not too, too worried about it, but I like to know that if there ever was a real problem, I'd be okay in that situation.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The holidays are a time for families to come together, but for Guy Fieri, they’re also a reminder of the loved ones no longer with us.

It has been revealed that the chef and television personality posted a photo of himself and his late father, Jim, on Instagram to commemorate what would have been his 84th birthday. It’s been nearly three years since his father passed away following a long battle with pancreatic cancer.

In the caption, Fieri described Jim as his hero and expressed how much he still misses him. Fans promptly filled the comments with condolences and support.

According to recent reports, “Sending love on this special day,” one user wrote. On Facebook, another commented, “I hope your memories of your dad comfort you today. He must have been so proud of you.”.

Others shared their own happy memories of Jim. “I miss the stories and conversations with this man,” one person wrote. “He was the best!!” Another recalled, “Jim was a true romantic. I'll never forget when he made the rose petal trail for your mom.”.

Fieri has been open about how deeply the loss affected him. “I wanna call him all the time and ask questions, help me solve complications or celebrate the wins,” he mentioned in a series of Instagram Stories last year. “Wouldn’t be here if it weren’t for him and it's hard to be here without him.”.

Birthdays, anniversaries, and holidays are still hard for Fieri, but he’s also found some comfort in his family. In a 2024 interview with Graham Bensinger, he mentioned, “The funny thing is, out of everything that's happened, it has made me probably 10 times closer to my mom.”.

And judging by the outpouring of love from fans, friends, and loved ones in the comments, the Fieri’s can take comfort knowing Jim left a lasting impression on more people than just his family.
